name: Adept-2
baseline: CppAD (measured in the benchmark); autodiff (autodiff/autodiff, measured); ADOL-C and Sacado (named in the user guide, qualitative)
workload: Time to compute all sensitivities (reverse-mode adjoint AD) for four quant-finance workloads: Heston Monte Carlo (8 sensitivities), SABR calibration (15), XVA CVA (40), LIBOR swaption (161).
claimed_speedup: Gradient time, Adept vs CppAD: Heston MC 91 ms vs 268 ms; SABR calibration 19 ms vs 32 ms (autodiff 38 ms); XVA CVA 7.1 s vs 8.0 s; LIBOR swaption 1.15 s vs 4.57 s (about 2.9x, 1.7x, 1.1x, 4.0x, derived from page data). autodiff did not finish (DNF) on three of four workloads. XAD, the benchmark owner's own library, is faster than Adept in every row, so Adept is the second-fastest tape library there. The Adept user guide says reverse-mode differentiation 'tends to be significantly faster and use less memory' than ADOL-C, CppAD and Sacado, and usually only a little slower than a hand-written adjoint (no numbers in the guide; numbers are in Hogan 2014, ACM TOMS 40, 26).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on all libraries, median of 10 measured iterations after warmup (ad-benchmarks README)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Ubuntu 24.04
license: Apache-2.0 (library); GNU all-permissive license for test and benchmark code
stars_or_usage: 189 stars; used in climate and weather codes (ECMWF)
tradeoffs: Operator-overloading AD with expression templates; Adept 2 adds array classes and optimizers; autotools build; reverse mode records a tape; optimized BLAS recommended for matrix work.
caveats: The A-tier benchmark is run and published by Xcelerit, the vendor of XAD (a competing library that wins every row), so it is a competitor's benchmark of Adept; ADOL-C and Sacado are not in it. The original claim is in the peer-reviewed Hogan 2014 ACM TOMS paper, which I could not open here (the user guide at doc/adept_documentation.tex only states it qualitatively); verifiers should open that paper for the 2014 numbers. The Adept margin over CppAD is small on XVA CVA (7.1 s vs 8.0 s). Last upstream commits are small additions (Oct 2025).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): ADBench (microsoft/ADBench) paper source Documents/ms.tex, surfaced by the query 'C++ automatic differentiation library benchmark comparison Adept CppAD ADOL-C Stan Math autodiff Sacado fastest'
WebSearch 'C++ automatic differentiation library benchmark faster than CppAD ADOL-C Adept' surfaced the ad-benchmarks repo; vcpkg has cppad but no adept port, conan has neither (config.yml 404).

name: bare-metal (hand-optimized SASS/CUDA ML kernels for RTX 3070 Ti Laptop)
baseline: cuBLAS (local reference harness; cuDNN and cuSPARSELt rows also measured and lost)
workload: FP16 tensor-core HGEMM (16-warp kernel) on square 2048^3 and 4096^3 problems, against cuBLAS measured on the same RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU under a no-throttle fair-run policy (median of 11 runs after 5 warmups).
claimed_speedup: HGEMM 16-warp 2048^3: 31,875 GFLOPS vs cuBLAS 28,631 GFLOPS (111.3%); 4096^3: 31,765 vs 29,708 GFLOPS (106.9%). The same table shows the project losing elsewhere: dense INT8 GEMM 68.7% of cuBLAS, sparse INT8 25.4% and 18.2% of cuSPARSELt, conv2d implicit GEMM 42.3% of cuDNN.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -arch=sm_86 -O2 (kernels via --cubin, bench harnesses use the CUDA Driver API; reference benches add -std=c++17 and link cublas, cublasLt, cudnn, cusparseLt); CUDA 13.2 (nvcc V13.2.78) per AGENTS.md
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU (GA104, sm_86) under a 150 W VBIOS cap; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: sm_86 (Ampere GA104) only; kernels are compiled to cubin and some are hand-edited at SASS level through the project's R package cuasmR, so they are not portable C++ source; reproduction needs CUDA, Nsight and R (make reproduce).
caveats: Only the two square HGEMM rows beat cuBLAS; every other row in the same table loses. Single laptop GPU with a power cap; README says several results are n=1 and that the repo disputes one of its own numbers with an open issue and footnote (29 open issues). Reference numbers recorded 2026-05-18. cuBLAS heuristics on this laptop part may be suboptimal, so the margin may not transfer to desktop GPUs. Tier A rests on the public reproducible harness (make reproduce, data/reference_baselines.json) plus stated flags and CUDA version; host CPU not stated. Flash Attention rows have no cuDNN reference locally ('not measured locally').
found_via: github.com/topics/flash-attention?l=cuda and github.com/topics/gemm?l=cuda listings ('hand-tuned NVIDIA SASS kernels ... no cuBLAS / cuDNN / PyTorch'), then opened README, docs/comparison_to_sota.md, AGENTS.md, Makefile and data/reference_baselines.json

claimed_speedup: Matmul N=4096: 763 TFLOPs vs cuBLAS 716 TFLOPs (about 1.07x, derived from page data); N=8192: 808 vs 795 TFLOPs (about 1.02x, derived from page data). Sum of 2^30 elements: 3240.11 GB/s vs CUB 3193 GB/s (about 1.01x, derived from page data).

hardware: NVIDIA H100 (SXM or PCIe variant, clocks and host CPU not stated)

name: FastGEMV (fp16/int8/int4 GEMV CUDA kernels)
baseline: PyTorch fp16 matrix-vector product (torch.matmul on a size x size fp16 matrix and size x 1 vector, baseline.py, kernel time via Nsight Systems)
workload: GEMV of an n x n fp16 matrix with an n x 1 fp16 vector for n=512..16384, plus int8 and int4 quantized-matrix variants that PyTorch cannot run directly; kernel runtime and estimated memory bandwidth.
claimed_speedup: README: max 2.7x speedup vs PyTorch on P100 and 1.4x on 3090 Ti. method_and_result.md, P100 fp16: 1.441x (n=512), 1.627x (1024), 1.551x (2048), 1.599x (4096), 2.695x (8192), 1.781x (16384); estimated bandwidth 602.0 GB/s vs PyTorch 320.8 GB/s at n=16384 (peak 732 GB/s). RTX 3090 fp16 kernel: 4372.4 ns vs PyTorch 6106.2 ns at n=1024 (about 1.40x, derived from page data); 609235 ns vs 691660.6 ns at n=16384 (about 1.14x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -m64 -std=c++17 with -gencode sm_60/sm_70/sm_75/sm_86 (Makefile); README requirements list CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2; PyTorch version not stated
hardware: NVIDIA P100 and RTX 3090 (README says 3090 Ti, results doc says 3090); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Square power-of-two sizes only (512..16384); per-tensor scale and zero point for int8/int4; blockDim must be tuned per size and GPU; no batching; tested on Pascal and Ampere only.
caveats: Benchmarks date from May-June 2023 against the PyTorch and cuBLAS of that time; modern PyTorch on Ada/Hopper may have closed the gap. The 2.7x peak is a single size (n=8192) on a P100; on the 3090 the gain is 1.1-1.4x. The int8/int4 columns compare against fp16 PyTorch and move far fewer bytes, so they are not like-for-like. README names a 3090 Ti while the results document says 3090. Timings are Nsight Systems kernel sums, not end-to-end wall clock. Host CPU not stated. Tier A is a judgment call: harness and flags are public, but PyTorch version and CPU are missing.
found_via: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels?l=cuda listing (description 'at most 2.7x speedup compared to pytorch baseline'), then opened repo, README, Makefile, baseline.py and method_and_result.md

claimed_speedup: analysis/attn/bkwd plot mi355x_gqa_non_causal_bkwd_plot.png: HipKittens 881 / 1007 / 1106 / 1155 / 1176 TFLOPS at sequence length 1024 / 2048 / 4096 / 8192 / 16384 versus AITER 300 / 351 / 375 / 384 / 389, Composable Kernel 368 / 428 / 447 / 463 / 465 and PyTorch SDPA 220 / 273 / 301 / 309 / 312; about 2.9-3.0x over AITER (derived from page data).

A tile-primitive DSL in C++ rather than a drop-in library: kernels are written per operation and shape configuration (matrix sizes are Makefile constants). name: HyperJet (hyper-dual number automatic differentiation)
baseline: Eigen AutoDiffScalar (nested), autodiff (dual2nd) and ceres::Jet
workload: Value, gradient and dense Hessian of a cable strain-energy sum (n = 3, 6, 12, 24 variables), median ns per evaluation over 7 repetitions with Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Second order, static size: HyperJet 101 ns vs Eigen AutoDiffScalar nested 328 ns and autodiff dual2nd 375 ns at n=6 (3.3x vs the faster of the two); 921 vs 2888 and 2425 ns at n=12 (2.6x); 12,214 vs 22,105 and 17,679 ns at n=24 (1.5x); 15 vs 18 and 127 ns at n=3 (1.2x). First order (gradient only) there is no winner: HyperJet 244 ns vs AutoDiffScalar 245 ns vs ceres::Jet 304 ns at n=24.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0, -O3 -DNDEBUG (Release CMake build; benchmark verifies identical values, gradients and Hessians before timing)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro, macOS 26.5; Eigen 3.4.0, autodiff v1.1.2, Ceres 2.2.0
tradeoffs: Header-only C++23 (Python bindings via pybind11); the fast variant needs the variable count at compile time, while the dynamic-size variant is 1.9x to 43x slower than the static one in the README's own text and, in its second-order table, is slower than both Eigen AutoDiffScalar and autodiff dual2nd at every size tested (n=3 to 24).
caveats: Author-run benchmark (first-party) on a single Apple Silicon machine, but the benchmark code is in the repository and the README is candid that there is no gain for gradient-only work. The Eigen baseline is AutoDiffScalar from Eigen's unsupported module, not Eigen Tensor. The README notes inlining decisions change absolute times by about 1.6x and that the benchmark forces inlining uniformly. Small project (17 stars).

name: Sleipnir
baseline: CasADi 3.8.0 (autodiff and NLP frontend) with Ipopt 3.14.20 and MUMPS 5.8.1
workload: Optimal-control NLP scalability benchmarks (flywheel with 100-5000 samples, cart-pole with 100-300 samples): problem setup time and solve time of Sleipnir's reverse-mode autodiff plus interior-point solver versus CasADi plus Ipopt.
claimed_speedup: Flywheel (ratios derived from page data CSVs): at 1000 samples solve 11.088 ms vs 59.015 ms (about 5.3x) and setup 0.368 ms vs 19.184 ms; at 5000 samples solve 75.124 ms vs 339.385 ms (about 4.5x) and setup 1.961 ms vs 91.157 ms. Cart-pole: setup 2.147 ms vs 194.851 ms at 300 samples, but solve is NOT faster there (2683.45 ms vs 1251.01 ms at 300 samples).
compiler_and_flags: g++ (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810; the root CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to RelWithDebInfo; explicit -O flags are not listed in the benchmark README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7840U, 64 GB DDR5-5600
tradeoffs: C++23 with Python bindings; pool-allocated expression-node reverse-mode autodiff that records linearity to cache constant derivatives; uses Eigen sparse solvers; the NLP DSL picks the solver from problem structure. It is an AD-plus-NLP-solver stack, not a general tensor autodiff library.
caveats: Compares a full AD plus interior-point stack against CasADi plus Ipopt plus MUMPS, so AD speed alone is not isolated; CasADi uses tuned options (expand=true etc.) while Sleipnir uses defaults. Sleipnir's cart-pole solve times are slower than CasADi from 150 samples up (for example 3065.18 ms vs 973.846 ms at 250 samples; the Sleipnir cart-pole CSV has no 200-sample row), possibly because of different iteration counts. Flags are implied by the RelWithDebInfo default rather than listed, so tier A is borderline. Author's own benchmark; commercial linear solvers could change Ipopt's numbers.

name: CoDiPack (operator-overloading AD, expression templates)
baseline: ADOL-C and Adept (other C++ operator-overloading AD tools); none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply
workload: Tape recording and reversal time and tape memory for a coupled Burgers-equation PDE test and for SU2 CFD (inviscid flow over the LM1021 supersonic aircraft), versus Adept and ADOL-C, with GCC and Intel compilers (per the TOMS paper as described by search results; paper not opened).
claimed_speedup: Paper reports CoDiPack roughly on par with Adept with slightly faster tape recording and reversal and about 7% (250 MB) less memory, and faster than ADOL-C; exact factors could not be verified because the paper pages were blocked (see caveats for unverified snippet numbers).
stars_or_usage: 119 stars; evaluated on the SU2 CFD suite in its paper and reported (search snippets) in the ISSM ice-sheet model; developed at TU Kaiserslautern (RPTU)
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++17 (2.x release for C++11). GPL-3.0 (other licensing on request), so linking proprietary code needs a commercial arrangement. Operator overloading with expression templates: needs the active type substituted into the code, tapes cost memory proportional to the number of operations, and performance depends on forced inlining (-DCODI_UseForcedInlines recommended in the README). Several tape types (RealReverse, RealReverseIndex, RealReversePrimal, RealReversePrimalIndex) trade memory against generality.
caveats: I could not open the evidence: the README of the repo (opened) cites the peer-reviewed paper 'High-Performance Derivative Computations using CoDiPack' (Sagebaum, Albring, Gauger, ACM TOMS 45(4), 2019, doi 10.1145/3356900, arXiv 1709.07229), but dl.acm.org, arxiv.org, ar5iv, researchgate, arxiv-vanity, groundai and scicomp.rptu.de were all blocked by the egress proxy. Everything below about numbers comes from web-search result snippets and is UNVERIFIED: (a) CoDiPack vs Adept performance quite similar, CoDiPack slightly faster at recording and reversal and 7% (250 MB) less memory; (b) SU2 LM1021 test with 5,730,841 interior elements: relative runtime factors of 3.1 to 4.47 for recording and 0.4 to 0.86 for interpretation of one flow iteration without preaccumulation (baseline of that ratio not confirmed); (c) an independent third-party paper (AD-HOC, arXiv 2412.05300, snippet only) lists first-order derivative-to-primal runtime ratios ADOL-C 8.36x, dco/c++ 3.03x, CoDiPack 3.63x, i.e. CoDiPack about 2.3x faster than ADOL-C there (derived from snippet data). Hardware, compiler versions and flags are unknown. The repo itself has no benchmark directory (tests/ has events, functional, general only) and its README and docs make no numeric performance claim. Tier B rests on peer review only; a verifier able to open the paper should confirm the numbers, the CPU model and the flags, which could move this to A (benchmark code for the paper may not be public) or down to C. Not a numerical-kernel library of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor): competes with other AD tools, so category fit is loose.

name: FlashAttention-4 (CuTeDSL, Hopper/Blackwell)
baseline: cuDNN 9.13.0 fused attention (also benchmarked: cuDNN 9.19.1.2, Triton 3.6.0, Gluon 3.6.0, FlashAttention 2.8.3)
workload: Attention forward (and backward) in BF16 on B200: head dim 64, 128 and (192,128), causal and non-causal, sequence 1K to 32K with total tokens fixed at 32K, hidden dimension 2048 (32 or 16 heads); TFLOPs/s from 4 * seqlen^2 * head_dim * heads (halved for causal, backward = 2.5x forward).
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: 'up to 1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x over Triton on B200 GPUs with BF16, reaching up to 1613 TFLOPs/s (71% utilization)'; Figure 4 caption: '1.1-1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13.0 and 2.1-2.7x over Triton across sequence lengths'. Figure 4 bar labels, head dim 128, non-causal, seq 1K/2K/4K/8K/16K/32K, TFLOPs/s: FA4 1355, 1468, 1532, 1579, 1601, 1613; cuDNN 9.13.0 1157, 1328, 1413, 1460, 1488, 1517 (FA4 about 1.06-1.17x, derived from page data); cuDNN 9.19.1.2 1346, 1474, 1552, 1585, 1609, 1613 (FA4 within about 1.3% either way, derived from page data); Triton 3.6.0 507 to 703; FA2 383 to 432. Causal, head dim 128, 32K: FA4 1576 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 1266 (about 1.24x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1 1540 (about 1.02x, derived); causal 1K: FA4 744 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 717 vs cuDNN 9.19.1 822 (slower).
compiler_and_flags: Per paper Appendix A.1: CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6, FlashAttention 2.8.3, cuDNN 9.13 and 9.19.1.2; 5 warmup runs then 10 repeats averaged. No nvcc-style flags (CuTe-DSL is JIT compiled).
hardware: NVIDIA B200 (the main text says B200; Appendix A.1 writes 'B100 180GB SXM6 (1000W)', apparently a typo); CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 25.1k stars (whole flash-attention repository, shared with FlashAttention-2 and -3); pip package flash-attn-4; paper by Princeton, Meta, Colfax, NVIDIA, Georgia Tech and Together AI authors, listed in MLSys 2026 proceedings per a WebSearch result
tradeoffs: Written in CuTe-DSL embedded in Python (paper claims 20-30x faster compile than C++ templates), so no C++ build step but a Python/CUTLASS-DSL dependency and JIT compile at first use; Hopper (sm90) and Blackwell (sm100/sm120) only, CUDA 13 recommended for best performance (cu13 extra). Forward and backward, GQA, varlen, paged KV, block sparsity and MLA kernels live in flash_attn/cute. Uses software-emulated exponentials and conditional softmax rescaling (paper abstract), which a numerics-sensitive user should check against a reference softmax.
caveats: The paper's own Figure 4 caption says: 'newer versions of cuDNN have incorporated many of the techniques described in this paper, yielding similar performance to FA4', and the bar labels confirm parity with cuDNN 9.19.1.2 (and cuDNN ahead at short causal sequences). So the 1.1-1.3x lead holds only against cuDNN 9.13.0, the version the authors compared at release. FlashAttention-3 'does not run on B200' (paper footnote), so there is no FA4 versus FA3 comparison on B200, and I found no H100 FA4 numbers in the paper text or README (the README says only 'optimized for Hopper and Blackwell GPUs (e.g. H100, B200)'); the lead asked for FA3/H100 figures, which I could not find. Backward-pass figures (Figures 6 to 8) were not read. Short of tier A because CPU model and flags are not stated, though benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py is public and its defaults (total 32K tokens, 16 heads at head dim 128, 5 warmup, 10 reps, backends fa2/fa3/fa4/cudnn) match the paper's stated settings. The paper was read from the PDF checked into the repo (assets/fa4_paper.pdf); arXiv 2603.05451, the MLSys proceedings page, the Together AI blog and the Colfax post were not opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED). Several authors work on cuDNN or FA4's vendors, so first-party in part, but peer reviewed. Shares a repository with FlashAttention-3 (use id paper:flashattention-4).
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention README (FlashAttention-4 section), flash_attn/cute/README.md, benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py and assets/fa4_paper.pdf; WebSearch 'FlashAttention-4 CuTeDSL B200 BF16 forward TFLOPs speedup over cuDNN and Triton paper' gave the abstract figures and the MLSys listing

name: FlashTP (SNU-ARC)
baseline: e3nn o3.TensorProduct (uvu, with torch_scatter) and NVIDIA cuEquivariance
workload: Channelwise (uvu) tensor-product layer of equivariant MLIPs (NequIP, SevenNet-type irreps configs in ir_config/), kernel microbenchmarks and end-to-end SevenNet-l3i5 inference and training.
claimed_speedup: Search snippets of the ICML 2025 abstract: up to 41.6x and 60.8x kernel speedups over e3nn and NVIDIA cuEquivariance; SevenNet-l3i5 4.2x and 3.5x speedup with 6.3x and 6.2x peak-memory reduction for inference and training.
tradeoffs: Drop-in only for channelwise 'uvu' e3nn TensorProduct; CUDA 12+ and PyTorch >= 2.4.1; kernels compiled at install (up to 10 minutes), per-architecture (auto-detect, A100/H100 fallback with PTX); README TODO lists performance work and a JIT implementation.
caveats: Paper (openreview, proceedings.mlr.press) and arXiv were EGRESS_BLOCKED; numbers are from WebSearch snippets only, so GPU model, precision, compiler flags and the config on which 41.6x/60.8x peak occurs are unverified. Repo README gives no numbers; it ships microbenchmarks (example/test.sh runs flashTP_test.py on ir_config/nequip/4_32_3_p_sc.txt, fp32) that a user can rerun, so reproducibility is plausible but the stated hardware and flags are not in the repo page. The 'up to' figures are maxima. OpenEquivariance issue #171 (opened at https://github.com/PassionLab/OpenEquivariance/issues/171) contains a user remark that FlashTP seems to outperform cuEquivariance a lot at higher angular momentum, but states no numbers and notes the FlashTP authors did not benchmark against OpenEquivariance, so the lead that FlashTP wins at high l against OpenEquivariance is not supported. Sobek's README lists FlashTP as a related library but its snippets name only OpenEquivariance as the main baseline.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SNU-ARC/flashTP README, WebSearch snippet of ICML 2025 paper, and https://github.com/PassionLab/OpenEquivariance/issues/171

name: KleidiAI (via the llama.cpp KleidiAI backend PR)
baseline: llama.cpp ggml CPU backend's own Arm Q4_0 kernels (master at the time: AArch64 i8mm/dotprod repacked kernels); not XNNPACK, oneDNN or Eigen
workload: llama.cpp prompt processing (pp128) and token generation (tg64) with a llama 1B Q4_0 model (727.75 MiB, 1.24 B params), CPU backend, 1 to 10 threads, KleidiAI I8MM and SME micro-kernels versus llama.cpp master, in llama.cpp PR #11390 (merged 2025-02-20).
claimed_speedup: Mixed, as posted by the PR contributors. Apple M4 Pro, SME kernels, 1 thread: pp128 205.39 t/s vs master 160.94, tg64 62.22 vs 47.84 (about 1.28x and 1.30x, derived from page data); 2 threads: pp 389.43 vs 312.10, tg 99.95 vs 87.31. At 4 threads SME is slower (pp 326.86 vs master 586.83, tg 110.52 vs 157.63) and at 10 threads slower again (pp 435.39 vs 1173.93, tg 162.36 vs 243.65). KleidiAI I8MM path on M4 Pro is about equal or slower (e.g. 4 threads pp 531.04 vs 586.83). Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) I8MM slower in every row (1 thread pp 174.13 vs 181.23); Galaxy A34 pp512 87.11 vs 84.25 but tg128 11.00 vs 13.79. The PR's own summary: 'KleidiAI SME excels with 1-2 threads but degrades significantly at higher core counts. I8MM kernels consistently underperform'.
compiler_and_flags: From the PR (the PR does not say which build produced which table): Apple Clang with 'cmake -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D GGML_METAL=OFF -D GGML_BLAS=OFF -D GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON -G Ninja'; or LLVM Clang 19.1.7 with CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=armv9.2a+nosve+sme', -D GGML_NATIVE=OFF -D GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH='armv9.2a+nosve+sme+dotprod+i8mm' -D GGML_OPENMP=OFF. Build 119d3bf.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (SME and I8MM) run by max-krasnyansky; Samsung Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) by the same contributor; Galaxy A34 (8 threads) by rmatif. Exact core configuration beyond thread counts not stated.
stars_or_usage: 187 stars on the GitHub mirror (official source is gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai); integrated in llama.cpp (GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI), XNNPACK (open and merged KleidiAI PRs listed on github.com/google/XNNPACK/pulls); ExecuTorch use was named in the task lead and not verified by me
tradeoffs: Arm-only (AArch64; SME/SME2, SVE, i8mm, dotprod variants; will not build on x86). Micro-kernels with caller-controlled output tiling, no threading, no allocation, no dependencies, plain .c/.h pairs (callable from C++); weights must be prepacked (RHS pack) and activations dynamically quantized and packed (LHS pack) per call, so end-to-end gain depends on the framework integration. API may change between releases (two releases per month). Dual license files: Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause in LICENSES/.
caveats: The only numeric comparison I could open is a third-party integration PR from February 2025, and it is not a clean win: faster only for SME at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro, slower at higher thread counts and for the I8MM path on the phones, against llama.cpp's own Arm kernels rather than a library on the project's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen). No XNNPACK-vs-KleidiAI numbers were visible: the open and merged XNNPACK KleidiAI PRs listed titles only, the KleidiAI README and CHANGELOG hold no comparative figures, and the repo's benchmark tool (benchmark/README.md) times KleidiAI variants against each other with placeholder output ('123 ns'). Arm's own published speedup claims (developer.arm.com blogs, ExecuTorch/MediaPipe posts) were not opened. The table values come from WebFetch's page summary; four values (205.39, 160.94, 62.22, 47.84) were cross-checked by a second fetch. Tier B is on the basis of independent contributors, public llama.cpp benchmark tooling, named CPU and build commands; it falls short of A because the PR does not tie each table to one compiler and flag set. KleidiAI has changed substantially since build 119d3bf (e.g. CHANGELOG lists later SME2/SVE GEMV/GEMM kernel improvements), so the numbers are dated; llama.cpp's current docs (docs/build.md) now say the backend selects the best compatible kernel at runtime rather than always using KleidiAI.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/ARM-software/kleidiai README, benchmark/README.md and CHANGELOG.md found no comparative numbers; then https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/11390 (ggml-cpu: Add CPU backend support for KleidiAI library) opened directly; XNNPACK PR list https://github.com/google/XNNPACK/pulls?q=is%3Apr+kleidiai for integration status

name: Nervana neon (GPU convolution kernels)
baseline: cuDNN R4 (fp16 and fp32, via Torch bindings)
workload: Full forward+backward pass time (ms) of AlexNet, Overfeat-fast, OxfordNet (VGG model A) and GoogleNet V1 convolution stacks on a Titan X in the convnet-benchmarks shootout.
claimed_speedup: OxfordNet model A fp32: neon 320 ms vs cuDNN R4 529 ms (about 1.65x, derived from page data); fp16: 254 vs 471 ms. GoogleNet V1 fp32: 270 vs 470 ms; fp16: 230 vs 462 ms. Overfeat fp32: 211 vs 268 ms; fp16: 176 vs 242 ms. cuDNN R4 won AlexNet: fp16 71 vs 78 ms, fp32 81 vs 87 ms.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X, Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64
tradeoffs: Python framework with custom GPU kernels; not callable as a C++ library. Intel discontinued the project, so there is no support for newer GPUs or cuDNN versions.
caveats: Numbers are from 2016 and compare against cuDNN R4 only; later cuDNN releases added Winograd and other algorithms, so today's gap is likely smaller or reversed (not measured here). The suite states CPU and GPU but no compiler or flags. neon's README itself claims '2x speed of cuDNNv4'. The suite's Nervana rows link to convnet-benchmarks/nervana/README.md, which was not opened, so it is not confirmed on the page that the benchmarked kernels are exactly the code in the neon repository.

name: OpenVINO (CPU inference runtime)
baseline: TensorFlow Lite with the XNNPACK delegate (XNNPACK)
workload: MobileNet V2 and ResNet 50 single-image inference latency/throughput on an 8-vCPU Google Cloud Ubuntu 16.04 VM, TFLite+XNNPACK vs OpenVINO.
claimed_speedup: ResNet 50: OpenVINO 62.55 ms vs TFLite+XNNPACK 118.3 ms (first table, thread count not labelled; about 1.9x, derived from page data); with 8 threads 16.70 ms vs 32.8 ms (about 2.0x, derived from page data). MobileNet V2 is a tie or a loss: 11.14 vs 11.48 ms (first table) and 3.56 vs 3.16 ms with 8 threads (XNNPACK faster). OpenVINO throughput-optimized mode reached 382.44 FPS vs 316.46 FPS for XNNPACK on MobileNet V2 with 8 threads.
hardware: Google Cloud VM, 8 vCPUs (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 16.04 LTS
tradeoffs: Large toolkit (model converters, plugins for CPU/GPU/NPU) rather than a small kernel library; not a drop-in replacement for XNNPACK kernels inside TFLite.
caveats: The benchmark is a small personal repository (undated, Ubuntu 16.04 era) with unstated CPU model, compiler, flags and library versions, so it falls short of tier A; the XNNPACK and OpenVINO versions are old. OpenVINO wins on ResNet 50 but not on MobileNet V2 at 8 threads. A separate user report (XNNPACK issue 1803, Aug 2021, EC2 T2.Large, MobileNet V1 and AlexNet) says OpenVINO took 50% of XNNPACK's latency, but it got no maintainer reply and is anecdotal.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): query 'github "faster than XNNPACK" OR "outperforms XNNPACK" CPU inference kernels benchmark' surfaced yaysummeriscoming/xnnpack_benchmarks

name: pytorch-qrnn (QRNN CUDA kernels)
language: Python (CUDA kernels compiled at runtime via CuPy and pynvrtc)
baseline: NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM
workload: Training speed of a two-layer 640-unit PTB language model (batch of 20 examples, 105 timesteps) and inference speed of a 320-unit QRNN layer alone vs an equal-sized cuDNN LSTM layer across batch sizes and sequence lengths.
claimed_speedup: README: 'betwen 2 and 17 times faster than the highly optimized NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM implementation depending on the use case'; repo description says 'up to 16 times faster than NVIDIA's cuDNN LSTM'; largest gains at small batch sizes or long sequences. AWD-QRNN 'trains over twice as quickly' as AWD-LSTM.
tradeoffs: QRNN is a different architecture, not a faster LSTM: gains come from batching the input matmuls and a light element-wise recurrence (ForgetMult kernel). Accuracy is described as similar, not identical. No bidirectional support, no PackedSequence support, needs cupy and pynvrtc. Archived 2022-02-12.
caveats: README reproduces Figure 4 of the paper (image only); GPU model, cuDNN version and framework version are not in the README and no benchmark script is in this repo. Peer-reviewed status taken from the README's citation of ICLR 2017; the paper page was not reachable. The comparison is architecture plus kernel, not an equal-model kernel swap. Old cuDNN (2016 era); modern cuDNN LSTM is faster.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'faster than cuDNN' sorted by stars

name: SageAttention (SageAttention, SageAttention2, SageAttention2++)
language: CUDA/C++ and Triton with Python API
baseline: FlashAttention2 (also FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention3-FP8)
workload: Quantized (INT8 QK^T, FP8 or FP16 PV) attention kernel TOPS on RTX 5090, RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100 and RTX 3090 (head dim 128), plus end-to-end video, image and language model speed.
claimed_speedup: Repo description: 'Quantized Attention achieves speedup of 2-5x compared to FlashAttention, without losing end-to-end metrics'. README: 'On RTX5090, SageAttention reaches 560T, 2.7x faster than FlashAttention2'; on Hopper 'matches the speed of FlashAttention3-FP8 but offers much better accuracy'.
hardware: RTX 5090 (560 TOPS stated in text); RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100, RTX 3090 shown in README figures; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: about 4.0k stars; ICLR 2025, ICML 2025 and NeurIPS 2025 (spotlight) papers
tradeoffs: Approximate attention: INT8/FP8 (and INT4 in SageAttention2) quantization with outlier smoothing, so outputs are not bit-identical to exact attention; plug-and-play replacement for F.scaled_dot_product_attention, but README warns not every model works by monkey-patching. Tensor-core GPUs only. Kernels are CUDA plus Triton.
caveats: Peer-review status is taken from the README (ICLR 2025, ICML 2025, NeurIPS 2025 spotlight); the papers could not be opened here. Most kernel numbers are in figure images; the README states the TOPS figures exclude quantization and smoothing overhead. Baseline is FlashAttention2/3, not cuDNN. README says it ships a benchmark/ directory comparing against FlashAttention2/3; the script was not opened.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'SageAttention', after WebSearch 'attention kernel faster than cuDNN benchmark github'
PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/sageattention/json (attention kernels distributed through PyPI).

name: SpargeAttn (SpargeAttention)
language: C++ (CUDA) with Python bindings; Triton example
baseline: FlashAttention2 (Figure 2 legend 'FlashAttn'; Table 1 'Full-Attention' does not name the implementation)
workload: Figure 2 (README image): attention kernel speed in TOPS versus sparsity on an RTX 4090, sequence length 22K, head dim 128; Table 1 (assets/exp_table.png): average per-layer attention speed in real generation runs for Llama3.1 (NeedleInAHaystack, 128K), CogVideoX (17K), Mochi (22K), Flux (4.5K) and Stable-Diffusion3.5 (4.5K), reported with accuracy metrics.
claimed_speedup: Table 1, speed in TOPS, Full-Attention vs SpargeAttn (sparsity): Llama3.1 156.9 vs 708.1 (0.54); CogvideoX 166.0 vs 507.9 (0.46); Mochi 164.2 vs 582.4 (0.47); Flux 158.2 vs 280.3 (0.38); StableDiffusion3.5 164.2 vs 293.0 (0.31); ratios about 4.5x, 3.1x, 3.5x, 1.8x and 1.8x (derived from page data). Figure 2 (values read from the chart, approximate): FlashAttn about 165 TOPS flat; SpargeAttn+Sage2 about 410 TOPS at sparsity 0.1 rising to about 875 at 0.6 (about 5.3x, derived); SpargeAttn+FA2 about 370 at 0.6 (about 2.2x over FlashAttn); SageAttention alone about 300. Accuracy in Table 1 stays near the dense baseline (e.g. Llama3.1 WikiText perplexity 6.020 vs 6.013 for full attention).
hardware: RTX 4090 stated for Figure 2; the GPU for Table 1 is not stated in the image.
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; ICML 2025 paper (arXiv 2502.18137); from the SageAttention group (thu-ml)
tradeoffs: Approximate attention: a training-free predicted block-sparse mask (block 128x64) skips work, so the 'topk' parameter trades accuracy for sparsity. The headline numbers stack sparsity on SageAttention's low-bit quantization (SpargeAttn+Sage/Sage2), so part of the gain over FlashAttention2 comes from quantized matmuls, not sparsity (SageAttention alone is about 300 vs FlashAttn about 165 TOPS in Figure 2, read from the chart). CUDA-only (CUDA 12.0+ Ampere, 12.3 Hopper fp8, 12.4 Ada fp8, 12.8 Blackwell), PyTorch 2.3+; older versions required per-model tuning, the recommended API now does not.
caveats: Peer reviewed (ICML 2025) and the numbers sit in the repo as images from the paper (the README states acceptance, and the rendered README shows Figure 2; Table 1 is in assets/exp_table.png, referenced only inside an HTML comment in the README). Short of tier A: no compiler, flags or CPU model, and I found no kernel benchmark script in the repo listing (evaluate/ holds model examples for CogVideoX, Flux, Hunyuan and Wan; tools/ holds gpu_process.py). The README comment says Table 1 and the paper used the SageAttention-based SpargeAttn and that the SageAttention2-based version is about 30% faster, so Table 1 and the current API differ. TOPS for sparse kernels may count only executed or dense-equivalent operations: not stated on the opened pages. The baseline is FlashAttention2, not a library on the project's list. Numbers were read from images using the image viewer; chart values are approximate.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/thu-ml/SpargeAttn README (assets/speed_comparison.png and assets/exp_table.png opened via raw.githubusercontent.com)

name: batmobile (CUDA kernels for equivariant GNNs)
baseline: e3nn (PyTorch library for E(3)-equivariant neural networks; generic implementation)
workload: Spherical harmonics (L=3), tensor product with Clebsch-Gordan coefficients (forward and backward) and fused SH+TP for MACE/NequIP/Allegro style models, N_atoms=1000, C=32, about 20 neighbours per atom, on RTX 3090.
claimed_speedup: README: spherical harmonics 0.142 ms (e3nn) vs 0.012 ms (11.8x); tensor product 1.847 ms vs 0.089 ms (20.8x); TP backward 3.21 ms vs 0.156 ms (20.6x); fused SH+TP 0.574 ms vs 0.413 ms (1.39x). At N_atoms=5000, C=64 the fused pipeline is 1.45x faster than the unfused batmobile pipeline (not vs e3nn).
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 12.x and PyTorch 2.0+ (README); flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Hand-written kernels for specific L_max and layouts; fused operators; PyTorch extension only.
caveats: Small project, first-party numbers from one GPU; README lists benchmarks/ scripts (not opened). Baseline is the generic e3nn, not an optimised library such as cuEquivariance. The 1.45x large-scale result compares fused vs unfused batmobile. Latest commit message credits Claude as co-author, so check code correctness before use.

name: BitBLAS
language: Python (TVM/TileLang code generation) with CUDA kernels
baseline: cuBLAS (W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMV/GEMM); also CUTLASS, bitsandbytes, FasterTransformer, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and Marlin
workload: Mixed-precision GEMV and GEMM for LLM layer shapes (BLOOM, OPT, LLaMA, LLaMA-2 matrix sizes) with FP16, INT8, FP16xINT4/NF4 and W_INT2 A_INT8 formats on A100 and RTX 3090.
claimed_speedup: README: W_INT2 A_INT8 GEMV/GEMM '8x/2x speedup over cuBLAS W_FP16 A_FP16 on A100'. benchmark/README.md: FP16 and INT8 Tensor Core GEMM only 'matches the performance of cuBLAS and CUTLASS' on RTX 3090; float16xnf4 'achieves 2x the speed of bitsandbytes and 4x the base float16 performance'; on A100 int4 dequantize 'outperforms bitsandbytes, faster-transformer, tensorrt-llm, vLLM, and Marlin'.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA 12.1; bitsandbytes 0.43.0; vLLM 865732342b4e3b8a4ef38f28a2a5bdb87cf3f970; FasterTransformer 1afbf20129647a35d108152fc6789bc1d029cda5; TensorRT-LLM 2bf3a0a4287069ac55ee3304c285b08592d3d1bc; CUTLASS 629f4653c3ea3db3264030382956fabe715f3436; Marlin 512f1b1ba39ff708bcc95419f11cfd1285cd31b3
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (24GB) and NVIDIA A100 (80GB); host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 770 stars; archived 2026-02-24; Ladder (OSDI'24) is the technical basis
tradeoffs: Gains come from low-bit weights (INT2/INT4/NF4), so accuracy depends on the quantized model; for plain FP16/INT8 GEMM it only matches cuBLAS. Integrates with PyTorch, vLLM, AutoGPTQ, GPTQModel and BitNet b1.58.
caveats: The 8x/2x figure compares W_INT2 A_INT8 against a W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMM, i.e. fewer bytes moved, not an equal-precision comparison. Result plots are images; the repo's text gives only the lines quoted. Archived in 2026. First-party. cuBLAS is not one of the category baselines.
found_via: GitHub: microsoft/BitBLAS README (Benchmark Summary) and benchmark/README.md, located while checking mixed-precision GEMM kernel libraries after the 'faster than cuBLAS' queries

hardware: Apple M2 Ultra; Intel Core i7-13700H
tradeoffs: Requires ternary-trained models; built on llama.cpp infrastructure.
caveats: Baseline is FP16 llama.cpp on a different (larger) weight format, so the speedup partly reflects 1.58-bit weights, not a like-for-like kernel win; compiler flags not stated; not one of the listed baselines.

name: Chipmunk (column-sparse attention and MLP kernels for diffusion transformers)
baseline: FlashAttention-3 (attention layer) and cuBLAS / torch.compile'd nn.Sequential (MLP layer); torch.compile'd reference repos for end-to-end
workload: Dynamic column-sparse attention and MLP layers inside HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev and Mochi diffusion-transformer inference on H100 GPUs; layer-level and end-to-end video/image generation latency.
claimed_speedup: 'Column Sparse Attention layer is ~9.3x faster than FlashAttention3 baseline; Column Sparse MLP layer is ~2.5x faster than cuBLAS baseline.' End-to-end: HunyuanVideo 720x1280x129 Chipmunk alone 1030 s -> 477 s (2.16x); Chipmunk + step caching 277 s on 1xH100 (3.72x) and 412 s on 8xH100 (2.50x); Wan2.1 up to 2.67x; FLUX.1-dev about 1.6x.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit >= 12.4 (12.8 recommended), conda cuda 12.8.0, torch.compile for baselines; nvcc flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA H100 (1x and 8x), Hopper required for the CUDA kernels; Ampere supported via Triton ports; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Approximate and training-free: it skips attention and MLP work by dynamic sparsity (column-sparse deltas against cached activations), so outputs differ from dense baselines (README reports VBench quality scores); Hopper-only CUDA kernels plus Triton ports; needs per-model integration; PyTorch-based.
caveats: Layer speedups compare a sparse method with dense baselines at undisclosed sparsity levels in the README; the microbenchmark scripts behind the 9.3x and 2.5x figures were not located, and the README's benchmark baselines are torch.compile'd reference repos. Workshop papers only (ES-FoMo at ICML 2025, YPS at MLSys 2025). Not a drop-in exact kernel replacement.
found_via: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels?l=cuda listing (description 'ColumnSparseGEMM 2.5x vs cuBLAS'), then opened repo, README and commits page

name: CodeJeNN (Keras-to-C++ inference header generator)
baseline: Keras eager-mode inference (TensorFlow backend for the MLP case, PyTorch backend for the CNN case)
workload: Single-thread, single-core inference of a small MLP and CNN, 10,000 loops each on fresh random samples, generated C++ vs Keras eager (and Keras JIT mode).
claimed_speedup: From a WebSearch summary of the arXiv paper 2607.02746 (paper not opened, snippet only): roughly 25x faster than Keras with the TensorFlow backend and nearly 38x with the PyTorch backend; about 2.5x and 9x faster than the JIT-enabled TensorFlow and PyTorch versions. The repo itself holds no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GCC from Homebrew (not Apple clang) in a conda environment with llvm-openmp; optimization flags not stated
hardware: MacBook with M1 Pro chip, single thread on one core
tradeoffs: Emits a standalone C++ header with inlined static weights and no Lapack or Eigen dependency; large models can become memory-bandwidth bound because of big static arrays (noted in the repo); input must be a Keras HDF5 model with supported layers only.
caveats: Speedup figures were not read on an opened page (arXiv blocked), so they are snippet-level and the two summaries seen were not identical in detail; the repo's speed test (tutorials/06_speed_test, run.sh) reproduces the setup but publishes no numbers. License is the NRL Open License (use and modify allowed, redistribution only under that agreement, grant-back of modifications to the US Government), which is not an OSI license, so treated as reference. Single commit in history. Baseline is Keras eager mode, which is slow for tiny models, so the comparison favors generated code.
found_via: WebSearch 'Show HN faster than PyTorch kernels written from scratch C++ CUDA OR CPU inference engine benchmark' restricted to news.ycombinator.com (surfaced the arXiv paper title), then WebSearch 'CodeJeNN github C++ neural network generator ...'

name: CTranslate2
baseline: PyTorch 1.13.1 (OpenNMT-py, Hugging Face Transformers), TensorFlow 2.11.0 (OpenNMT-tf), Marian 1.11.0, FasterTransformer 5.3 (GPU)
workload: Translating the En-De newstest2014 test set with Transformer base models (OpenNMT-tf WMT14, OpenNMT-py WMT14, OPUS-MT/Marian); target tokens generated per second, aggregated over several runs, CPU with 4 threads and GPU.
claimed_speedup: CPU, OpenNMT-py WMT14 model: CTranslate2 3.6.0 658.8 tokens/s vs OpenNMT-py/PyTorch 275.8 (about 2.4x, derived from page data); int8 860.2 vs PyTorch int8 323.3. CPU, OPUS-MT model: CTranslate2 525.0 vs Transformers/PyTorch 147.3 (about 3.6x, derived) and vs Marian 344.5 (about 1.5x, derived). GPU, OPUS-MT model: 5876.4 vs Marian 3241.0 and Transformers/PyTorch 1022.9 tokens/s. GPU, OpenNMT-py model: fp32 CTranslate2 6634.7 vs FasterTransformer 5.3 at 6979.0 (CTranslate2 slower), but CTranslate2 float16 10990.7 vs FasterTransformer float16 8592.5. Max memory also lower (CPU OPUS-MT 721MB vs Marian 7605MB).
hardware: CPU: 4 threads on an AWS c5.2xlarge instance, Intel Xeon Platinum 8275CL. GPU: AWS g5.xlarge, NVIDIA A10G, driver 510.47.03, CUDA 11.

tradeoffs: Supports a fixed list of Transformer architectures only (encoder-decoder, decoder-only LLM, encoder-only); models must first be converted to its own format; int8/int16/float16 quantization changes outputs slightly (BLEU 26.64 to 26.82 in the table); CPU backends are third-party (Intel MKL, oneDNN, OpenBLAS, Ruy); C++ and Python APIs.

Benchmarked versions are old (CTranslate2 3.6.0 vs repo release 4.8.2; PyTorch 1.13.1, TensorFlow 2.11.0, early 2023), so the ratios may have changed. Compiler and flags not stated (prebuilt wheels). Benchmark scripts are public under tools/benchmark in the repo (not opened). Baselines are general-purpose frameworks, not tuned inference engines, except Marian and FasterTransformer, which CTranslate2 only partly beats. faster-whisper (SYSTRAN) is a Python wrapper over this engine and should fold into this entry.

name: CUDA-L1
language: CUDA (kernels generated by a contrastive reinforcement-learning LLM) with Python
baseline: KernelBench PyTorch reference implementations (default PyTorch eager, which calls cuDNN/cuBLAS), torch.compile, torch.compile reduce-overhead and CUDA Graph
workload: 250 KernelBench PyTorch workloads (levels 1 to 3) evaluated on A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20 and L40.
claimed_speedup: README table, mean speedup vs Default: A100 3.12x, 3090 2.51x, H100 3.85x, H20 2.38x, L40 3.13x; vs Torch Compile on A100 2.77x; vs Torch Compile RO 2.88x; vs CUDA Graph 2.81x; maximum single-task speedup 120x.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, RTX 3090, H100, H20, L40; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Kernels are released as per-GPU code snippets (JSON, a separate version for each device: A100, 3090, H100, H20, L40), each specialised to a KernelBench task. Not a library.
caveats: The README itself reports that RL exploited timing and caching reward hacks; they added stream timing sync and removed caching, but more hacks may remain. KernelBench reference code is naive eager PyTorch with many small ops, so much of the speedup is fusion rather than a better cuDNN-class kernel. Baselines are not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen; a 'cuDNN backend flags' comparison is listed as done in the to-do list but no numbers were read for it.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels (neighbour of CUDA-L2), then CUDA-L1 README evaluation tables

name: Decoding Attention (Bruce-Lee-LY)
baseline: Flash-Decoding (FlashAttention v2.6.3) and FlashInfer v0.1.6 decode attention
workload: Decode-stage multi-head attention (32 heads, head dim 128, FP16) on an RTX 3090, sweeping sequence length and batch size; MLA on an H20 is also plotted.
claimed_speedup: README text: better than Flash-Decoding and FlashInfer when sequence length is below 1536 (FlashInfer and Flash-Decoding win above 1536), and 'regardless of batch size' better than both at sequence length 128. Reading the batch-size plot by eye (approximate, derived from page data): about 1.5x Flash-Decoding and about 1.0x FlashInfer at batch sizes of 128 and above.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (CUDA 12.1); H20 (CUDA 12.4) for MLA
tradeoffs: Uses CUDA cores, not tensor cores; decode stage only; MHA, MQA, GQA and MLA with FP16/BF16; C++ and Python APIs.
caveats: Single-developer repository whose results are plots with no numeric tables (y-axis labelled only 0 and 1); no compiler flags; the repository has two commits. Baselines are FlashAttention-family kernels, not cuDNN. The README concedes the baselines are faster at long sequences.

name: Effort (bucketMul approximate matrix multiplication for LLM inference on Apple Silicon)
baseline: Apple MPS default matrix multiplication (benchmark.swift labels it 'comparable to llama.cpp')
workload: Weight-matrix multiplication during LLM inference on Apple Silicon, timed by benchmarks/benchmark.swift at several 'effort' levels against the default MPS matmul.
claimed_speedup: README: 'At 50% effort, it performs as fast as regular matrix multiplications on Apple Silicon chips; at 25% effort, it is twice as fast while still retaining most of the quality.'
hardware: 'Apple Silicon chips'; the specific chip is not stated in the README or benchmark.swift.
tradeoffs: Approximate computation: it skips the least important weights, so quality drops as effort falls; needs converted weights; written in Swift and Metal for macOS only, with no C++ API; the author describes it as a demo with 'ton of things to fix'.
caveats: First-party claim with no hardware, model size or raw timings in the repo; the benchmark script prints timings only when run. At 50% effort the claim is only parity with regular matmul. The author notes real generation speed is slower than the matmul benchmark because of implementation overhead. The quality claim ('most of the quality') was not checked, and the project page and blog (kolinko.github.io) are egress-blocked. Last commit is 2024-07-01. Repo identity inferred from the HN title and README (HN thread not opened).

name: faster-enhancer.c
baseline: ONNX Runtime fp32 graph of the same FastEnhancer-Medium weights
workload: Streaming 48 kHz speech enhancement with FastEnhancer-Medium, measured as per-frame real-time factor over 5569-frame clips on Apple M2 and Galaxy S23+ cores.
claimed_speedup: Repository description: '3.3x faster than the ONNX Runtime graph, same quality'. README: real-time factor 0.069 on one Apple M2 core (I8MM) and 0.096 on Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2); quality PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060 for the fp32 ONNX graph over 824 VoiceBank-DEMAND utterances.
hardware: Apple M2 (one core) and Samsung Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2)
tradeoffs: One fixed model with W8A8 post-training quantization; six hand-written int8 GEMM kernel tiers (ARM NEON, DOTPROD, I8MM; x86 AVX2, AVX-VNNI, AVX-512 VNNI) chosen at init with no scalar fallback and no heap allocation after startup; draws on ggml, XNNPACK, oneDNN and Arm kernel patterns.
caveats: The 3.3x figure appears in the repository description; the README text shows real-time factors but not the ONNX Runtime timing, which lives in the linked paper (arXiv 2607.25350, not opened). The comparison is int8 against an fp32 graph, so precision differs. The x86 tiers are not timed in the README. A paced real-time callback costs 4.2x more per frame than the racing benchmark. Single-model runtime, not a general kernel library. Compiler flags are not stated.
found_via: WebSearch '"faster than oneDNN" OR "outperforms oneDNN" OR "beats oneDNN" github C++ kernels'
WebSearch 'C++ library faster than XNNPACK OR oneDNN inference kernels benchmark GitHub' (result faster-enhancer.c).

name: FasterTransformer
baseline: TensorFlow XLA FP16, PyTorch TorchScript FP16, Megatron (GPT)
workload: BERT-base encoder inference at small and large batch size and sequence length, translation decoder/decoding throughput, both on T4 (FP16/INT8), and GPT-89B/175B tensor-parallel generation on 8xA100 versus Megatron.
claimed_speedup: BERT base vs TensorFlow XLA FP16 on T4: about 3x for small batch and sequence length, about 5x for large with Effective FasterTransformer plus INT8-v2. Vs PyTorch TorchScript: 4x to 6x small, about 5x large. Translation vs TensorFlow: FT-Decoder 1.5x-3x, FT-Decoding 4x-18x; vs PyTorch: FT-Decoder 1.2x-3x, FT-Decoding 3.8x-13x. GPT vs Megatron on A100 is shown only as a figure.

name: FBGEMM
baseline: Intel MKL FP32 GEMM (via a cited Microsoft paper), caffe2/perfkernels (embedding SpMDM), a prior 64-bit GEMM implementation
workload: Low-precision GEMM, convolution, embedding and sparse operators for server-side inference, as summarized on the FBGEMM wiki page 'Recent feature additions and improvements'.
claimed_speedup: Wiki page: a Microsoft NMT paper found FBGEMM INT8 had 2x throughput vs MKL FP32 at batch size 1 and 1.3x at batch size 32; JIT'ed EmbeddingSpMDM about 2x over caffe2/perfkernels; 64-bit GEMM 10.5 GOps/s vs 3 GOps/s (3.5x) on Xeon Gold 6138 with turbo off; 60x for 3D groupwise convolution vs the fused im2col base implementation; 2x-4x for 90% sparse operations.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6138 (turbo off) for the GEMM number and Xeon D-2191 for the ResNet-50 thread-scaling number; other results state no hardware
stars_or_usage: 1.6k stars; the CPU backend of PyTorch quantized inference
tradeoffs: INT8, FP16 and sparse kernels that need quantization-aware model changes; x86 (AVX2, AVX-512) JIT-generated kernels; separate FBGEMM_GPU and GenAI packages exist in the same repo.
caveats: Most speedups compare reduced precision against FP32 or against older internal code, so accuracy trade-offs apply; the MKL comparison is a third-party paper that the wiki cites and was not opened or re-run here; many wiki claims state no hardware or flags. The MLSys 2021 paper (arXiv 2101.05615) could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked) and may carry stronger peer-reviewed evidence. Baselines are not oneDNN, cuDNN or XNNPACK.
found_via: WebSearch 'github C++ GEMM kernels int8 CPU faster than oneDNN FBGEMM benchmark README' surfaced the FBGEMM paper; wiki page opened

name: FeatherCNN
baseline: Caffe2 with Eigen, Caffe with OpenBLAS, Caffe2 with NNPACK, TensorFlow Lite, ARM Compute Library, TVM
workload: End-to-end CNN inference time in ms (VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-50, SqueezeNet, MobileNet, DenseNet-121) on ARM CPUs: Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72), iPhone 7, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3.
claimed_speedup: Huawei D05, best thread count, vs Caffe2+Eigen: VGG-16 12.84x, GoogleNet 4.45x, ResNet-50 2.29x, SqueezeNet 1.25x, MobileNet 2.65x; vs Caffe+OpenBLAS: VGG-16 10.86x, GoogleNet 13.7x, ResNet-50 3.88x, SqueezeNet 1.68x, MobileNet 4.03x, DenseNet-121 3.08x. VGG-16 on iPhone 7: 284 ms (2 threads) vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms. TX2 VGG-16 at 1 thread: 1325 ms vs Caffe2+NNPACK 5876 ms (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
hardware: Huawei D05 (Hi1616, 2x32 Cortex-A72 @ 2.40 GHz), iPhone 7 (A10 Fusion), Galaxy S8, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3B
tradeoffs: Loads Caffe models converted to its own .feathermodel format; targets ARM CPUs on iOS, Android and embedded or ARM-server Linux; small library with no external dependencies.
caveats: Eigen is the Caffe2 CPU backend, not the Eigen Tensor module directly. Baselines are 2018-2019 versions (Caffe2+Eigen scales badly at high thread counts, which inflates ratios such as 12.84x); speedups are computed from the best thread count; TVM on RK3399 (1293 ms) beat FeatherCNN at 2 threads (1420 ms); some wiki table cells are blank or unlabeled; compiler flags are not stated. The repository has no root LICENSE file (the README badge links to a missing one) but source headers state BSD 3-Clause, and some code is derived from ncnn.

name: FFPA (ffpa-attn, Faster Flash Prefill Attention for large head dimension)
baseline: PyTorch SDPA (F.scaled_dot_product_attention); FlashAttention-2 supports head dim only up to 256, FP8/FP4 variants also compared with SageAttention 2/3
workload: Exact attention for large head dimension (D 320 to 1024) forward and backward, plus FP8/FP4 attention for D 64 to 256, on L20, RTX 5090, H800, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 5000 (for example B1 H32 N8192 D512).
claimed_speedup: README: '1.5x~15x speedup over PyTorch SDPA'; D=512 on B200 via CuTe-DSL: 1517 TFLOPS forward and 763 TFLOPS backward, '6x~15x' over standard PyTorch SDPA; FP4 on RTX 5090 850-980 TOPS (D=128-256), '3.8x~4.4x' over PyTorch SDPA; FP8 on L20 '1.5x~1.8x' (D=64~224).

tradeoffs: Targets head dimensions above 256 where FlashAttention-2 does not apply; CUDA backend is forward only, Triton and CuTe-DSL backends cover forward and backward. FP8/FP4 attention trades accuracy for speed and is sm_120 (RTX 50) or Ada only.
caveats: For D>256 PyTorch SDPA falls back to non-flash backends, so the largest ratios are against a weak baseline; for D<=256 the README claims are only for FP8/FP4. Speedups are shown in figures; the bench/ directory exists but was not opened. First-party. cuDNN SDPA is not a stated baseline.
found_via: GitHub: xlite-dev/CUDA-Learn-Notes (LeetCUDA) README -> ffpa-attn; github.com/topics/cuda-kernels

name: Flash Attention PTX/CUDA (hand-written PTX prefill attention for RTX 5080)
baseline: FlashAttention-2 as bundled in vLLM 0.23.0 (vllm.vllm_flash_attn.flash_attn_varlen_func, FA2 path)
workload: Causal fp16 attention prefill over 34 shapes (B=1..8, H=12 or 32, S=512..8192, D=64 or 128) on an RTX 5080, same-process interleaved timing with shared random inputs; plus end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode and prefill against vLLM.
claimed_speedup: Beats or matches vLLM FA2 at 23 of 34 shapes. Latency-based gains: D=64 H=12 B=1 +18.5% (S=512), +31.9% (S=1024), +8.9% (S=2048); D=128 H=12 B=1 +16.6% (S=512), +12.6% (S=1024). Losses up to -4.8% (B=8 S=4096 D=64) and -4.5% (B=8 S=8192 D=128). Peak about 202 TFLOPS vs vLLM about 212. End-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode B=1: 4.70 ms/token vs vLLM 5.12 ms/token; B=8: 5.28 vs 5.43 ms/step.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build, CUDA Toolkit 12.0+ (tested with 13.1), C++17, sm_120; full nvcc flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5080 (84 SMs, sm_120, 234.8 TFLOPS FP16 theoretical), Windows/WSL2 for the vLLM comparison; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Consumer Blackwell (sm_120) only; mma.sync-based, no WGMMA/TMA; forward/prefill kernels with paged-KV decode glue; PyTorch bindings (fa_ptx) and a C++ API; the default branch shown on GitHub is dev/FlashAtt.
caveats: Loses at the largest batch x context shapes (-2 to -5%) and wins mainly at B=1 and short or mid context. The same-process vLLM harness (fa_sweep2.py) lives in the author's WSL environment and is not in the repo, so the comparison is not reproducible from the repo alone (hence tier C); in-repo benchmark is src/bench.cu. Baseline is FlashAttention-2 because FA3 does not run on sm_120; no cuDNN comparison. Single GPU, first-party, history of about one week.
found_via: WebSearch 'attention kernel written from scratch CUDA C++ beats cuDNN flash attention benchmark blog' (surfaced the repo), then opened README and docs/vllm-comparison.md

name: flash-attention-minimal (forward-only FlashAttention in about 100 lines of CUDA)
baseline: naive PyTorch attention (eager matmul + softmax + matmul)
workload: One profiled forward call of attention with batch 16, 12 heads, sequence length 64, head dimension 64, FP32, on a T4 (bench.py).
claimed_speedup: README sample output on a T4: manual attention Self CUDA time total 52.545 ms vs minimal flash attention 3.908 ms (about 13x, derived from page data); Self CPU time total 52.389 ms vs 11.452 ms; the README says 'Speed-up achieved!'.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O2 (extra_cuda_cflags=['-O2'] in bench.py via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load); CUDA, PyTorch and compiler versions not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA T4 (AWS g4 instance); host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Educational forward pass only (no backward); FP32 rather than FP16; block size fixed at 32 at compile time; one thread per output row, which makes the matmuls slow.
caveats: Weak evidence. The win is only over a naive eager PyTorch attention at deliberately tiny sizes: a comment in bench.py says 'Use small model params, otherwise slower than manual attention', and the README admits it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes. Each variant is timed with a single profiled call and no warm-up is visible in bench.py, so one-time CUDA/cuBLAS initialisation may inflate the manual attention figure. No comparison with cuDNN, the official flash-attention or PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention. A 'tensorcore' branch exists but was not assessed. Repo identity inferred from the HN title (HN thread not opened).
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN CUDA kernel faster than cuDNN cuBLAS attention softmax from scratch' surfaced item 39726781 'Show HN: Flash Attention in ~100 lines of CUDA'; repo located by title and verified on github.com.

name: FlashKDA
baseline: flash-linear-attention (fla) Triton chunk_kda kernel, and fla chunk_gated_delta_rule (GDN) as a second reference
workload: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) forward pass, T=8192, H=96 and H=64, D=128, fixed-length and variable-length batches, on Hopper H20 and Blackwell GB200.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARK_H20.md (T=8192, H=96, D=128): flash_kda 2.6220 ms vs fla_chunk_kda 4.8388 ms (1.85x) fixed; 2.06x and 2.29x for the two varlen cases; H=64: 1.95x, 1.91x, 2.31x. BENCHMARK_GB200.md (H=96): 2.31x fixed, 2.71x and 3.27x varlen. Versus fla GDN kernel only 1.17x to 1.80x.
compiler_and_flags: warmup=30, iters=200, repeats=5; fla_chunk_kda with use_gate_in_kernel=True, use_qk_l2norm_in_kernel=True, use_beta_sigmoid_in_kernel=True, lower_bound=-5, transpose_state_layout=True; generated by benchmarks/generate_benchmark_hopper_h20_md.py; requires CUDA 12.9+, SM90+, PyTorch 2.4+. fla and PyTorch versions used for the numbers are not stated on the benchmark pages.
hardware: NVIDIA H20 (Hopper) in BENCHMARK_H20.md, generated 2026-04-22; NVIDIA GB200 (Blackwell) in BENCHMARK_GB200.md, generated 2026-05-26; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; auto-dispatched as a backend by flash-linear-attention's chunk_kda
tradeoffs: KDA forward only (the benchmark pages cover forward); requires SM90 or newer GPUs and CUDA 12.9+; uses bf16 inputs and a custom forward-substitution inverse, so results are checked against fla_chunk_kda for accuracy.
caveats: First-party benchmark with no software versions or CPU model on the benchmark pages. H20 is a low-compute, high-bandwidth SKU, so H20 numbers may not transfer to H100. Baseline is the FLA Triton KDA kernel, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. Only the forward pass is benchmarked.

name: FlashQLA
baseline: FLA Triton kernels (flash-linear-attention chunk_gated_delta_rule) and FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel
workload: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) chunked-prefill forward and backward kernels at Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 head configurations (TP1 to TP8, d=128), single-sequence and varlen batches up to 32768 tokens, CUDA-graph timing on H200 and GB200.
claimed_speedup: README: '2-3x forward speedup and 2x backward speedup over the FLA Triton kernel'. benchmark_results_H200.txt, forward, 397B/122B TP8, 1x32768: FlashQLA 0.348 ms vs FLA 1.019 ms (2.93x) vs FlashInfer 1.645 ms (4.73x); 1x4096: 1.19x vs FLA; TP4 4096x8: 3.18x vs FLA but 0.64x vs FlashInfer. Across the 171 forward rows: 1.18x to 3.32x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.07x, derived from page data); across the 32 backward rows: 1.38x to 5.47x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.56x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: torch 2.8.0+cu128, fla 0.5.1, flashinfer 0.6.13, tilelang 0.1.12; Warmup=10, Repeats=100, Backend=cudagraph (README text names FLA 0.5.0, Triton 3.5.1, FlashInfer 0.6.9, TileLang 0.1.8). No compiler flags stated.
hardware: NVIDIA H200 (benchmark_results_H200.txt) and NVIDIA GB200 (benchmark_results_GB200.txt); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Specific to Gated DeltaNet chunked prefill (Qwen3.5/3.6 linear-attention layers), not general attention. Needs Hopper or Blackwell GPUs (SM120 forward only) and the TileLang toolchain. Uses an algebraic reformulation of the GDN forward/backward flow that the authors say keeps numerical precision.
caveats: First-party benchmark; host CPU and compiler flags not stated, which is why this is tier C rather than A (benchmark script benchmark/bench_gated_delta_rule.py and the result files are public, so a verifier may be able to re-tier). Baselines are the FLA Triton and FlashInfer GDN kernels, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. Speedup is shape dependent: forward 1.18x to 3.32x vs FLA, and FlashInfer is faster than FlashQLA in 56 of the 171 forward rows (as low as 0.62x, mostly small-batch varlen rows). name: Lucebox Megakernel (single-launch CUDA forward pass for Qwen 3.5-0.8B)
baseline: llama.cpp (BF16, CUDA backend) and PyTorch + HuggingFace Transformers (BF16)
workload: Batch-1 prefill of 520 tokens (pp520) and decode of 128 tokens (tg128) for Qwen 3.5-0.8B in BF16 on an RTX 3090, with all 24 layers fused into one persistent CUDA kernel launch.
claimed_speedup: RTX 3090 RESULTS.md: prefill pp520 21,347 tok/s vs llama.cpp BF16 11,247 (README states 1.9x) and PyTorch HF 7,578; decode tg128 413 tok/s vs llama.cpp 267 (1.55x) and PyTorch HF 108 (3.8x). Also 1.87 tok/J at a 220 W power limit.
compiler_and_flags: setup.py: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_<auto-detected, sm_86 for RTX 3090> --use_fast_math -std=c++17 plus NUM_BLOCKS/BLOCK_SIZE defines; host -O3; CUDA toolkit version for the RTX 3090 run not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 24GB (also RTX 2080 Ti, DGX Spark GB10 and Apple M5 Max 36GB for the efficiency comparison); host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Hard-wired to one small hybrid DeltaNet/attention model (Qwen 3.5-0.8B); batch size 1 only (README says to use vLLM or SGLang for batched throughput); BF16 on Ampere (FP16 path for Turing, NVFP4 path for Blackwell); built as a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension, so it is not a general kernel library.
caveats: First-party benchmark. llama.cpp baseline is 'latest release at time of testing, default settings' with no version or commit, and no host CPU is stated. The model is only 0.8B parameters, where per-token kernel-launch overhead dominates and llama.cpp has no fused DeltaNet path, so the result may not transfer to larger models. The 413 tok/s decode figure is quoted at a 220 W power limit while llama.cpp is quoted at 350 W, which if anything understates the gap. A search summary of the HN thread quoted 37,800 tok/s prefill, which differs from the 21,347 on RESULTS.md; only RESULTS.md numbers are used here. HN thread itself not opened (egress blocked); the repo was renamed from luce-megakernel to lucebox and now also hosts speculative-decoding projects (DFlash, PFlash) not assessed here.

name: Marlin (FP16xINT4 LLM matmul kernel)
baseline: FP16 PyTorch matmul (calls CUTLASS) and other 4-bit kernels: torch-nightly, exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes
workload: 16-bit x 4-bit (group size 128) matrix multiplication on a 72k x 18k weight matrix on an NVIDIA A10 across batch sizes 1-128, plus the linear layers of Llama and Falcon models at batch size 16 on A10, 3090, A6000 and A100.
claimed_speedup: Plot of speedup over FP16 PyTorch on the A10 (values read from the README plot, approximate, derived from page data): Marlin about 3.9x at batch sizes 1 to 16 and 3.8x at 32, about 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128; at batch 16 torch-nightly about 1.4x, exllamav2 about 0.7x, AWQ about 0.3x, bitsandbytes about 0.4x. Model layers at batch 16: roughly 3.4x to 4.25x on A10, 3090 and A6000, and about 2.2x to 3.6x on A100. README text: 'close to ideal (4x)' up to batch sizes of 16-32.
hardware: NVIDIA A10 (peak plot); A10, RTX 3090, A6000 and A100 (model layers); CUDA >= 11.8, torch >= 2.0
tradeoffs: Weight-only FP16xINT4 inference kernel for Ampere/Ada GPUs (compute capability >= 8.0); the README says it is not yet optimised for Hopper; needs quantised, reshuffled weights; PyTorch extension.
caveats: First-party README results shown only as plots (no tables; compiler flags and host not stated); an arXiv paper (2408.11743) is cited but is a preprint and was not opened. The baseline is FP16 PyTorch matmul, which the plot labels as calling CUTLASS, not cuDNN or cuBLAS directly, and the headline compares 4-bit weights to 16-bit weights, so part of the speedup is the memory-traffic saving of quantisation rather than a faster FP16 kernel. Speedups fall off above batch size 32 (1.55x at 128) and are lower on A100.

name: nanoinfer (int8 GEMM vs cuBLAS)
baseline: cuBLAS int8 GEMM; ONNX Runtime
workload: Hand-written CUDA int8 GEMM (WMMA + shared memory) vs cuBLAS at n=256..4096; CPU conv engine vs ONNX Runtime on Apple M4 Pro.
claimed_speedup: CUDA int8 GEMM ahead of cuBLAS (NN layout) up to n=1024, e.g. 2.09x at n=256, but about 30% behind at 2048+; README itself says cuBLAS TN path is 1.6x-4.5x faster than the hand kernel at every size. CPU engine at parity with ONNX Runtime on dense models (e.g. MNIST 49 us vs 48 us), 1.3-1.7x slower on depthwise

name: NNPACK (Winograd/FFT convolution)

claimed_speedup: NNPACK 31.95 ms and 76.17 ms (91.4 and 89.3 GFLOPS) vs XNNPACK 1345.8 ms and 3060.0 ms (about 7.07 and 7.05 GFLOPS): roughly 42x and 40x lower time (derived from page data); the reporter says 3-5x slower on their real networks on arm64 and x86.
hardware: 6-core CPU at 4300 MHz, caches L1/L2/L3 32 KiB/256 KiB/9216 KiB (model not named), Ubuntu

caveats: Evidence is one user's GitHub issue (June 2020, user Kepnu4) with the CPU model, compiler and flags not stated; the roughly 7 GFLOPS XNNPACK result looks low for the stated CPU, so it may not reflect XNNPACK's best path (unverified), and the issue was closed with no maintainer explanation visible. Effective GFLOPS compare different algorithms. The GitHub repository is no longer maintained (last commit February 2023).

name: OpenEquivariance
language: Python/C++ (JIT-generated CUDA, HIP and SYCL kernels)
baseline: e3nn (torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs in the harness); also compared with NVIDIA cuEquivariance and FlashTP
workload: Clebsch-Gordan tensor products and fused equivariant graph convolutions for MACE, NequIP, DiffDock and e3nn tetris-poly problems, forward and backward, float32 and float64, run by tests/benchmark.py (uvu, uvw, roofline and conv suites; 100 warmup and 100 timed iterations, PRNG seed 11111).
claimed_speedup: README: 'We provide up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with the latest version of NVIDIA cuEquivariance, which has a closed-source kernel package'. Docs (tests_and_benchmarks.rst) and CHANGELOG v0.4.0: 'OpenEquivariance exhibits up to 2x speedup over FlashTP's fused kernels'. No per-problem figures appear on the opened pages; they are in the paper (SIAM ACDA25, arXiv 2501.13986), which was egress-blocked.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (kernels are JIT-compiled at runtime; README asks for PyTorch and GCC 9+).
hardware: NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory for the paper's benchmarks (docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst); the docs also list V100, A100-40GB, A5000, T4, H100, MI250x and MI300x as run-tested platforms (not benchmarked). CPU not stated.
stars_or_usage: 169 stars, 17 forks; pip package 'openequivariance'; works with MACE and NequIP
tradeoffs: Supports most 'uvu' and 'uvw' e3nn tensor products, not all of e3nn. Results equal e3nn up to rounding for many configurations; for 'uvw' connection modes the weights must be reordered (reorder_weights_from_e3nn/to_e3nn). Fused convolution has an atomics mode that is non-deterministic and a deterministic mode needing receiver-sorted indices plus a transpose permutation. JIT compile at first use; needs a CUDA, HIP or SYCL (beta) toolchain; PyTorch and JAX frontends.
caveats: The headline figures are first-party README statements with no per-problem numbers on the pages I could open, so tier C is a floor. The paper (SIAM ACDA25) is peer reviewed and the benchmark code is public with A100-SXM-80GB stated and exact reproduction commands in docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst, so a verifier with paper access may justify tier B, or A if the paper states compiler and flags. The README sentence is garbled ('up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn perform on par with...'), which is quoted as is. The harness removes e3nn's torch-compile variant for float64 'benzene' because it runs out of memory, and for 'limited-memory' GPUs drops expensive tests. The 2x claim over FlashTP is against FlashTP's fused kernels only. Opened: README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md, docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst and tests/benchmark.py via raw.githubusercontent.com, plus the repo tree and commit pages on github.com.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/PASSIONLab/OpenEquivariance README and docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst

The repo is derived from llama.cpp but GitHub does not mark it as a fork. Compiler flags are not stated.

name: QuACK (CuTe-DSL memory-bound kernels)
baseline: cuDNN v9.10.1 (RMSNorm only), torch.compile (PyTorch 2.7.1, default mode) and Liger Kernel v0.5.10
workload: Memory-bound kernels (RMSNorm, softmax, cross-entropy; forward and backward), batch 8k to 32k rows, reduction dimension 256 to 262k, FP32 and BF16 inputs, measured as model memory throughput on H100.
claimed_speedup: Blog: 'achieves nearly 50% more throughput (e.g., 3.01 TB/s vs 1.89 TB/s for FP32 softmax)' than torch.compile at reduction dim 262k; about 3 TB/s (~90% of peak) for reduction dim larger than 4k; 'significantly outperforms all baselines when reduction dim >= 65k for all 3 kernels' (cuDNN baseline covers RMSNorm only).
compiler_and_flags: PyTorch 2.7.1 torch.compile default mode, Liger Kernel v0.5.10, cuDNN v9.10.1; QuACK requires CUDA toolkit 12.9+ and Python 3.12 (README). JIT-compiled CuTe-DSL kernels, no compiler flags stated.

tradeoffs: Needs H100, B200/B300 or RTX 50 series GPUs, CUDA 12.9+ and Python 3.12. The advantage comes from cluster reduction (thread-block clusters with distributed shared memory) on Hopper, so it targets very long reduction dimensions. Also ships Hopper/Blackwell GEMM-with-epilogue kernels.
caveats: First-party blog numbers; the per-size results are in a figure, the text gives only the 262k softmax ratio and the >=65k claim. The repo has benchmarks/ and microbenchmarks/ directories, but the scripts were not opened, so the figure was not reproduced here. cuDNN is only compared on RMSNorm. The blog is dated 2025-07-10 and the baselines are older versions. Below about 4k reduction dim no advantage is claimed.

workload: Single-sample real-time-factor (48 kHz audio) of Dense, Conv1D, GRU, LSTM layers and activations at layer sizes 4 to 64, RTNeural compile-time and run-time APIs with Eigen, xsimd and STL backends vs libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite.

LSTM layer size 4: RTNeural Eigen (static) about 270x real time vs ONNX Runtime about 1.4x and libtorch about 0.38x; at size 64: about 6.5x vs about 1.1x and about 0.27x. Dense layer size 4: RTNeural xsimd (static) about 6000x vs TensorFlow Lite about 150x, ONNX Runtime about 7.5x, libtorch about 2.3x; at size 64: about 75x vs TensorFlow Lite about 41x (about 1.8x).

The benchmark is by the RTNeural author, on one x86 Mac, with prebuilt ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite binaries and no stated compiler flags; layers are tiny, so per-call framework overhead dominates the baselines, and the advantage shrinks as layer size grows (STL backend falls to about the ONNX Runtime level at size 64 for GRU/LSTM). baseline: cuBLAS SGEMM (CUDA 12.6)
workload: FP32 SGEMM, NN layout, square m=n=k from 1024 to about 12800 in steps of 128, RTX 3090, with clocks unlocked and with clocks locked at 1395 MHz, both at 350 W.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no text numbers, only two plots (assets/perf.png, perf_locked.png). Reading them by eye at m=n=k near 12800: about 25,300-25,500 GFLOP/s vs cuBLAS about 24,300 with unlocked clocks (about 4-5% faster), and about 23,000-23,500 vs about 21,800 with locked 1395 MHz clocks (about 6-7% faster); approximate, derived from page data. The HN title claims 'up to 24% faster than cuBLAS on a 4090' (snippet only, not on the repo page).

Margins in the plots are small (single-digit percent) at large sizes and sgemm.cu is slower than cuBLAS at small sizes (for example near m=n=k=1280 about 17,000 vs about 19,300 GFLOP/s unlocked). The 24% on an RTX 4090 claim from the HN title is not reproduced on the repo page, which shows RTX 3090 only. Repo identity was inferred from the HN title and README content (HN thread not opened); the same plots also show a Simon Boehm / tinyBLAS kernel at about 16,500 GFLOP/s, which is slower than cuBLAS.

name: Sobek (streaming equivariant tensor-product convolutions)
baseline: OpenEquivariance (primary), also cuEquivariance and e3nn
workload: Edge-conditioned equivariant tensor-product convolution (uvw and uvu operator families), forward, backward and double backward, on capacity-matched grids (16-profile UVW grid, 9-profile UVU grid); also peak memory.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of arXiv 2607.18074 abstract: faster in all 75 capacity-matched comparisons across two operator families and all three differentiation orders, 1.2x to 49.7x, peak allocated memory reduced by up to 99%; at the last degree point shared with OpenEquivariance, OpenEquivariance allocates 24.1-27.1 GiB vs Sobek 0.1-0.4 GiB; runs workloads up to two orders of magnitude beyond OpenEquivariance capacity.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit 13.3 recommended (CUDA 12.9 builds about 25% slower per README); PyTorch >= 2.12 JIT extension builder; float32 with ieee or tf32 GEMMs; nvcc flags not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA/PyTorch only, float32 only; requires CUDA toolkit for JIT compile (first call per problem compiles specialised kernels). Supports uvw and homogeneous uvu contractions, fused radial projection so the caller must pass the compact radial embedding plus final projection weight. Deterministic, no atomics, bounded scratch (receiver_scratch_bytes).
caveats: The paper (arxiv.org) and mirrors were EGRESS_BLOCKED in this session, so the numbers are from WebSearch snippets of the abstract and could not be checked against tables; GPU model and per-case numbers unknown. Repo ships a benchmark CLI (suites minimal, scaling, throughput, uvu-throughput; 'matched' command for OpenEquivariance-capacity-matched timing) but the paper PDF is not in the repo (tree: sobek/, tests/, LICENSE, NOTICE, pyproject.toml). Preprint, not peer reviewed; authors are the repo owners (Cortex Discovery GmbH). Speedups are over a partly different formulation (Sobek fuses the radial projection while baselines take precomputed edge weights), and the comparison is capacity-matched against OpenEquivariance, so 1.2x-49.7x is a range over cases, not a typical figure. No evidence found of a Sobek benchmark against FlashTP in the paper snippets (README only lists FlashTP among related libraries). Oldest repo commit window is 2026-07-20 to 2026-07-24 (4 commits).

No results are published.

The README makes no performance claim and the repo stores no results; the timing scripts only print GFLOPS for 'mlx' and 'tk' side by side (time_attn.py also prints 'diff' as a percentage). The accompanying Hazy Research blog post (hazyresearch.stanford.edu/blog/2024-11-28-tk-mlx) was egress-blocked; a WebSearch snippet for it says only that an M2 Pro has about 200 GB/s memory bandwidth and about 6.5 TFLOPs and that very simple kernels without producer/consumer asynchrony work well there. No speedup figure was visible to me.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated. Xcode (Metal compiler) for the MSL path, or CMake C++17 with nanobind against MLX for the Python path (kernels/CMakeLists.txt); no optimization flags beyond those defaults.
hardware: Not stated anywhere I could open (Apple Silicon chip unspecified).

The attention kernel (kernels/attn_fwd/attn_fwd.metal) is bf16 only with head dim 64 or 128 (static_assert) and forward only; the GEMM is a custom bf16 matmul. The repo has no LICENSE file of its own (only the vendored MLX tree carries an MIT license), so the ThunderMittens code is treated as reference-only. The repo history is two commits, both 'revive thundermittens' on 2025-08-26, after the repository had disappeared (ThunderKittens issue #132, 2025-07-02, unanswered). Benchmark script quirks that weaken any future number: in time_attn.py the 'tk' timing loop's warmup calls MLX's SDPA instead of the ThunderMittens kernel, scale=1 is passed to MLX SDPA while the TK kernel call takes no scale, each iteration calls mx.eval (synchronizing launch overhead into the time), and correctness against MLX is not checked in the scripts. A verifier with blog access could find M2 Pro numbers and justify tier C.
