name: blip_mp
baseline: GMP 6.3.0 (mpz_t; built with assembly and with --disable-assembly)
workload: Own bench executable (blip_mp_bench) timing add/sub/mul/divMod/powm/invMod on pre-built pools of values at sizes from i64-range up to 98304 bits, e.g. 5M iterations of r = pool[i % 256] + pool[(i+1) % 256], against mpz_* in a C program using the same libc malloc.
claimed_speedup: On Apple Silicon: all i64-fitting values 1.95-2.66x faster than GMP; RSA 1024/2048/3072-bit mul 1.19-1.45x; RSA-2048 mul 1.16x, divMod 1.31x, powm 1.11x (README also says 13% faster powm at RSA-2048, 21% at 1024-bit); add at 768 bits and up 1.04-1.28x; sub at 256 bits and up 1.03-2.11x; 2048/1024-bit long division 24% faster. Loses to GMP-with-asm on x86_64 (GMP asm is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP-noasm on Zen 4) and on 128-bit add/sub, 16384+ bit multiply (0.55-0.87x) and modular inverse (2.5-4x behind).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 ReleaseFast for blip_mp; GMP 6.3.0 from nixpkgs compiled with clang -O3; libc malloc for both; built with `nix build .#bench`
hardware: Apple M4 (aarch64-darwin, macOS 26.x) headline; cross-check on AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4, ~5.0 GHz boost) under NixOS
tradeoffs: Variable-length self-describing byte storage with small-buffer optimization instead of limb arrays; pure Zig, no inline assembly, C FFI exists. Integers only (no mpf/mpq/mpfr). FFT multiplication is implemented but disabled because Toom-3 still wins in the supported range, so it falls behind GMP past ~16K bits. Win is specific to Apple Silicon: on x86_64 GMP's hand-written assembly beats it by 1.5-4x on large operands.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (LICENSE, LICENSE-MIT and LICENSE-APACHE all 404 on raw); README says 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)', so license is treated as unclear and usability is reference. Research-grade; numbers are single-run or 3-run hand medians on one machine, with no statistical sampling, and the bench is the author's own. The author reports the GMP asm advantage on aarch64 is about 0% on M-series, so the win partly reflects GMP's weaker arm64 tuning. Very new repo (BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md has a run dated 2026-04-30, nearly all commits are from May 2026), 1 star.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github multiprecision integer library AVX-512 IFMA faster than GMP mpz_mul benchmark' surfaced pmarreck/blip_mp
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic pages gmp and bignum -> pmarreck/blip_mp description 'Beats GMP at i64 (1.95-2.66x)'

name: CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)
baseline: GMP 6.1.2 (OpenMP, 20-core Xeon)
workload: Batched fixed-size unsigned big-integer operations (add, sub, low multiply, Montgomery reduction, odd modular exponentiation, div/qr, sqrt, gcd, modular inverse) at 128 to 8192 bits, one CUDA cooperative group of 4/8/16/32 threads per number, versus GMP calls spread over 20 CPU cores with OpenMP.
claimed_speedup: README speed-up table, Tesla V100 vs Xeon E5-2698v4 (GMP+OpenMP), average over 128-8192 bits: add 77.4x, sub 77.1x, mul (low) 43.5x, mont_reduce 29.3x, powm_odd 21.4x, div_qr 14.4x, sqrt 11.3x, gcd 6.9x, mod inv 4.1x; per-size extremes: 128-bit add 174.3x, 128-bit mul (low) 172.9x, 8192-bit powm_odd 16.8x, 8192-bit mod inv 4.0x
compiler_and_flags: GPU side: nvcc -arch=sm_<arch> xmp_tester.cu -lgmp (perf_tests/Makefile, no explicit -O flag, nvcc defaults); CPU side: g++ gmp_tester.cc -lgmp -fopenmp (no -O flag in the Makefile); GMP 6.1.2 built by the user
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU vs Intel Xeon E5-2698v4, 20 cores at 2.2 GHz
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA (Kepler through Ampere targets in the Makefile). Fixed-size unsigned integers only, 32 to 32K bits in 32-bit steps, 4/8/16/32 threads per number, written inside CUDA kernels with a fixed number of bits per kernel. It pays off for large batches of independent numbers, not for one big number. No floating point, no arbitrary-size operands.
caveats: A GPU is compared with a 20-core CPU running GMP, so the ratios say a V100 beats one Xeon socket, not that the algorithms are better per core. The README table does not say whether host-to-device transfer time is included. Numbers date from the 2018 beta release (V100, GMP 6.1.2). The Makefile has no -O flag for the g++ GMP harness, though the work happens inside libgmp. gcd and modular inverse gains are small (about 2.5x to 8x per size). The README table is first-party, though perf_tests/ lets anyone reproduce it (make gmp-run, make <arch>, then xmp_tester).

name: dashu (dashu-int)
baseline: GMP (mpz via the rug 1.30.0 crate, GMP 6.x)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add/sub/mul/div/gcd/pow/modular ops swept over 10 to 10^4 bits, plus small-value (<=128 bit) workloads and string round-trips, dashu-int 0.4.2 vs rug (GMP), ibig, num-bigint and malachite.
claimed_speedup: Third-party report: dashu faster than rug (GMP) in 123 of 205 head-to-head cases and in 98 of 153 small-value cases; ubig_add at 100 bits 3.7 ns vs 21.9 ns, ubig_add_by_class one_word ~3.3 ns vs ~21 ns (typically 2-6x faster on tiny values). GMP wins from ~1000 bits up, e.g. ubig_mul at 10^4 bits rug ~4.5 us vs dashu ~12.8 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (2025-12-08); cargo bench (default bench/release profile implied, no explicit flags stated); criterion 1 s warm-up, 2 s measurement, 100 samples; rug 1.30.0 linked to GMP 6.x
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (arm64)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline storage for values up to two words, so no heap allocation for small integers. Slower than GMP from about 1000 bits upward (GMP has tuned assembly and asymptotically faster algorithms). Rust API, so usable from C++ only through FFI. Not an mpz-compatible API.
caveats: The benchmark code and report live in a separate third-party repo (DRMacIver/rust-bigint-benchmarks, originally written for but not merged into dashu) whose own report calls the numbers 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative'. Single laptop (Apple M2 Max), short measurement time, bit-width sweep capped at 10^4 bits, so the large-operand regime where GMP dominates is not covered. Compiler flags are the cargo bench default (optimized bench profile) and are not spelled out in the report, so tier A is borderline; drop to C if an explicit flag listing is required. The dashu README itself makes no GMP speed claim. Another benchmark (tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, 71 stars, large-number e/fib tasks) shows rug/GMP fastest overall and dashu slower.

name: ECM-ELF (ECM stage 1, AVX-512 IFMA 8-curve batch backend)
language: C/C++ (GitHub lists C as primary; the AVX-512 kernels are .cpp; CUDA and OpenCL backends also exist)
baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (ecm-zen3.exe, built on GMP, curve family -param 0); the same table also compares Prime95 v31.04b05 (GWNUM FFT)
workload: Elliptic-curve-method stage 1 only (B2=0 or B2=B1), Suyama sigma Montgomery curves, one thread on one physical core, on Mersenne numbers 2^k-1 (M127 to M19701), per-curve seconds; the SIMD backend runs 8 curves per batch (time divided by 8). Directly measured case: N = M4001 = 2^4001-1 at B1 = 1e5, 1e6 and 2e6.
claimed_speedup: docs/ECM_Montgomery_STAGE1.md section 14.2, M4001, per curve: B1=1e5 0.596 s vs GMP-ECM 1.787 s (3.00x faster); B1=1e6 6.264 s vs 15.008 s (2.40x faster); B1=2e6 13.455 s vs about 30 s (scaled, about 2.2x). Section 14.5 size sweep at B1=1e6: M1277 0.979 s vs 2.484 s (2.54x), M2203 2.285 s vs 5.804 s (2.54x), M3001 4.137 s vs 9.586 s (2.32x), M3500 5.164 s vs 11.656 s (2.26x), M4001 6.290 s vs 14.624 s (2.32x); about 1.7x (fitted) at M5755 and M8527. Against Prime95: 32.7x at M127, 10.4x at M521, 3.94x at M1277 but 0.90x at M4001 and 0.17x at M19701 (fitted); the doc says the new code is worthwhile below about 3700 bits and Prime95's FFT is the better choice above about 6000 bits, with mixed results in between. Section 10.4 (earlier, before clocks were pinned), M1277 B1=1e6: 1.418 s vs 3.551 s per curve (2.50x).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC Release build (build_vs18\Release\ecm.exe, MSVC /O2 per README); the two AVX-512 translation units src/cpu/simd_mont_ifma.cpp and simd_edwards.cpp get /arch:AVX512 (or -mavx512f -mavx512ifma -mavx512dq on GCC/Clang) in CMakeLists.txt. Commands are in section 14.1 and 14.4: echo (2^4001-1) | ecm.exe --mont --mont-backend simd --mont-threads 1 -gpucurves 8 --sigma 4242 <B1> 0, versus ecm-zen3.exe -param 0 -c 2 <B1> <B1>. The GMP-ECM baseline is a prebuilt multiarch Windows release (ecm-2025.10.28, --enable-asm-redc); its compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (Strix Point, Zen 5 plus Zen 5c, 256-bit FPU datapath so 512-bit IFMA runs as 2 x 256-bit); clocks pinned at 3990 MHz on the Zen 5 cores (logical CPUs 0-7) and 2995 MHz on Zen 5c; Windows (exe paths). Single-thread numbers stated reproducible to about +-3%.
tradeoffs: Stage 1 only (stage 2 is handed to Prime95 or GMP-ECM through compatible .save files). The fast path needs AVX-512 IFMA hardware (explicit error otherwise; auto falls back to a slow scalar mpn backend). Gains come from 8-lane batches, a Mersenne fold domain for N = 2^k-1 (about 2x faster than general N per the README) and affine differential ladder; general N uses Montgomery CIOS. Cost grows about n^1.66 in word count, so Prime95's FFT overtakes it above about 3700 bits. GPL-3.0 copyleft. Windows-first build; Chinese-language README (README.en.md exists). Renamed from OpenCL-ECM.
caveats: Strong methodology but one author, one laptop-class machine with hand-pinned clocks, mostly Mersenne inputs (special form), and a prebuilt third-party GMP-ECM binary without stated compile flags; the doc does not say whether GMP-ECM's special-form handling for 2^k-1 was active. Only the M4001 rows (section 14.2) and the section 10.4 rows are direct same-machine measurements; a footnote under the section 14.5 table says the own-implementation points for 1277 to 4001 bits use an extrapolation from the author's fit (about 2.98e-7*k^2 + 3.79e-4*k seconds) and its wording does not make clear which rows are direct measurements, M5755 and larger are fitted for all columns, and the Prime95 column is a FFT-length model calibrated on one measured M3001 point (5.65 s) plus the M4001 run at B1=1e7. The 'about 30 s' GMP-ECM figure at B1=2e6 is scaled, not measured. The doc itself notes Prime95 was running during the measurements and that the section 10.4 numbers predate clock pinning. The repo changes daily (the 2026-10-01 commits are on the GPU and stage 2 paths; one says a mathematically wrong optimisation was caught), and no bug in the CPU IFMA path turned up, but the numbers are dated 2026-09-24 and were not re-run against HEAD. The scalar GMP mpn backend of this repo is only a cross-check (about 5.6 s/curve at M1277, B1=1e5 versus 0.135 s/curve for SIMD in the same doc), so there is no win against raw GMP mpn arithmetic to claim. The GPU backends (CUDA CGBN, OpenCL) are compared with CGBN, not GMP, and are not covered here. Evidence-tier call (A) rests on public code, stated CPU, MSVC /O2 and /arch:AVX512, and exact commands; a verifier may lower it to C because the baseline binary's flags are unknown.

name: libzahl
baseline: GMP (also TomsFastMath and LibTomMath)
workload: Per-function micro-benchmarks of integer operations (set, swap, neg, abs, bit operations, comparison, add, sub, multiply, square, string conversion, gcd and more) on operands of 1 to 4097 bits, run through translation layers in bench/ for each library.
claimed_speedup: STATUS file: zset, zswap, zbtest, zsave, zload, zneg(a,b), zabs(a,b), ztrunc(a,b,c), zbits, zcmpu 'always fastest'; zadd 'fastest after ~90 (clang), ~260 (gcc+musl), or ~840 (gcc+glibc)'; zsub 'always fastest'; zlsh 'not too fast anymore'; zrsh 'gmp is almost always faster'; zmul and zsqr 'slowest'; zgcd '21 % of gmp'
compiler_and_flags: libzahl built with gcc+glibc, gcc+musl and clang+glibc; other libraries with gcc+glibc; config.mk CFLAGS = -std=c99 -O3 -flto; no CPU extensions or assembly extensions used
hardware: Intel Core 2 Quad Q9300 (x86-64), Linux, 50 us timer slack, benchmark process pinned to one CPU
tradeoffs: C library with long-jump error handling, allocation caching and no thread safety. Wins on cheap and small-operand operations; multiplication, squaring and many derived operations (modular multiply, pow, primality test) were still the slowest, so it does not beat GMP on arithmetic-heavy work. Plain C code, no assembly.
caveats: Mixed result, not a general win over GMP: the STATUS file's own multiply and square rows say 'slowest'. Measured on a 2008 Core 2 Quad with no vector extensions, so modern GMP assembly paths (mulx, adx, AVX) are not represented. The GMP numbers come through the repo's translation layer (bench/libgmp.h) and the GMP version is not stated; STATUS notes GMP does no failure checking while libzahl does, and TomsFastMath has a compile-time size limit. Repository archived 2024-10-06, last commit 2022-07-20. The README itself gives no numbers.

name: midint-arithmetic (Oancea/Watt GPU midsize-integer add and multiply)
baseline: CGBN (NVIDIA CUDA Cooperative Groups Big Numbers); GMP is used only to validate results, not timed
workload: Batched block-level big-integer addition (1-Add and 6-Add, GB/s) and quadratic multiplication (1-Mul = a*b; Poly = (a*a+b)*(b*b+b)+a*b) on an A100, precision 2^12 to 2^19 bits with the instance count chosen so bits x instances = 2^32, hand-written CUDA prototype ('CudaP', the cuda/ folder of this repo) versus CGBN.
claimed_speedup: Quadratic multiplication: CGBN is slower than CudaP by 1.21x at 2^16 bits, 4.48x at 2^17 and 35.1x at 2^18 (1-Mul); Poly 1.22x, 21.0x and 49.9x at the same sizes; CGBN is equal or slightly faster at 2^12 to 2^14 bits (CGBN/CudaP 0.91 to 1.01 on 1-Mul). Addition 1-Add (GB/s, CudaP vs CGBN): 1046 vs 369 at 2^18 bits, 1209 vs 368 at 2^17, 1358 vs 376 at 2^16, i.e. about 2.8x, 3.3x and 3.6x (derived from page data); comparable at 2^12 to 2^13 bits. Abstract of the Springer paper: outperforms CGBN above 32K bits, comparable below. Division (fork code): CGBN is 3.64x to 7.36x faster at 2^13 to 2^15 bits and does not support larger sizes.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_80 (from cuda/Makefile and cuda/cgbn-tests/Makefile, both linked with -lgmp); nvcc and CUDA versions not stated; paper text says RHEL 8.10
hardware: NVIDIA A100 GPU (6912 cores, 1555 GB/s peak bandwidth, 19.5 TFLOP/s FP32) per the preprint; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPU only (CUDA, sm_80 tuned); operates on integers that fit one CUDA block (about 2^12 to 2^19 bits, about 410,000 bits max after the erratum for the FFT path) and needs large batches (instances = 2^32 / bits) to fill the GPU, so it is not a single-number latency replacement for GMP. Contains an outdated early Futhark version (futhark-ninja) and a Futhark version (futhark-reg) that needs an archived custom Futhark compiler tarball. Addition, subtraction, multiplication only in the CUDA folder; division lives in the Futhark folder and in the separate division fork.
caveats: Same research codebase as the already-listed fork aske0778/midint-arithmetic-division, which is the parent's fork adding CUDA division (CASC 2026 paper [33] by Marchioro, Raahauge, Lovenskjold, Oancea, Watt; the fork's own GMP numbers, 11.3x at 2^18 bits and so on, come from arXiv 2606.06386 which I could not open). This parent repo's evidence is versus CGBN, not GMP or MPFR, so it is off the listed baselines. The numbers I quote are from the repo's own preprint 'High-Level Big Integer Arithmetic in Futhark for GPUs' (submitted to SYNASC per the README, tables I to III, opened as a PDF via raw.githubusercontent.com), whose 'CudaP' columns are the cuda/ prototype of the Springer essay 'GPU Implementations for Midsize Integer Addition and Multiplication' (LNCS essays for Alan Mycroft, pp. 51-79, doi 10.1007/978-3-032-08187-2_4, published as a Springer essay-volume chapter; arXiv 2405.14642 not opened). First-party results (the authors compare their own prototype with CGBN); CGBN is a 2018 beta and is far faster for small sizes and division, so the win applies only above 2^15 bits. No LICENSE file in the repo (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md, LICENSE.txt, COPYING all 404) so code is reference only. README erratum: FFT prime fields use 10 of 16 and 25 of 32 bits, lowering max precision (PrimeField64 about 410,000 bits). Tier A given public benchmark code, nvcc flags in the Makefile and A100 stated, though nvcc version and host CPU are missing; the results table is in a preprint, not a committed results file.

stars_or_usage: 2 stars (benchmark repo); the algorithms are also in MultiFloats.jl with 159 stars
tradeoffs: Fixed expansions of 2 to 4 doubles (about 2x to 4x double precision, roughly 106 to 212 bits) with the exponent range of double; not arbitrary precision and not correctly rounded like MPFR. Header MultiFloats.hpp (multifloats/ folder) uses x86 SSE/AVX/AVX-512 intrinsics and an ARM variant (multifloats-arm) where NEON was disabled in the latest commits. Designed for data-parallel kernels; scalar single-operation latency gains are not the claim.
caveats: Could not open the evidence: the SC '25 paper (Zhang and Aiken, 'High-Performance Branch-Free Algorithms for Extended-Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic', doi 10.1145/3712285.3759876, pp. 695-710) and its hosts (dl.acm.org, theory.stanford.edu, springer, dkzhang.com, purl.stanford.edu) were blocked; the speedup figures are from a search-result snippet of the abstract and the CPU model, thread count and kernel behind '35.6x' are unverified. The repo is only the harness: README is a one-line title and no benchmark JSON outputs are committed (bench_linux.sh writes MultiFloats-GCC-32.json style files at OMP_NUM_THREADS 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 but none are in the tree), so a reader must build and run it (needs Google Benchmark, GMP, MPFR, CLN, FLINT, Boost, QD, CAMPARY via download_campary.sh) to reproduce. Comparison fairness: MultiFloats kernels are hand-vectorized on split arrays while MPFR and GMP are scalar per-element calls with per-thread temporaries; MPFR is correctly rounded with a huge exponent range. Tier B (peer-reviewed) rather than A because the CPU model and committed results could not be confirmed; if the paper states the CPU model and flags, A is justified since the harness and flags are public. The same algorithms are verified in Rocq (MultiFloatProofs) per the author profile.

name: GNU MPFR with CUDA/CGBN backend (gnu-mpfr-cgbn)
baseline: MPFR 4.2.1 scalar functions (GMP 6.3.0) on one CPU core
workload: Correctly rounded mpfr_mul, add, div, sqrt and fma on batches of 1 to 16384 operands at 128 to 65536 bits of precision, GPU batch interface (with PCIe transfer) and device-resident vectors, versus the plain scalar MPFR function in a loop.
claimed_speedup: Peak batch speedups at n = 1024: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. Device-resident at n = 16384: fma 284x at 8192 bits, mul 230x at 4096, div 157x at 16384, add 120x at 8192, sqrt 115x at 16384. A single operation is always slower on the GPU (launch floor about 6.5 us resident, 16 us with transfers); batch add never beats the CPU (<= 0.7x); div and sqrt above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU.
compiler_and_flags: Backend built with NVCCFLAGS -O3 -arch=$cuda_arch -Xcompiler -fPIC (set by configure --enable-cgbn); CPU baseline is the stock MPFR 4.2.1 / GMP 6.3.0 build, its flags are not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs at 2.41 GHz), CUDA 13.2; CPU baseline is 'one core, the same machine' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Results are bit-identical to MPFR (same correctly rounded value, ternary value and flags for all five rounding modes); without --enable-cgbn the library is plain MPFR. Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA. Precision above 65536 bits runs on the CPU, all results in one batch must share a precision, device calls are serialized on a mutex, and only mul/add/sub/div/sqrt/fma are offloaded.
caveats: Tier C because the CPU model is not stated (everything else is public: the cgbnbench code, GPU, CUDA, MPFR and GMP versions). The repository is a single initial commit on 2026-09-12 with 3 stars, so it has had no outside use yet. Baseline is one CPU core against a whole GPU. The tree is GNU MPFR 4.2.1 with a patch, not a GitHub fork. It builds on steleman/nvidia-cgbn, a fork of NVlabs/CGBN that adds signed integers, Ada/Blackwell support and sizes up to 256K bits but publishes no new speed numbers.

baseline: GMP (mpf) and MPFR backends of the same library, at their default 512-bit precision
workload: Rgemm (multiple-precision matrix-matrix multiply) with square matrices on a Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, double-double and quad-double backends (with and without OpenMP) versus the GMP and MPFR backends, plus a CUDA double-double Rgemm on A100/V100 GPUs.
claimed_speedup: Manual section 9 peaks for Rgemm: reference GMP 19 MFlops and 693 MFlops OpenMP; reference MPFR 11 MFlops and 390 MFlops OpenMP; reference quad-double 33 MFlops and 1.3 GFlops OpenMP; reference double-double about 365 MFlops and 11.2 GFlops OpenMP. Derived from page data: double-double OpenMP is about 29x MPFR and 16x GMP, quad-double OpenMP about 3.3x MPFR and 1.9x GMP. README: CUDA double-double Rgemm and Rsyrk reach about 450 GFlops on a V100. Benchmark logs in the repo show the A100-box CUDA double-double kernel at 486,829 MFLOPS (n = 562).

tradeoffs: Faster only by giving up precision: double-double is about 32 digits (106 bits) and quad-double about 64 digits (212 bits), while the GMP and MPFR runs use 512 bits. The manual itself says double results 'are not competitive to OpenBLAS or Intel MKL'. The author notes MPFR is about twice as slow as GMP, possibly because of the C++ binding copies. name: VROOM (RNS Montgomery arithmetic with AVX-512 IFMA, BLS12-381 and BN254)
baseline: BLST (supranational/blst at 8065152, a modified vendored copy in blst/ with benchmark wrappers); GMP is used only for parameter generation and validation, not timed
workload: Google Benchmark ns per operation for BLS12-381 field and curve operations (Fp mul, Fp2, Fp12, G1/G2 add, double, scalar multiplication, Miller loop, final exponentiation, full pairing), VROOM RNS code against BLST on the same machine; ratio = blst_ns / rns_ns.
claimed_speedup: results/bench_bls12_381_vs_blst.txt, MatrixNoK (the production configuration), VROOM ns vs BLST ns: full pairing 128145.9 vs 500035.1 (ratio 3.902); Miller loop 49888.2 vs 215023.1 (4.310); final exponentiation 82491.2 vs 285421.3 (3.460); Fp12 mul 257.1 vs 1563.4 (6.082); Fp12 sqr 224.4 vs 1126.2 (5.019); G1 add 154.2 vs 585.8 (3.799); G1 scalar mult (GLV) 30647.5 vs 75949.8 (2.478); G2 scalar mult (GLS) 41245.7 vs 146934.4 (3.562); Fp mul 21.8 vs 29.0 (1.332 for a single mul, up to 2.272 amortized in a batch of 10). The slower row: Fp12 inversion with the BLST inverter 7599.8 vs 5560.4 (0.732); the RNS-assisted inversion reaches 3406.7 (1.632). The plain Matrix variant gives pairing 151066.7 vs 500035.1 (3.310).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 21.1.0 (LLVM 21 prebuilt, llvm-project 3623fe6) with Google Benchmark at 04ccbd8 (v1.9.4-89), --benchmark_min_time 0.5s (scripts/reproduce_cpu_bench.sh). VROOM benchmark: -std=c++20 -O3 -march=native -mavx512ifma -D__ADX__ (src/Makefile CXXFLAGS_BENCH). BLST baseline: blst/Makefile CFLAGS -O2 -fno-builtin -fPIC -D__x86_64__ (+ -D__ADX__ when /proc/cpuinfo shows adx), CC auto-detected as clang if present, field arithmetic from assembly_small.S.
hardware: AWS c7i.metal-24xl, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (Sapphire Rapids), Amazon Linux 2023 (kernel 6.1.x); raw JSON committed (results/bench_bls12_381.json, bench_blst_complete.json, run dated 2026-06-17, Google Benchmark reports 96 CPUs). Thread count of the benchmarks not stated; they look single-threaded.
stars_or_usage: 5 stars, 1 fork; research artifact (README refers to paper numbers, a camera-ready update and artifact evaluation)
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 IFMA hardware (a slow integer fallback exists for correctness only) and, per the README, clang 21.x for paper-comparable timings, because GCC and older clang are significantly slower on the IFMA path. Gains are largest on batched or compound operations (Fp12, pairing, scalar mult); a single Fp multiply is only 1.33x. Ships parameter sets for BLS12-381 and BN254 only; the MatrixNoK parameter search is exponential in the number of radix words, so it suits small moduli. README says: research-grade, not vetted or audited for security. The blst/ subtree stays Apache-2.0; baselines/ vendors arkworks, zkcrypto, zksync and gnark with their own licenses.
caveats: Tier capped at C under the project rule for numbers measured on code later fixed for correctness bugs: the committed results and the camera-ready README are from 2026-06-17, while commits of 2026-08-14 (2785394, 145f864) and 2026-08-28 (0131695) fixed the radix-to-RNS conversion (floor instead of ceiling, reported by an outside reviewer) and the MatrixNoK negative-input conversion; results/ was not touched afterwards. The commit diffs change precomputed constants and add a rounding mode, not operation counts, so a verifier may judge tier A defensible (public code, committed raw JSON, stated CPU, compiler and flags, artifact-evaluated). The same-machine pair is clean, but BLST is built at -O2 with assembly field arithmetic while VROOM uses -O3 -march=native; the pairing figure uses BLST's own inverter inside the RNS pairing (BM_Pairing_RNS_BLST_Inverter); amortized batch rows exclude any batching cost on the caller side; BLST is a modified vendored copy. The paper 'VROOM: Accelerating (Almost All) Number-Theoretic Cryptography' (IACR ePrint 2026/393) appeared in a WebSearch result but eprint.iacr.org was blocked by the egress proxy, so the paper's own numbers and venue were not opened. The task lead's baselines (GMP, MPFR) are not what this repo benchmarks against; BLST is the relevant incumbent for BLS12-381.

name: libMetalFloat64 (philipturner/metal-float64; emulated FP64 on Apple GPUs)
baseline: Native hardware FP64 on the Apple Silicon CPU (NEON) in the README table, and OpenCL FP64 in the precision table; the listed baselines GMP and MPFR are not compared
workload: Theoretical maximum scalar giga-operations per second per operation (FFMA, FADD, FMUL, FCMPSEL, FCMP, FRECIP, FDIV, FRSQRT, FSQRT) for a reference system with an 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU (four 128-bit vector ALUs per core) and a 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU, computed from instruction counts and not measured.
claimed_speedup: README table of theoretical Gops, CPU FP64 vs GPU FP32x2 (double-single) emulation: FFMA 392 vs 590, FADD 196 vs 482, FMUL 196 vs 758, FCMPSEL 196 vs 2123, FCMP 196 vs 1769, FRECIP 49 vs 196, FDIV 49 vs 183, FRSQRT 49 vs 171, FSQRT 49 vs 189 (ratios 1.5x to 10.8x, derived from page data). The 'GPU eFP64' column, the IEEE-compliant mode, is empty. Text: additions and multiplications 'will have 1/32-1/64 the throughput of their 32-bit counterparts', an estimate.
hardware: README reference system: 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU and 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU; the chip is not named.
tradeoffs: Swift package that builds a Metal dynamic library and headers; needs an Apple6-family or newer GPU (A13 and later, Metal 3) and macOS Ventura on Intel Macs. Two precisions: float64_t is IEEE-compliant but the README gives no throughput for it, while float32x2_t has 1+47 mantissa bits, flushes denormals and has undefined INF/NaN results. Larger functions are called through the dynamic library, so inlining is partial. The planned 64-bit atomics use a lock buffer and the README warns that a missing useResource call can freeze half the GPU. Matrix types, division, square root and transcendentals were still planned; the README states the library is 'not a finished library'.
caveats: The README says 'Still in the planning stage - this is not a finished library!'. There is no measured benchmark anywhere I could open: the table is labelled 'maximum theoretical performance', the eFP64 (IEEE) column is blank and the precision table is mostly '???'. The related philipturner/openmm-benchmarks FP64Emulation folder holds only Trial1.swift, Trial2.swift, Trial3.cl and a chat transcript, and I found no timing numbers in the trial files. The comparison is against the CPU's hardware double, not against the category baselines GMP or MPFR (software arbitrary precision), so it does not fit this category; it is filed here because the assignment placed it there. I set tier D because no real workload was timed; the README does contain theoretical numbers, so a verifier could treat it as C. Abandoned and archived.

name: libQD3 (double-double, triple-double, quad-double, extended-double)
baseline: MPFR (the task lead also names original QD; the only numbers found put the upstream QD library against MPFR and GMP)
workload: No benchmark of libQD3 itself found. Indirect lead: MPLAPACK's Rgemm (dense matrix multiply) benchmark with the upstream QD library as the quad-double back end, against MPFR and GMP back ends, on one machine.
claimed_speedup: None in the libQD3 repo or its release notes. Indirect numbers from the MPLAPACK 2.0.1 manual (section 9, upstream QD, not libQD3): peak Rgemm reference versions quad-double 33 MFlops, GMP 19 MFlops, MPFR 11 MFlops; OpenMP versions quad-double 1.3 GFlops, GMP 693 MFlops, MPFR 390 MFlops (ratio to MPFR about 3.0x single-threaded and 3.3x OpenMP, derived from page data).
hardware: For the indirect MPLAPACK numbers: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, 256 GB DDR4-3200 ECC, Docker, GCC 9.3.0 (flags not stated).
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks; MPLAPACK (same author) now uses libQD3 as its QD back end per the MPLAPACK README
tradeoffs: Fixed-precision floating point built from 2 to 4 binary64 limbs (about 106, 159, 212 bits) or two binary80 limbs (EDD): binary64 exponent range, not correctly rounded, not arbitrary precision. Sloppy add, multiply and divide are on by default (a few bits of accuracy traded for speed); optional branch-free arithmetic (QD_ENABLE_BF*), FMA selection and x86-64-v3 or native code generation. C, C++ and Fortran interfaces. EDD needs binary80 long double (x87), with known MinGW/Wine trigonometry test failures.
caveats: Why tier D: libQD3's own text has no timing against MPFR or against original QD. What it has: docs/td.tex flop counts (for example TD add 41 flops vs QD 84, multiply 116/206 vs QD 182/332 with and without FMA, FMA speedup about 1.8x to 2.7x for multiplication, derived from counts rather than timings) and tests/qd_timer.cpp (a timer with no MPFR). The README says the fork 'keeps the original double-double and quad-double functionality' and adds TD, EDD, complex types, optional branch-free arithmetic, MPFR oracle tests; recent commits (2026-09-18) fix qd sqrt rescaling. The indirect MPLAPACK numbers (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nakatamaho/mplapack/master/doc/manual/manual.pdf, section 9, same author, arXiv 2109.13406 v2 of 2022) predate libQD3 (they used upstream QD), compare precisions that differ (quad-double about 212 bits against MPFR and GMP at their 512-bit default), go through MPLAPACK's C++ wrappers (the author suspects the MPFR wrapper copies needlessly because MPFR ran at half of GMP speed), and are not peer reviewed. Another web-search result title mentions a QD vs MPFR/GMP (212 bits) matrix-multiplication timing table of unknown authorship; it was not opened. A verifier may re-tier to C if it accepts the lineage argument. Benchmark data for the 2022 run sit in nakatamaho/mplapack benchmark/results/2022 (directory listing opened, files not read).

name: primefactors (CPU GMP/GMP-ECM reference plus CGBN GPU factoring programs)
baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (libecm, on GMP): the repo's own CPU reference path is GMP plus libecm, and the GPU programs are measured against it
workload: Prime factorization of semiprimes: Pollard's rho on GPU (CUDA with the author's CGBN fork) against CPU ECM on the same number, 16-digit factor; CPU ECM wall clock on a 32-core box for 30-, 35- and 40-digit factors.
claimed_speedup: None: the project claims no speedup and says the opposite. README 'Performance reality': the GPU programs 'do not beat the CPU for hard inputs'; for integers below 2^64 they are 'much slower than their GMP-ECM equivalent'; on an RTX 4080 a 16-digit factor takes about 8.7 s with GPU rho versus about 2 s for CPU ECM on the same number (about 4x slower, derived from page data), and 19-digit and larger factors are impractical. CPU path wall clock (32-core box, equal-size prime semiprime): 30-digit factor about 10.5 s, 35-digit about 20.6 s, 40-digit about 5.7 min.
compiler_and_flags: CPU: /usr/bin/gcc -O3 -std=c17 -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize -ftree-slp-vectorize -fopenmp, link -lecm -lgmp -flto=32. GPU: nvcc (CUDA 12.9, also tested 13.2) -O3 -arch=sm_89 (sm_120 on Blackwell), OpenMPI 5.0.5, GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (all from the Makefile and README).
hardware: Tested on a laptop with RTX 4080 Ada (sm_89) and Core i9-14900HX, and an Intel NUC 13 Extreme with RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120) and Core i9-13900K, Fedora 41 and 44; the 32-core CPU box for the ECM timings is not identified.
tradeoffs: Hobby research code. primefactors.c is arbitrary precision through GMP mpz_t with trial division, Pollard's rho and GMP-ECM curves spread across cores by OpenMP (memory grows with threads times B1). The two CUDA programs (cgbnprimefactors.cu, ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi.cu) need CUDA, the author's CGBN fork and OpenMPI; GPU rho gains only about sqrt(k) from k parallel walks. Single-machine ECM tops out around 45 digits per the README; MPI scaling was never tested beyond one node.
caveats: Does not qualify as faster than its baseline: the README and primefactors-design.pdf both state that neither GPU program is intended to beat the CPU GMP-ECM path, and the CPU path simply calls GMP and GMP-ECM, so no baseline is beaten. Kept as a record so the shortcoming is documented (not faster). The only comparison is first-party and has no methodology beyond the GPU model (8.7 s vs 2 s, one number). The ~37 s to ~8.65 s improvement in the design doc is GPU-against-GPU tuning. The README states the author used Claude Opus 5.0 for the Pollard's rho code and for testing and bug finding. Related: the author's CGBN fork (steleman/nvidia-cgbn) was not examined.

stars_or_usage: 2.7k stars; 2023 James H. Wilkinson Prize for Numerical Software (per the repo README page)
tradeoffs: ISO C99 framework with BLAS, CBLAS and its own typed/object APIs, so it links from C++ directly. Runtime sub-configuration selection ('auto'). It provides BLAS-like operations only, so full LAPACK needs libflame or another LAPACK on top. MKL stays faster on Intel hardware (SkylakeX) per the same page.
caveats: Results were gathered 2019-2021 against OpenBLAS 0.3.5/0.3.10/0.3.17 and MKL 2018-2020, so OpenBLAS (which later gained better AVX-512 kernels) and MKL have since changed. Run by the BLIS developers, though the benchmark driver code is public (test/3 in the repo). Win over MKL on AMD may reflect MKL's CPU dispatch rather than kernel quality (the authors speculate this on the page). Win over OpenBLAS is stated for SkylakeX only in text; other platforms need the graphs read. Explicit BLIS compiler flags are not listed, so tier A rests on the public driver, compiler version, CPU model and configure line.
found_via: PyPI simple-index scan for names matching blis/gemm/blas surfaced the 'blis' wheel (explosion/cython-blis, which bundles BLIS); then GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/blas?l=c and https://github.com/topics/dgemm list flame/blis; docs/Performance.md and docs/PerformanceSmall.md read from the repo. vcpkg and Conan Center have no BLIS port.

name: cpp-matmul (talhasaruhan)
baseline: Eigen MatrixXd product built with EIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL (so Intel MKL dgemm, 12 threads, TBB), also multithreaded NumPy on MKL
workload: Multithreaded double-precision square matrix-matrix multiplication, one C = A*B timing per run, N up to about 15,000, compared against Eigen with the MKL backend.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Current implementation runs identically or slightly faster than Eigen (MKL+TBB) for all test cases (tested up to N=15K)'. NumPy (MKL) was 'consistently slower than Eigen(MKL+TBB)'. The result is shown only as a graph (Benchmark1.png) and benchmark.xlsx; no ratio is given in the text.
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2017, x64 Release plus /O2 /Ot /Gy /arch:AVX2 /fp:fast /std:c++17; hand-written AVX/FMA intrinsics, software prefetching, runtime-detected block sizes. The Eigen benchmark (Benchmarks/EigenBenchmark.cpp) defines EIGEN_USE_MKL_ALL and sets 12 threads.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-8700K (12 threads), Windows
tradeoffs: Windows only (Win32 processor-mapping and thread-affinity calls, cpuid), x86-64 with AVX/FMA only, double-precision square matrices, no BLAS-style API (README says to copy CPUUtils.*, ThreadPool.h and MatrixMul.cpp into a namespace), plain O(N^3) with no Strassen. Block sizes are detected at run time from cache sizes.
caveats: No license file (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.md and LICENSE.txt all 404, repo page shows none), so the code is reference-only. Tier A is assigned because benchmark code (EigenBenchmark.cpp, NumpyBenchmark.py), compiler, flags and CPU are all public, but the numbers exist only as a PNG graph and an xlsx, and the text claim is qualitative ('identically or slightly faster'); a verifier should open the graph and could reasonably re-tier to C. The Eigen/MKL/TBB versions are not stated, and the benchmark times one multiplication with 12 threads on a single desktop CPU. README text is partly stale: it strikes out 'Still a factor of 2 to achieve MKL performance' and also says that on this CPU the build without software prefetching is about 15% faster. Single author, last commit Nov 2018.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'small matrix multiplication library outperforms Intel MKL OpenBLAS Eigen C++ github benchmark blog' listed https://github.com/talhasaruhan/cpp-matmul (title 'cpp matmul'); then opened the repo page, README, Benchmarks folder, EigenBenchmark.cpp and the commit list.

name: cpu_gemm_opt
baseline: OpenBLAS 0.3.4 sgemm (README: 'most of the size exceed openblas(0.3.4)'; the driver times cblas_sgemm from the OpenBLAS it links)
workload: Single-core row-major SGEMM, square sizes 48 to 3264, alpha=beta=1, hand-written AVX2 6x16 micro-kernel with per-size tuned block parameters, hyperthreading off.
claimed_speedup: 78.31 GFLOPS (96.38% of peak) vs 75.11 for the reference column at 960^3; 78.12 vs 73.65 at 1920^3; 78.20 vs 73.41 at 3264^3; 75.79 vs 68.14 at 192^3; 60.13 vs 43.05 at 48^3. About 4-7% faster at sizes from 960 up (derived from page data). Slower than the reference at 144^3 (55.85 vs 64.26).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ 7.0.0, -pthread -std=c++11 -Wall -O3 -m64 -mfma -msse -msse2 (src/build.sh)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6142, one core at 2600 MHz, hyperthreading off, theoretical 81.25 GFLOPS (AVX2 FMA)
tradeoffs: SGEMM only, single core, row-major driver; AVX2 kernel (the Xeon Gold 6142 also has AVX-512, which it does not use); needs a per-machine tuned parameter database (sgemm_tuned.db), hyperthreading off and ideally turbo off to reach peak.
caveats: OpenBLAS is version 0.3.4 (2019) and its build TARGET is not stated, so it may not have been the best kernel for that CPU; the gflops_ref column is not labelled in the README (identified as OpenBLAS from the README sentence and the driver/build script); the win is small (a few percent) and reverses at some sizes below 768; the README says it is still being tuned; results are 7 years old.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'beats OpenBLAS'; opened the repo page, README and src/build.sh.

name: emugemm-cdna
baseline: rocBLAS native FP32 sgemm on AMD MI250 (per-shape tuned solutions)
workload: FP32 GEMM emulated by splitting inputs into three BF16 slices (bf16x3) multiplied on the matrix cores, on one MI250 GCD, across the tested shapes, with the native rocBLAS side also tuned per shape.
claimed_speedup: 1.20-1.22x faster than native FP32 on every shape tested, after per-shape solution tuning of both sides (README table).
compiler_and_flags: hipcc -O3 -Wno-deprecated-declarations --offload-arch=gfx90a, ROCm 7.2.3
hardware: AMD MI250 (gfx90a), 1 GCD, 104 CU
tradeoffs: Not bit-compatible with FP32: accuracy floor of 4.4355e-6 relative error with the bf16x3 scheme, with a request API (max_rel_err) that reports 'TARGET UNREACHABLE' instead of silently under-delivering; only gfx90a was tested; needs a tuning table per GPU and ROCm version; speed ceiling on MI250 is 1.33x.
caveats: GPU, not CPU. The README itself records that an earlier 2.1x was really 1.21x because the baseline ran rocBLAS's default kernel, and ties the investigation to ROCm/rocm-libraries issue 9985 (rocBLAS default solution losing to another solution in the same library), so the win depends on how well the native baseline is tuned. Written with AI assistance (commits co-authored by an AI assistant). Baseline rocBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'topic:gemm language:C++'; opened the repo page, README and build example.

name: gemm (johnnyw3, AVX/AMX kernels)
baseline: OpenBLAS or Intel MKL, whichever was faster on each machine (OpenBLAS built with BUILD_BFLOAT16=1 for AMX)
workload: fp32 (AVX2, AVX-512) and bf16-input/fp32-output (AMX) GEMM, n=4096, single-threaded and 4 threads, average of 10 runs.
claimed_speedup: AMX on Granite Rapids Xeon 6972P: 1279 vs 1229 GFLOPS single-threaded (1.04x) and 4810 vs 4675 with 4 threads (1.03x); but slower on AVX2 Kaby Lake i5-8350U (78 vs 103, 0.76x; 213 vs 282 with 4 threads) and AVX-512 Tiger Lake i5-1135G7 (106 vs 122, 0.87x; 380 vs 465 with 4 threads).
compiler_and_flags: clang++ (version not stated; clang 16+ or gcc 13+ required for AMX), -march=$(TARGET) -O3 -flto (Makefile)
hardware: Intel Xeon 6972P (Granite Rapids), Core i5-1135G7 (Tiger Lake), Core i5-8350U (Kaby Lake)
tradeoffs: x86 only (AVX2, AVX-512, AMX); the AMX path takes bf16 inputs; multithreaded code does not scale well beyond 8 threads; README says the best results are single/lightly threaded; no license file.
caveats: Beats the baseline only on AMX hardware (3-4%); on AVX2 and AVX-512 it is 13-24% slower; the baseline is the better of OpenBLAS and MKL chosen per machine; no LICENSE file in the repository, so the code cannot be copied; one size (n=4096); compiler version not stated.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'AMX GEMM'; opened the repo page, README and Makefile.

name: gpu-compute (SGEMM for Blackwell)
baseline: cuBLAS cublasSgemm with CUBLAS_PEDANTIC_MATH (true FP32) on an RTX 5080
workload: Hand-written row-major FP32 SGEMM, square sizes N=32 to 256 (and larger sizes for contrast), timed with CUDA events and checked against cublasSgemm; a 32x32-tile kernel runs one to 64 CTAs.
claimed_speedup: Faster than cuBLAS FP32 on every square N from 32 to 256 measured: 8.1 us vs 16.5 us at 32^3 (2.02x), 9.5 vs 16.2 us at 64^3 (1.71x), 10.9 vs 16.2 us at 128^3 (1.49x), 11.9 vs 16.9 us at 192^3 (1.42x), 13.6 vs 17.8 us at 256^3 (1.30x). Not a win on tall-skinny shapes (4096x64x4096 is 0.90x), and at 4096^3 the README's throughput table (units not labelled) shows the auto kernel at 23.05 vs 36.79 for cuBLAS FP32.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.3 via CMake, C++17, --use_fast_math -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native; Windows PowerShell build script
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5080 (Blackwell sm_120, 84 SMs, 15.9 GB)
tradeoffs: Only wins in the launch-bound small-square regime (N<=256, used up to about 384); loses on large and tall-skinny shapes; fixed 32x32 tile with one output per thread; row-major C = A@B; includes a labelled WMMA TF32 kernel that does not beat cuBLAS TF32.
caveats: The win is cuBLAS's roughly 16 us per-call launch and heuristic floor on tiny matrices, not arithmetic throughput; the license was changed from MIT to a view-only 'all rights reserved' text, so the code cannot be copied; one GPU and one build; compiled with --use_fast_math; the README does not give run counts or variance.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'outperforms cuBLAS'; opened the repo page, README, gemm/README.md, CMakeLists.txt and LICENSE.

name: MaxMulSK
baseline: OpenBLAS (tuned build reaching its own SME kernels, one thread) and Apple Accelerate
workload: Single-thread FP32 GEMM over 35 shapes (squares, LLM-shaped, DeepSeek-V3 and LLaMA shapes) with allocation, packing and writeback inside every timed call, on an Apple M4 using Arm SME2.
claimed_speedup: README: v5.1 (development kernel, code not yet published) is 1.86x tuned OpenBLAS (geometric mean of paired ratios, ahead on 33 of 35 shapes, tied on 2) and 1.16x Apple Accelerate (behind at 256^3: 0.74x). For the published v3 kernel (2026-09-09 session): 1.40 to 1.77 TFLOP/s end to end on squares 256^3 to 4096^3, 1.01x to 1.31x OpenBLAS on squares and 1.36x to 2.23x on LLM shapes, but 5 to 17% behind Accelerate at most sizes.
compiler_and_flags: LLVM/Clang from Homebrew, CMake with -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 -march=armv8.7-a+sme+sme2 (CMakeLists.txt); OpenBLAS thread count 1 (OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, OPENBLAS_DIRECT_LIMIT=1792), Accelerate pinned to one thread via BLASSetThreading
hardware: Apple M4, macOS 26.6.2, AC power
tradeoffs: C++20 library for Apple M4 only (needs SME/SME2); single-threaded FP32 row-major C = A*B with packing and blocking done internally; Homebrew clang and libomp required. Not a BLAS ABI drop-in.
caveats: The headline v5.1 numbers are from kernel code that is not yet in the repository (published code is v3 and v4c), so only the v3/v4c claims are reproducible from the repo. Versus Accelerate (Apple's own SME-aware BLAS) the margin is 1.16x geomean and it loses at small sizes; the 1.86x figure is against an OpenBLAS build the README says reaches its SME kernels only when built from develop with DYNAMIC_ARCH (the stock Homebrew build cannot). Small-size results depend on call order (matrix-unit frequency effects), acknowledged in the README. Single M4 machine, author's measurements, zero stars.
found_via: GitHub repository search 'SME GEMM Apple Silicon'; opened the repo page, README and CMakeLists.txt.
GitHub: topic page github.com/topics/gemm sorted by recently updated; opened README and CMakeLists.txt

name: MTGEMM-A
baseline: Apple Accelerate sgemm/dgemm (also OpenBLAS develop and 0.3.34, Eigen master, LIBXSMM, KleidiAI)
workload: FP32/FP64 GEMM on Apple M4 Pro using Arm SME2: the paper's 24 workloads and square sizes 512-4096, row- and column-major, one thread and default threading, geometric mean GFLOPS.
claimed_speedup: FP32 geomean 2777 vs 2363 GFLOPS for Accelerate on the paper's 24 column-major workloads at default threading (1.18x); 1.19x (column-major) and 1.26x (row-major) on one thread for the paper's 24 workloads; 1.25x row-major / 1.19x column-major vs Accelerate in the paper-comparison table; 3.7x faster than OpenBLAS 0.3.34 (row-major) and 2.2x faster than LIBXSMM (column-major), 1.7x faster than KleidiAI (one thread); Eigen master 1044 GFLOPS vs 2777 at default threading
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21 (macOS 27.0), -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=armv8.6-a+sme2+sme-f64f64
hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 8 performance cores in two clusters of 4 (two SME units, SVL 512 bits), 48 GB
tradeoffs: Apple M4-family (SME2) only for the SME backend; an AMX backend covers M2/M3-class chips; no transposed operands (computes C = alpha A B + beta C only); GEMM only, not full BLAS; macOS cannot pin threads to an SME cluster so two-thread results depend on scheduling.
caveats: Reproduction of the paper arXiv:2512.21473 (MpGEMM, whose authors released no code), by a single author, measured on one machine (8 P-core M4 Pro vs the paper's 10 P-core); at default threading it is slower than Accelerate on 10 of 484 shapes; the OpenBLAS 0.3.34 figure in the LIBXSMM/KleidiAI comparison is one Homebrew-build measurement that falls back to NEON at M=4096; OpenBLAS develop's own SME kernels reach 0.50x-0.78x of MTGEMM-A on one thread. The repo also carries an OpenBLAS port (branch sme2-gemm of the author's OpenBLAS fork, not yet submitted) and an Eigen SME GEMM backend developed from this code. Wave 8 leads.md already lists this repo as a candidate for the MpGEMM paper entry.
found_via: Wave 8 leads.md (from the MpGEMM verifier); GitHub repository search 'SME GEMM Apple Silicon'; opened the repo page and README.

name: Octavian.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS and Intel MKL (also BLIS)
workload: Dense matrix multiplication GFLOPS across sizes 10 to 1000 (square), run with BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl; headline row is 1000x1000x1000 with 36 threads.
claimed_speedup: 1000x1000x1000: Octavian median 1816 GFLOPS (max 1895) vs OpenBLAS median 1254 (max 1385), MKL median 1348 (max 1589), BLIS median 1051 (max 1476). README states 'Octavian has the fastest CPU performance' among the listed Julia packages.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.7.0-DEV.1124 (2021-05-19), LLVM 11.0.1 ORCJIT cascadelake, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=36; benchmark via BLASBenchmarksCPU.jl (public)
hardware: Intel Core i9-10980XE @ 3.00GHz
tradeoffs: Pure Julia, built on LoopVectorization.jl; BLAS-like gemm-style API (matmul) rather than a full BLAS/LAPACK ABI, so it is not directly callable from C++. Task scheduling can interfere with Base.Threads tasks (README docs note).
caveats: The headline figure is from one 2021 run on a 36-thread Skylake-X/Cascade Lake part with a Julia dev build; MKL and OpenBLAS may be better tuned for other sizes or newer versions. The README says the full size sweep took 2h25m. Newer LoopVectorization/Julia versions may change results. Not a C++-callable library.

name: PureBLAS.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build) and AOCL-BLIS (AMD's BLIS fork); the repo's gate is max(OpenBLAS, AOCL)
workload: Single-threaded Float64 and ComplexF64 BLAS 1-3 and LAPACK routines across sizes on three AMD microarchitectures (2619 op/size/machine cells), measured with ABBA-interleaved rounds at locked clock frequency and the median ratio reported.
claimed_speedup: README: about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL), single-threaded. Median PureBLAS/OpenBLAS ratios (Zen3/Zen4/Zen5) from bench/gen_table.md: gemm 1.17/1.08/1.23, potrf 1.11/1.46/1.49, geqrf 1.55/1.79/1.66, getrf 1.17/1.20/1.31, gesvd 1.30/1.27/1.30, syev 1.40/1.44/1.34. Versus AOCL (gen_table_aocl.md): gemm 1.06/1.08/1.07, potrf 1.72/1.37/1.20, geqrf 1.64/1.30/1.24. notes.md: gemm at n=4096 is 1.252/1.280/1.308 (Zen4/Zen3/Zen5) against the faster of OpenBLAS and AOCL.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (README requires Julia 1.13) with LLVM; benchmark is `taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench` with BLAS.set_num_threads(1) and frequency locking via bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (methodology.md); no extra compiler flags stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3), Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4), Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5); measured 2026-09-23 (bench/provenance.md)
tradeoffs: Pure Julia BLAS and LAPACK (about 36k lines) that derives block sizes from detected cache and vector sizes. Inside Julia it reroutes LinearAlgebra through libblastrampoline with PureBLAS.activate(). It can also build libpureblas.so (ILP64 BLAS symbols, embedded Julia runtime) via juliac --trim, which the README calls experimental; that route makes it linkable from C/C++/Rust. Single-threaded only (multithreading deliberately on hold). Singular vectors only for Float64 and complex.
caveats: All measurements are the author's, on AMD hardware only (no Intel), single-threaded, Float64/ComplexF64 only. The win over OpenBLAS is larger than over AOCL, and roughly 13% of cells are below the gate (listed in docs/src/notes.md; some trmm/trsm/solve cells are 0.78-0.94 of AOCL). About 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity and the methodology page says run-to-run noise moves the below-gate count by 10-15 cells per sweep. notes.md says large-n gemm uses Strassen-Winograd (1.2-1.4x at large n), which has weaker numerical error bounds than classical gemm. The OpenBLAS version and AOCL version are not stated in the pages read. Repository is days old (first visible commits 2026-09-26) with 0 forks and no external users.

name: TCCG / GETT (Tensor Contraction Code Generator)
language: Python (generator that emits vectorized C code)
baseline: TTGT (transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose) tensor contraction built on Intel MKL sgemm/dgemm (the repo's default BLAS in config.cfg is MKL); TTGT is TCCG's own backend, not a third-party tensor library
workload: Dense tensor contractions from the repo's benchmark v0.1 (CCSD, AO2MO and intensli test cases, up to 6-D tensors, largest tensor 200 MiB), single and double precision, GFLOPS on one core; GETT versus LoG versus TTGT, and TCCG versus the best of CTF/naive (single) or CTF/TT/naive (double).
claimed_speedup: No numeric table; values read by eye from benchmark/GETT_LoG_TTGT.png. Single precision on one Haswell core: abcde-efbad-cf GETT about 20.5 GFLOPS vs TTGT about 15 (about 1.4x, derived from figure); abcdef-dfgb-geac GETT about 55.5 vs TTGT about 25 (about 2.2x, derived from figure). On compute-bound cases TTGT ties or beats GETT (for example abcd-aebf-fdec about 67 vs about 75 GFLOPS single precision). benchmark.png (Fig. 11): TCCG about 55 GFLOPS vs best-of(CTF, naive) about 13 on abcdef-dfgb-geac. README text only says GETT is 'especially outstanding' for bandwidth-bound contractions.
compiler_and_flags: Intel icpc 16.0.1 20151021, -O3 -xhost -mkl (benchmark/README.md)
hardware: Single core of an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 (Haswell); ECC enabled, Intel SpeedStep and TurboBoost disabled
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; GETT is the contraction method behind TCL and the subject of ACM TOMS 2018 / arXiv 1607.00145
tradeoffs: Generator written in Python 2.7 that emits C with AVX2 (AVX-512 experimental; CUDA only for TTGT and LoG); needs Intel icc 15+ (g++ 4.8+ experimental), a BLAS such as MKL, and the HPTT library. GETT has a stated limitation: the product of free-index sizes of each input tensor must be a multiple of 24. Auto-tuning explores up to N candidate implementations at generation time (--maxImplementations). Parallel GETT only on the v0.2.0 branch per the changelog; the published benchmark is single-core.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repository (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md and COPYING all returned 404 and GitHub shows none), so the code is reference-only even though the sibling HPTT is BSD-3-Clause. The TTGT baseline is the authors' own implementation (HPTT-style transposes plus MKL GEMM) rather than an independent library. Results are single-core, 2016-era hardware and compiler; figures are images, so values are read by eye and approximate. GETT does not win everywhere: on compute-bound contractions TTGT is on par or faster. benchmark.py also drives libtensor, TBLIS, CTF and Eigen scripts (with a hard-coded author path) but the README publishes only the GETT/LoG/TTGT and TCCG-vs-best-of-others figures. The peer-reviewed paper (Springer and Bientinesi, ACM TOMS 2018, arXiv 1607.00145) is not opened (arXiv, ACM and the author's PDF host are blocked); its abstract, seen only as search-engine snippets, reports up to 12.4x over existing approaches for bandwidth-bound contractions and up to 91.3% of peak on compute-bound ones; those numbers are not used above. Abandoned since 2017.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/HPAC/tccg (README, benchmark/README.md, benchmark/benchmark.py, benchmark/GETT_LoG_TTGT.png, benchmark/benchmark.png)

name: Zynum
baseline: OpenBLAS 0.3.34 (also Apple Accelerate)
workload: GEMM GFLOP/s over 42 NN column-major shapes for each of sgemm/dgemm/cgemm/zgemm (168 cases), six interleaved fresh-process runs per library, on an Apple M5 with 10 threads.
claimed_speedup: sgemm 1024x1024x1024: 1998.7 GFLOP/s vs OpenBLAS 472.6 and Accelerate 1924.8; dgemm sq1024: 556.5 vs OpenBLAS 252.4 and Accelerate 505.8 (gemm.csv). Median Zynum/OpenBLAS GFLOP/s ratio over all 168 cases is 2.15x (derived from page data), Zynum faster in 146 of 168 cases. Versus Accelerate the median ratio is 1.11x, with Zynum ahead in 100 of 168 cases (derived from page data) and behind on sgemm medians (0.93x).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build -Dcpu=baseline -Ddispatch=dynamic -Doptimize=ReleaseFast; OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=10 OPENBLAS_DYNAMIC=0; OpenBLAS 0.3.34
hardware: Apple M5, 10 logical CPUs, macOS 27.0 (feat_sme/sme2 detected)
tradeoffs: Zig-native BLAS exposing CBLAS and Fortran-ABI entry points plus C headers (include <zynum/blas/cblas.h>, link zynum_blas), so it is callable from C++. Needs Zig 0.16 to build. LGPL-3.0-or-later (GPL-3.0 text also shipped). Level 1-3 BLAS only; no LAPACK. Beta, API and dispatch policy may change.
caveats: Single host (Apple M5), measurements by the author. Zynum appears to dispatch SME/AArch64 kernels while OpenBLAS 0.3.34 on M5 likely runs NEON kernels, which probably explains the 3.9x median sgemm gap; Accelerate (Apple's vendor BLAS) is the fairer comparator and Zynum is roughly even to slightly slower on sgemm/dgemm medians (0.93x and 0.99x of Accelerate's GFLOP/s). Some shapes (e.g. m17_n2048_k257) are slower than both rivals (sgemm 107.2 vs Accelerate 429.1, OpenBLAS 203.5 GFLOP/s). The dataset is marked dirty (uncommitted working-tree sources hashed in source.json), correctness is sampled-checked only, and the metadata reader reports a kernel_coverage_invalid_document diagnostic. Repo is days-to-weeks old with no external users. Level 2 timings include Python/ctypes overhead.

name: CLBlast
baseline: clBLAS 2.12, NVIDIA cuBLAS

name: COSMA
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also Cray LibSci, Cray LibSci_acc, CARMA, CTF)
workload: Distributed matrix-matrix multiplication (communication-optimal, with a ScaLAPACK pxgemm wrapper): CP2K RPA benchmark of 128 water molecules (46 tall-and-skinny pdgemm calls) and square matrices, on Piz Daint.
claimed_speedup: README: 'speedups by factor of up to 8.3x over the second-fastest algorithm'; 'approximately 2x faster' than Cray-libsci_acc for CP2K pdgemm on 1024 GPU nodes; GPU version '25-27% faster than the second best' on 128 nodes (MKL, Cray-libsci, libsci_acc compared); CPU COSMA reaches peak and is compared against Intel MKL ScaLAPACK 19.0.1.144 on square matrices (plots).
hardware: Piz Daint (Cray XC50 GPU nodes and XC40 CPU nodes), 128 and 1024 nodes
tradeoffs: MPI-based, needs a local BLAS (MKL, LibSci, OpenBLAS, BLIS, cuBLAS, rocBLAS) and optionally ScaLAPACK for the wrapper; distributed-memory only; speedups depend on matrix shape and node count; the ScaLAPACK-layout wrapper costs some throughput versus the native layout.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SC19 Best Student Paper, ACM DL link in README) but this run could not open the paper, so the numbers cited are the README's; the 8.3x is over the second-fastest algorithm (not necessarily MKL); the result tables are SVG images; compiler and flags are not stated on the README; results are from 2019 with MKL 19.0.1.144 and Cray LibSci 19.06/19.10.
found_via: WebFetch of github.com/eth-cscs/spla README which links COSMA; GitHub topics/matrix-multiplication?l=c++ page; then the COSMA README.

name: faer

workload: Dense matrix multiplication, QR and eigenvalue decomposition, plotted as n^3 over run time versus matrix size, with Eigen compiled with -fopenmp.
claimed_speedup: JOSS paper text: 'State of the art algorithms are used for each decomposition, allowing performance that matches or even surpasses other low level libraries such as OpenBLAS, LAPACK, and Eigen.' No numeric table in paper.md (results are PDF plots).
compiler_and_flags: Eigen built with -fopenmp; Rust flags not stated in paper.md
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i5-11400 @ 2.60GHz, 12 threads
stars_or_usage: 2.6k stars (GitHub mirror; project moved to codeberg.org/sarah-quinones/faer)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust dense linear algebra (matmul, Cholesky, LU, QR, SVD, EVD) with its own API, not a drop-in BLAS/LAPACK ABI; a faer-ffi directory exists in the repo for C bindings. Explicit SIMD on x86-64 and AArch64 NEON. Uses Rayon for threading.
caveats: Numbers are only in plots I could not read (faer.veganb.tw benchmarks page and the JOSS site were unreachable from this container), so the size of the win is not verified here. The paper concedes it is usually on par with OpenBLAS and slower than MKL on the author's desktop (author statement quoted in search results, not opened). Rust optimization flags are not stated. Benchmarks are first-party. The GitHub repo is now a mirror of the Codeberg repo.

name: fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard)
baseline: Intel MKL dgemm
workload: Sequential square dgemm (N = 1000 to 7500) comparing MKL against Strassen and other fast matrix multiplication algorithms with 1 to 3 recursion levels; run times in ms, median of five trials, data checked into data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data: Strassen with 2 recursion levels takes 4836 ms vs MKL 5361 ms at N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 ms vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x); 3 levels 15561 ms at N=6000 (1.16x); 1.04x at N=2000. The PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README) reports better performance than MKL dgemm on a shared-memory machine.
compiler_and_flags: C++11 with OpenMP and Intel MKL; flags set in make.incs/make.inc.linux (not read)
hardware: NERSC Edison (data/README.md says all data was collected on Edison; sequential results should be scaled to 3.2 GHz because of Turbo Boost); CPU model not stated in the files read
tradeoffs: Code-generated implementations of Strassen, Bini (approximate) and many other fast algorithms for sequential and shared-memory parallel use, calling MKL for base cases; requires MKL. Fast algorithms have weaker numerical stability (README reports errors about 1e-14 to 1e-15 for exact algorithms and larger for approximate ones) and only win for large matrices.
caveats: The 1.11-1.16x figures are derived from raw timing files and exclude the approximate (Bini) algorithm, which is faster still but numerically lossy; some rows in the data are noisy (for example one-level Strassen at N=1000 takes 405.8 ms vs 108.2 ms for MKL). The speedup applies only to N of about 2000 and above, and the machine is a 2014-era supercomputer node, so the ratio against current MKL on modern CPUs is unknown. The paper itself (arXiv 1409.2908) could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked); the paper claim is from the README citation and a search snippet.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github Strassen algorithm implementation faster than MKL OpenBLAS dgemm'; opened README, data/README.md and the checked-in timing files

name: fmm-gen (Generating Families of Practical Fast Matrix Multiplication Algorithms)
baseline: conventional GEMM (the paper's classical dgemm; the opened pages do not name the library, so BLIS, MKL or OpenBLAS as comparator is unconfirmed)
workload: Generated Strassen-like fast matrix multiplication (20+ algorithm variants, multi-level, arbitrary matrix sizes and shapes) with the matrix additions fused into GEMM packing and micro-kernels, run on single-core and multicore systems and compared with a performance model.
claimed_speedup: README abstract: 'Our implementations demonstrate a performance benefit over conventional GEMM on single core and multi-core systems.' No numeric speedup appears on any opened page.
tradeoffs: Python scripts generate and compile C code per algorithm and partition (OpenMP, config.py and SLURM scripts for cluster runs). Fast matrix multiplication trades numerical stability and extra additions for fewer multiplications, and only helps above some matrix size; no BLAS-compatible drop-in interface is shown.
caveats: Tier B rests on the IPDPS 2017 paper (Huang, Rice, Matthews, van de Geijn) cited in the README's BibTeX; the paper PDF host was blocked in this container, so no speedup number, CPU, compiler or comparator library was read. The README says only that results should follow the paper's curves and that absolute GFLOPS differ by machine. Repo has had no commits since 2017. The related arbenson/fast-matmul project is already catalogued separately.
found_via: Related-links section of the flame/tblis-strassen README (opened), then the fmm-gen README, repo page, commits page and LICENSE (opened).

name: RecursiveFactorization.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia LUFactorization default) and Intel MKL (MKLLUFactorization)

The benchmark output page has only a plot; reading it (approximate, derived from page data), RFLUFactorization reaches about 33 GFLOPs at N=500 versus about 18 for OpenBLAS LUFactorization and about 23 for MKLLUFactorization, and is roughly 2x OpenBLAS around N=100-250.

name: TBLIS (Tensor-Based Library Instantiation Software)
baseline: BLAS-based TTGT tensor contraction (transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose around a BLAS GEMM such as OpenBLAS or MKL)
workload: Tensor contraction (a multi-dimensional generalisation of GEMM) done natively with BLIS-style micro-kernels, without the explicit tensor transpositions that a GEMM-based approach needs.
claimed_speedup: Wiki home page: TBLIS implements tensor contraction 'with essentially zero overhead compared to matrix multiplication'. The numeric comparison against TTGT is in the linked SISC paper (arXiv:1607.00291), which this agent could not open; no number is claimed here.
tradeoffs: C and C++ interfaces (tblis.h header in the repo); builds on BLIS-style kernels and its own threading; the wiki lists build/usage pages. Tensor operations only, not a drop-in BLAS replacement.
caveats: Evidence tier B rests on the peer-reviewed paper that the wiki's Research page cites (it says 'submitted to SISC'), but arxiv.org and the publisher were blocked in this container, so the speedup numbers, CPU, compiler and flags were not read. The repo README and wiki home contain no benchmark numbers. A verifier should open the paper and upgrade, downgrade or fill compiler/hardware.
found_via: Web search 'TBLIS tensor contraction library GitHub devinamatthews performance versus TTGT BLAS' after bassoy/ttv (already in this wave) benchmarked TBLIS 1.0.0 as a comparator; the PyPI scan also showed the pytblis and pyscf-tblis binding wheels. Pages opened: repo, wiki home, wiki Research page, commits page.

name: TTM / TLIB(TTM) (in-place tensor-times-matrix via loops-over-GEMM)
baseline: Eigen (Tensor module) and LibTorch tensor-matrix products, plus Intel MKL batched GEMM; the paper reports parity with TBLIS
workload: Mode-q tensor-times-matrix product on dense tensors of many shapes and orders, large tensor slices highlighted, as reported in the author's Journal of Computational Science 2025 paper (details not seen).
claimed_speedup: SNIPPET ONLY (search-engine summary of the paper abstract; the paper was not opened): best-performing algorithm reaches a median 2.47 TFLOPS on an Intel Xeon Gold 5318Y and 2.93 TFLOPS on an AMD EPYC 9354 for large tensor slices; 'outperforms batched GEMM implementation of Intel MKL by a factor of 2.57 with large tensor slices'; 'on average at least 6.21% and up to 334.31% faster' than frameworks implementing state-of-the-art approaches including Libtorch and Eigen; 'on par with TBLIS' for the majority of tensor shapes. The repo README gives no numbers ('For large tensors reaches peak matrix-times-matrix performance').
compiler_and_flags: Paper build not seen. Repo example/Makefile: g++ -Wall -O3 -std=c++17 -fopenmp with the BLAS chosen through BLAS_FLAG (OPENBLAS, MKL or BLIS makefile fragments).
hardware: Per the search snippet only: Intel Xeon Gold 5318Y and AMD EPYC 9354.
stars_or_usage: 5 stars, 1 fork; Python bindings (ttmpy) in repo; the README asks users to cite the Journal of Computational Science 2025 article (vol. 87, art. 102568)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 but requires an external BLAS (BLIS, MKL or OpenBLAS makefile fragments provided), so performance follows the chosen BLAS. float and double only, contiguously stored tensors, OpenMP 4.5 or newer for threading. In-place: no tensor transposition and no extra memory. Runtime choice of contraction mode, tensor order, extents and any linear layout. Task-loop parallelism added in late 2024.
caveats: I could not open the evidence: tore.tuhh.de returned EGRESS_BLOCKED and ScienceDirect, arXiv and ICCS pages are listed as blocked, so every number above is from one WebSearch result summary and is UNVERIFIED. Tier B rests on peer review (the README cites the paper as the article to cite) and on the snippet; it is the author's own benchmark of his own library, with the low end of the claimed range (6.21% average) marginal and TBLIS a tie. Whether the baselines were built with comparable flags, the compiler used, and whether the benchmark code is public are unknown. The repo has no baseline comparison: example/measure.cpp (g++ -O3, 10 iterations, 32 MB cache flush between runs) times only TTM's own parallel/slicing/fusion variants, and the wiki has no performance page (three of four wiki pages failed to load). The README badge says GPL while LICENSE.txt is the GNU LGPL version 3 (GitHub also shows LGPL-3.0). A verifier able to open the paper should confirm numbers, CPUs and flags and check for a public artifact repo, which could move this to A.

name: apple-bottom
baseline: Apple Accelerate DGEMM on AMX (and OpenBLAS 6-thread in a Quantum ESPRESSO run)
workload: DGEMM GFLOP/s using double-float (FP32 pair) arithmetic on Metal GPU kernels versus the CPU Accelerate AMX path, plus end-to-end Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 wall time.
claimed_speedup: M2 Max: DGEMM 2048^2 552 GFLOP/s vs Accelerate 468 (+18%), 4096^2 643 vs 566 (+14%). Quantum ESPRESSO Si64: 2:01 with apple-bottom vs 2:28 with OpenBLAS 6-thread (22% faster wall time, 47% less CPU usage); Si128 +12% wall.
hardware: Apple M2 Max (38-core GPU, 64 GB unified memory)
tradeoffs: Metal compute shaders with a C API (apple_bottom.h) and a Fortran bridge that routes calls under 100M FLOPs to OpenBLAS/Accelerate and large calls to the GPU; callable from C++. Not IEEE FP64: precision is about 1e-15 (double-float), so results are not bit-exact; ZHERK is slower than the CPU path; single calls under N=1024 are dominated by about 100 us GPU overhead; max dimension 46,340.
caveats: First-party numbers on one machine with no compiler flags or methodology details; margins are modest (+14-18%) against Accelerate, which is not in the category baseline list; the OpenBLAS comparison is an application-level run on 6 threads rather than a GEMM microbenchmark. Double-float arithmetic is not equivalent to native FP64, and the README warns against it for pivoted LU and eigensolvers. Last commit is about five months old.

name: cbk (Compact Batch Kernels)
baseline: Intel MKL compact kernels (mkl_dgeqrf_compact, mkl_dpotrf_compact, mkl_dtrsm_compact pipeline) and per-matrix LAPACKE (LAPACKE_dgels, LAPACKE_dposv, LAPACKE_dgeqrf)
workload: Batched QR, Cholesky and unpivoted LDL^T factorizations and solves for pools of many small double-precision matrices (n=10..120) in the compact interleaved layout, one thread.
claimed_speedup: QR solve (1000 matrices, n=10..120, 1 RHS): cbk gels 2.7x geometric mean over LAPACKE_dgels (1.5x at n=100) and cbk-batch 1.25x over MKL-batch; at 64 RHS the gels win drops to 1.3x and cbk-batch to 1.12x over MKL. SPD solve (512 matrices, 1 RHS): fused compact solve 2-9x over LAPACKE_dposv at orders 8-48, 1.4-2.2x at 60-105, geometric mean 1.7x, level with MKL's compact pipeline (0.9-1.0x geomean).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native (CMake Release); MKL compact paths linked against sequential MKL, all paths driven with the same thread count
hardware: '4-core AVX-512 container' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs the compact (interleaved) layout and packing; many small matrices only; the win disappears for larger matrices; unpivoted LDL^T (no Bunch-Kaufman pivoting); optional MKL-compatible API layer; GCC/Clang vector extensions, OpenMP over groups of V matrices.
caveats: Hardware is not identified beyond '4-core AVX-512 container', so tier C; the benchmark page labels the runs 'indicative'; pack/unpack time is excluded from the timed region; per-matrix LAPACK wins from about n=128-168 (0.25x at n=256) and at nrhs=64 is level or ahead at several sizes; SPD solve only matches MKL compact; the README states most of the library, tests and benchmarks were written by Claude models with human review. The LAPACKE backend used in the baseline is not named on the page.

The chgemm README repeats 18.6 GFLOPS on RK3399 and about 23 GFLOPS on one AWS A72 core.

GFLOPS here count int8 operations, so comparison with fp32 libraries is not like-for-like. Baseline gemmlowp is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS. Last commit June 2020. The same tutorial repo also shows a CUDA kernel above cuBLAS on an RTX 3080 as a graph with no numbers; not reported separately (GPU, off-baseline, no numbers).

name: COSTA (communication-optimal distributed matrix redistribution and transpose; ScaLAPACK pxgemr2d/pxtran replacement)
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 pdgemr2d (matrix redistribution between block-cyclic layouts)
workload: pdgemr2d redistribution of square double-precision matrices with n = 20000 to 100000 between block-cyclic layouts, once with identical layouts (128x128 blocks) and once with different block sizes (36x36 to 128x128), on 8 Piz Daint nodes of 36 cores each with 16 MPI ranks (4x4 grid); COSTA run without rank relabelling and without memory pools.
claimed_speedup: README chart data labels (docs/costa-same.svg and docs/costa-diff.svg, rendered locally; time in ms, COSTA vs MKL). Same layout: n=20000 14 vs 292; 40000 56 vs 1100; 60000 128 vs 2487; 80000 208 vs 4402; 100000 324 vs 6702 (chart caption '~20x faster'; ratios 19.4x to 21.2x derived from page data). Different layouts: n=20000 188 vs 406; 40000 702 vs 1987; 60000 1608 vs 4579; 80000 2900 vs 8012; 100000 4557 vs 12737 (chart caption 'up to 3x faster'; ratios 2.2x to 2.9x derived from page data). README overview text also says it 'outperforms other scalapack implementations by orders of magnitude in some cases'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. CMakeLists.txt adds -funroll-loops (or -Munroll) and a build_type.cmake default that was not read; MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 is named as the baseline; the MPI implementation and compiler are not given.
hardware: Piz Daint (Cray XC40, CSCS), 8 nodes x 36 cores, 16 MPI ranks as a 4x4 grid; the CPU model is not stated on the page.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars, 8 forks; used by COSMA, which is used by CP2K (README)
tradeoffs: Needs MPI 3 and OpenMP and CMake 3.12 or newer. Drop-in ScaLAPACK wrappers (pdgemr2d, pstran, pdtran, pctranu/c and complex variants) take effect when COSTA is linked before ScaLAPACK. Handles arbitrary irregular layouts, not only block-cyclic, and can transform several layouts in one communication round at the cost of larger messages and more memory. caveats: The baseline is MKL's ScaLAPACK redistribution routine, not a BLAS or LAPACK kernel, so it only loosely fits the blas-lapack baselines. The identical-layout case (about 20x) most likely reflects MKL's slow generic path when no data needs to move (my inference, not stated by the authors). The charts are first-party; the number of repetitions, whether times are mean or minimum, and the MKL and MPI settings are not stated (the miniapp default is n_rep=2). The README says the benchmark code is public (miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, pxtran_miniapp.cpp) but the compiler, flags and CPU model are missing, so not tier A. The peer-reviewed paper (Kabic, Pintarelli, Kozhevnikov, VandeVondele, ISC 2021, Springer; arXiv 2106.06601) is cited in the README but was not opened (Springer and arXiv are blocked in this session), so I kept tier C; a verifier who can open it should consider B and check whether the paper's numbers match the README charts. name: fast_matmul (NinjadenMu; didactic BLIS-style SGEMM for Apple M4)
baseline: OpenBLAS as called through NumPy (float32 A @ B in scripts/openblas.py)
workload: Square float32 matrix multiplication for n = 100, 200, 300, ... each run once until a cumulative 5 s budget is used (scripts/driver.py), custom BLIS-style code versus NumPy with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 and with default threads.
claimed_speedup: README text: the single-threaded BLIS-style implementation is 'comparable to an OpenBLAS build targeting Apple Silicon (with the difference being too small for me to reliably measure)' and the multi-threaded one is 'noticeably faster (probably due to better load balancing on my particular M4 spec)'; '~200x faster (40x with just one thread)' is against the project's own naive loop, not OpenBLAS. Read by eye from plots/plot.png: single-threaded OpenBLAS reaches n=3100 at about 4.55 s cumulative versus BLIS-style n=3000 at about 4.08 s (curves overlap); multi-threaded BLIS-style reaches n=4500 at about 4.08 s versus multi-threaded OpenBLAS n=4200 at about 4.7 s.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: clang -O3 -ffast-math -march=native (commented alternative -mcpu=apple-m4), OpenMP via Homebrew libomp, -fno-vectorize on the early didactic versions. The clang version is not stated and neither are the NumPy or OpenBLAS versions.
hardware: Apple M4 (README: 'my Apple M4'); core configuration and RAM not stated.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; same author as MuBLIS (which is already on the known list)
tradeoffs: Teaching code: float32 only, square matrices only, column-major, no transposes or alpha/beta and no BLAS interface. ARM NEON intrinsics (Apple Silicon only; the README says x86 needs retuned block sizes and AVX kernels). Fixed 12x8 register tile, cache block sizes tuned by scripts/tuner.py, OpenMP dynamic scheduling for the parallel version. No LICENSE file, so the code cannot be copied.
caveats: The benchmark treats the two sides unequally. The custom side runs ./bench with one untimed warm-up call and one timed call into a pre-zeroed output buffer (utils/bench.c). The baseline times a single NumPy A @ B call inside Python with no warm-up and with the result matrix allocated inside the timed region. There is one measurement per n, no repeats or variance, the metric is 'largest n within a cumulative time budget' rather than GFLOPS, and the custom code is built with -ffast-math. The README does not record whether NumPy used OpenBLAS or Accelerate on the M4. Parity is the only single-thread result, and the author himself attributes the multi-thread gap to load balancing on his particular M4, which may be a P/E-core scheduling artifact. Numbers are read by eye from the plot image. By the literal tier-A rule (public script, clang flags, Apple M4) this would be A, but I held it at C because of the asymmetric method; a verifier may revisit. The author's deep-dive post on ninjadenmu.github.io is egress-blocked. No license.
