compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 darwin/arm64 (CGO=0 pure Go); FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle with NEON, plans FFTW_MEASURE threads=1; numpy 2.5.0 and scipy 1.18.0 pinned single-threaded
hardware: Apple M4 Max (12P+4E), macOS 26.5
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, so not callable from C++ without a wrapper. Arbitrary lengths: mixed radix for 13-smooth lengths, Rader for primes whose N-1 is 7-smooth, large-prime convolution otherwise (BENCHMARKS.md shows FFTW ahead at primes 1,009 and 10,007 by 1.26x and 2.15x). AVX2 and NEON SIMD butterflies. Plan creation is far cheaper than FFTW_MEASURE (e.g. 14,808 ns vs 3,434,000 ns at N=1,024).
caveats: Does not beat FFTW on the single-threaded rows; the only wins are 2-D shapes where go-fft fans rows and columns across goroutines while FFTW, numpy and scipy are single-threaded, so the 2-D comparison is not apples-to-apples. The report states real 1-D transforms lag FFTW by 1.51x to 3.20x. Recent commits are co-authored by an AI assistant and the repo is a few months old (earliest visible commit 2026-06-20). The README attributes part of the scipy gap at small N to Python FFI overhead on the scipy side, so the scipy comparison there is not like-for-like. Listed mainly because it is a benchmark-backed pure-Go FFT that beats the Go incumbent gonum and, at some sizes, scipy.fft.

name: PFT (Partial Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (real-to-complex 1D, FFTW_ESTIMATE), Intel MKL DFTI, FFTW pruned FFT, Goertzel algorithm
workload: Computing only M of the N Fourier coefficients of a real-valued time series (repo defaults N = 4194304, M = 131072; datasets are synthetic random vectors of power-of-two length, Urban Sound, Air condition and Stock series) and comparing against full FFTs from FFTW and MKL, FFTW pruned FFT and Goertzel.
claimed_speedup: Order of magnitude speedup for sufficiently small output sizes without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming FFTW, MKL, pruned FFT and Goertzel (KDD 2021 paper, arXiv 2008.12559). Text seen only as a WebSearch snippet of the paper abstract; it is not on any page I opened and I could not read the paper's tables.
tradeoffs: Approximate, not exact: error is selectable from e-1 to e-7 through precomputed polynomial coefficient files (src/precomputed). The sample code is written for real-valued input and a target output range centered at zero (the file header says a small modification removes this limit). Single precision throughout. Needs Intel MKL and IPP (mkl.h, mkl_dfti.h, ipp.h, ipps.h) plus fftw3.h. Gains only when M is much smaller than N (O(N + M log M) instead of O(N log N)). Research sample code, not a packaged library.
caveats: (1) Paper numbers, CPU model, compiler and flags were not obtainable: arXiv, dl.acm.org, openreview and yongchanpark.github.io (the author PDF) are egress-blocked here, so the headline claim comes from a search snippet only; hardware is null. B rests on the peer-reviewed KDD paper, not on numbers I read. (2) The repo does not carry a timing harness: PFT.cpp prints only the first and last coefficients and the relative L2 error against the MKL full FFT (single precision, DFTI_REAL, not in place) and contains no timers; FFTW.cpp declares clock_t variables but never reads them; src/PrunedFFTW.cpp is the FFTW web-page pseudocode with an unfinished body that does not compile as is. README says MKL code is included in src/ but src/MKL.cpp returns 404, MKL DFTI is inside PFT.cpp. So tier A is impossible from the repo. (3) FFTW baseline in src/FFTW.cpp is a 1,048,576-point float r2c transform with 4 threads planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE (the FFTW_MEASURE alternative is only a comment), a weaker plan than a tuned FFTW; FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h. (4) Last commit date and the README-only nature of the last two commits (last substantive source commit is 'Update PFT.cpp', 2021-06-03) were read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch. (5) A later multidimensional follow-up exists (snudatalab/Auto-MPFT, KDD 2024) and may be a better-documented entry; its repo was not opened.

tradeoffs: Specialised to radial trajectories and CUDA (needs cuFFT, nvcc); gridding code only, not a general uniform FFT or arbitrary-trajectory NUFFT; reproducing the paper needs MATLAB, BART and gpuNUFFT.
caveats: Peer-review tier rests on the Magnetic Resonance in Medicine paper linked in the README (onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mrm.27497), which was not opened. GPU model, compiler and flags are not on the page, so not tier A. The speedups are for the gridding step against gpuNUFFT and IRT, not against FFTW/MKL/KissFFT, and the repository description ('radial Fast Fourier Transform') overstates it as an FFT. Latest commits (Jan 2026) only add zipped MATLAB files; the CUDA code dates from 2018-2021.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/fft?l=cuda (registry route gave no new claim-bearing libraries)

hardware: NVIDIA A100, Tesla T4

name: VkFFT

name: cuSpFFT
baseline: cuFFT (dense 2D real-to-complex) and SpFFT (eth-cscs/SpFFT, CUDA backend)
workload: Single-precision 2D real-to-complex FFT of binary sparse matrices from SuiteSparse (benzene 8,219 x 8,219, density 0.36%), median of 10 runs after one warm-up, CUDA-event timing.
claimed_speedup: benzene: custom binary-sparse pipeline 14.65 ms vs dense cuFFT 23.64 ms ('1.61x faster, 10.7x less memory'); variant using cuFFT inside 9.60 ms ('2.46x faster, 10.4x less memory'); SpFFT about 32 ms ('0.74x speed'). pct20stif (52,329 x 52,329): dense cuFFT plan creation failed and SpFFT ran out of device memory, the sparse variants completed in 2,569 ms and 893 ms.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA Toolkit 12.5.82, CMake 3.20+, C++17, -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 24 GB (compute capability 8.9), driver 555.42.02, Linux x86_64; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Only for binary (all-ones) sparse 2D inputs in CSC form; Bluestein convolution at a smooth length; needs CUDA; the custom variant is less accurate than dense cuFFT (max_abs vs FFTW CPU reference 2.0e-01 vs 4.7e-02 on benzene).
caveats: Course project (CSC 766) with no licence file, so code must not be copied. The README itself reports losses: on sstmodel dense cuFFT is 0.85 ms vs 1.39 ms or 3.62 ms for the sparse variants, and on the power-of-2 delaunay_n14 matrix dense cuFFT takes 7.81 ms vs 68.56 ms and 304.76 ms. SpFFT figure is a single run. The baseline is a dense GPU FFT that the workload is deliberately unfavourable to; not a general FFT speedup.
found_via: GitHub topic pages https://github.com/topics/bluestein and https://github.com/topics/cufft (registry route gave no new claim-bearing libraries)

baseline: FFTW
workload: Multi-dimensional FFTs in single precision (README design notes)
claimed_speedup: README: multi-D double precision 'fairly similar' to FFTW_MEASURE; single precision 'can be significantly faster'; no numbers. Concedes 1D is somewhat slower than FFTW
license: GPL-2.0 (BSD for FFT components per repo page)

name: eFFT (event-based FFT)
baseline: FFTW (fftw_plan_dft_2d, full N x N 2D FFT recomputed after every event or event packet)
workload: Incrementally maintaining the exact 2D FFT of an N x N event-camera frame (N = 16 to 256) as random single events (250 per iteration) or packets of 100 to 5000 events arrive, versus re-running a full FFTW 2D transform after each update.
claimed_speedup: Faster than FFTW for incremental event-stream updates: the README says FFTW3 'served as the benchmark for testing and evaluation' and the repo ships paired Google Benchmark cases (BenchmarkFeedWithEvents vs BenchmarkFeedWithEventsFFTW, BenchmarkFeedWithPackets vs BenchmarkFeedWithPacketsFFTW). No numeric result or speedup ratio is printed on any page I could open.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated (CMake default toolchain). benchmarks target in the root CMakeLists.txt: -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -finline-functions -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math, defines NDEBUG, EIGEN_STACK_ALLOCATION_LIMIT=0 and EFFT_USE_FFTW3; C++17, Eigen >= 3.4, FFTW3 >= 3.3.8, Google Benchmark.
stars_or_usage: 23 stars, 2 forks; PyPI package efft; Docker image; TPAMI 2024 and JORS 2026 papers
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 on top of Eigen; frame size is a compile-time template parameter and must be a power of two (radix-2 tree); keeps a tree of intermediate matrices (about log2 N levels of N x N complex floats) so memory is well above one frame; single-precision complex (float) output; GPLv3 copyleft; Python bindings via nanobind. It is not a drop-in FFT: it only wins when the input changes by a few pixels between transforms (event streams) and needs one initial full transform.
caveats: (1) No benchmark numbers and no CPU model appear in the repo or on any page I could open; the TPAMI paper (doi 10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3422209), the JORS paper (doi 10.5334/jors.642), IEEE Xplore, PubMed and Zenodo are egress-blocked here. Only a WebSearch snippet of the paper abstract was seen (snippet only, not on benchmark_url): exactness PSNR > 55 dB and SSIM > 0.999, event processing time < 1 microsecond for packets of more than 40 events and < 0.5 microsecond for packets of more than 200 events at 128 x 128. That snippet states absolute eFFT times, not a ratio against FFTW. Retier to B if the TPAMI paper confirms the FFTW numbers. (2) The in-repo FFTW baseline is deliberately weak: initializeGroundTruth plans with FFTW_ESTIMATE | FFTW_UNALIGNED | FFTW_NO_SIMD | FFTW_PRESERVE_INPUT, uses double-precision complex while eFFT uses float, recomputes the whole N x N 2D transform for every single event, and getGroundTruthFFT() also copies and casts the whole N x N result to a float Eigen matrix each call while eFFT.getFFT() returns a const reference. Any speedup measured with this harness is inflated relative to a tuned FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE, SIMD, float, no copy). (3) Different problem from a plain FFT: incremental update after sparse input changes versus a from-scratch transform, so the comparison is only meaningful for event-stream use. (4) benchmark.cpp seeds events from std::random_device, so runs are not bit-reproducible. (5) Repo last commit date (2026-09-22) was read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/raultapia/efft (README, benchmarks/efft_benchmark.cpp, root CMakeLists.txt, include/efft.hpp); one WebSearch for the paper abstract

name: FastAndFourier (FAF, JIT-compiled DSP/FFT library)
baseline: KissFFT (and FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE/FFTW_MEASURE, which beat it); also NotoriousFFT
workload: Single-transform C2C latency in double precision at N=8 to 65536, first on macOS x86_64 (2026-02-22) and then Linux aarch64 interleaved FP64 (2026-09-03).
claimed_speedup: x86_64 macOS, 2.3 GHz AVX2: at N=65536 907 us vs KissFFT 3253 us (README: 3.2-3.6x faster; 3.6x derived from page data) but slower at N=64 (4.40 vs 1.11 us), 1024 (75.3 vs 27.1 us) and 16384 (1595 vs 634 us); FFTW3 measure is 3-10x faster than everything. Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz: 53.8 ns vs 95.3 ns at N=8, 0.778 vs 0.850 at N=64, 16.5 vs 21.7 at N=1024, 2238 vs 2735 at N=65536 (slightly slower at N=16: 0.161 vs 0.149).
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -march=native -ffast-math -funroll-loops for the x86 run (README); -O3 -march=native for the aarch64 run; compiler name not stated
hardware: x86_64 2.3 GHz with AVX2 under macOS Ventura and Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz; CPU models not named
tradeoffs: Runtime JIT: transforms are lowered to C and compiled by a system C compiler (falls back to a VM interpreter without one). Sizes up to 2^16, 5-smooth sizes plus codelets and Rader primes, optional Bluestein. Part of a larger DSP library with a scripting language, DWT and CWT.
caveats: The README itself says FFTW3 wins at nearly every size and that small N is not the library's race (about 1 us VM floor); the win over KissFFT on x86 only appears at N=65536 and on aarch64 at four of five sizes. The README flags the x86 table as the old VM-floor result. First-party numbers, CPU models not named. NotoriousFFT, by the same author, is faster than FAF on aarch64 by 1.2-2.15x. Possible duplicate decision with Notorious-FFT.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"faster than kissfft"' returned NotoriousLOB/FastAndFourier README.md

claimed_speedup: On Core i7-870 (SSE4.2, no AVX) FFTS 1.11x-1.88x faster than FFTW across sizes (issue #28); but on i5-3340M (AVX) FFTW is faster for N>=64 and FFTS 30-50% slower

name: GPU_FFT (Raspberry Pi VideoCore IV, hello_fft)
language: C with VideoCore QPU assembly kernels
baseline: FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE) running on the Raspberry Pi 1 ARM CPU
workload: Single-precision complex power-of-two FFTs from 2^8 to 2^22 points: per-transform runtime on the BCM2835 GPU (batch of 1 and 10) against FFTW_MEASURE on the same Pi 1.
claimed_speedup: Doc text: 'ten times more data throughput than is possible on the 700 MHz ARM of the Pi 1'. Per-transform milliseconds, GPU_FFT (batch 1) vs FFTW_MEASURE: 2^8 0.033 vs 0.092; 2^12 0.25 vs 3.0; 2^15 3.5 vs 31; 2^16 7.0 vs 83; 2^20 194 vs 1600; 2^22 786 vs 8800. That is 2.8x, 12x, 8.9x, 11.9x, 8.2x and 11.2x (derived from page data).
hardware: Raspberry Pi 1 (BCM2835, 700 MHz ARM, VideoCore IV GPU, L2 cache enabled)
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars (raspberrypi/userland, archived 2025-08-27); shipped as the hello_fft demo with Raspbian
tradeoffs: Tied to the BCM2835 VideoCore IV 3D hardware and the Raspberry Pi mailbox device (the demo runs under sudo). Single-precision only, power-of-two lengths from 256 to 4,194,304, and a transpose helper for 2D. Per the doc, accuracy is 0.33 to 1.5 ppm rms and FFTW is still one order of magnitude more accurate. C API, so callable from C++.
caveats: First-party table from the library's own doc file (release 3.0, 2015), measured on 2015-era Pi 1 hardware. It compares GPU offload against a CPU FFTW on the same SoC; the FFTW version, precision, build flags and thread count are not stated and no compiler is given. The benchmark code (hello_fft.c) is in the repo but no compiler or flags are recorded. The repo is archived and deprecated by its maintainers. The author's blog page for GPU_FFT was not opened; all numbers come from gpu_fft.txt. The last commit date is for the hello_fft directory.
found_via: Blogs / talks: recalled the well-known Raspberry Pi GPU_FFT blog and library; opened hello_fft/gpu_fft.txt in raspberrypi/userland. The blog page itself was not opened.

name: gpu_fftw
baseline: FFTW3 (running on the Raspberry Pi CPU)
workload: Binary-compatible FFTW3 replacement that offloads power-of-two complex FFTs (log2 N from 8 to 21, float) to the Raspberry Pi GPU (Andrew Holme's GPU_FFT); the README self-test compares ffts per second against CPU fftw3.
claimed_speedup: Self-test output: 'GPU FFTW 7.11652 times faster (11523.3 ffts/sec, 86.781 usec/fft, fftw3: 1619.23 ffts/sec)'. README: 'They can be up to ten times faster than running fftw3 by itself.'
compiler_and_flags: Makefile cross-compiles with RPICC/RPICXX using -march=armv6 -mfloat-abi=hard -mfpu=vfp -O3 -ffast-math (-std=c99, -std=c++11); the README example run does not state the flags used
hardware: Raspberry Pi (model not stated in the README; the Makefile targets armv6, i.e. original Pi class)
tradeoffs: Float only (double only through lossy 'double squashing'), power-of-two sizes 2^8 to 2^21, 1-D complex only (no 2-D/3-D/real), copies arrays to GPU memory, needs root, falls back to FFTW3 otherwise. Early alpha by the author's own words.
caveats: First-party numbers from one sample self-test output; FFT size, Pi model and CPU clock not stated in the README. Single Raspberry Pi generation from 2015 (pre-Pi 4); the GPU_FFT code it relies on belongs to a different author and its license was not checked. Repo is abandoned since January 2015.
found_via: WebSearch 'FFT library faster than FFTW benchmark github' result page for gpu-fftw/gpu_fftw

name: heFFTe (Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale)
baseline: Distributed 3-D FFT libraries fftMPI, SWFFT, AccFFT and P3DFFT (FFTW-MPI-class); FFTW is heFFTe's own CPU backend
workload: Distributed-memory 2-D/3-D complex FFTs (e.g. 1024^3 on Summit nodes) with pencil or slab decomposition; the repo's speed3d benchmark reports heFFTe's own GFlops/s per backend.
claimed_speedup: No competitor numbers on any page I could open. The repo benchmarks (speed3d_c2c/r2c/r2r.cpp, convolution.cpp) time heFFTe with a chosen backend (stock, FFTW, MKL, cuFFT, rocFFT, oneMKL) and print 'Performance: <x> GFlops/s'. Paper claims seen only through WebSearch result summaries, not verified: ICCS 2020 paper 'heFFTe: Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale' reports more than 40x speedup of GPU local kernels over CPU state-of-the-art libraries and over 2x for the whole FFT, about 90% of roofline peak at 1024^3 on Summit; a follow-up reportedly shows heFFTe about 2x faster than fftMPI and SWFFT on GPU and up to 2x faster on one node and 1.65x on two nodes than another distributed library.
hardware: Not stated on any opened page; README acknowledges OLCF resources (Summit per the papers).
stars_or_usage: 59 stars; DOE Exascale Computing Project library (ICL UTK / ORNL)
tradeoffs: MPI-based distributed FFT; local 1-D/2-D kernels are delegated to FFTW, MKL, oneMKL, cuFFT or rocFFT backends, so heFFTe is a communication/decomposition layer and does not beat FFTW on a single core. Needs MPI and a backend library; also Fortran and Python bindings. Optional GPU-aware MPI.
caveats: The numbers that matter (papers at icl.utk.edu, iccs-meeting.org, netlib, Springer, arXiv) were all EGRESS_BLOCKED, so no competitor figures were opened and tier C is a floor: the ICCS 2020 and IPDPS-W 2022 papers are peer-reviewed and a verifier with access may justify tier B (or A if the artifact is public). The headline '40x' compares GPU kernels with CPU kernels, which is hardware not software. The AccFFT GPU runs reportedly failed correctness on Summit. The repo itself contains no head-to-head against other distributed FFT libraries. Docs site (icl-utk-edu.github.io/heffte) is blocked.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/icl-utk-edu/heffte README, benchmarks directory and WebSearch 'heFFTe distributed 3D FFT performance compared FFTW P3DFFT AccFFT Summit speedup paper'

name: JTransforms
baseline: FFTW 3 through the ezFFTW Java wrapper (single-threaded)
workload: Java JMH benchmark: full real-to-complex forward FFT, zero the DC bin, then inverse FFT, for 1-D (1,024 to 10,000,000 elements) and 2-D (1280x720 to 5000x5000) arrays, in the third-party FFTBench repo.
claimed_speedup: Pure-Java JTransforms vs FFTW wrapper: 1-D 10,000,000 elements 3.205 s vs 4.560 s; 1-D 1,024 elements about 1e-4 s vs 0.006 s; 2-D 1280x720 single array 0.058 s multithreaded and 0.137 s single-threaded vs 0.155 s; 2-D 1920x1080 0.125 s / 0.331 s vs 0.360 s. FFTW is faster at 1-D 98,304 to 1,000,000 (e.g. 1,000,000: 0.175 s vs 0.290 s) and at 2-D 1087x1931 single-threaded (0.998 s vs 2.132 s).
compiler_and_flags: Java with JMH; Java version and JVM flags not stated
hardware: Not stated ('observations for my machine')
tradeoffs: Pure Java, multithreaded by default, DFT/DCT/DST/DHT derived from Ooura's FFT package; JVM warm-up and GC apply.
caveats: Mixed result: the benchmark author's own conclusion is that no library wins everywhere. FFTW is reached through a Java wrapper (ezFFTW, written by the benchmark's author), so JNI and copying overhead may favor JTransforms. CPU, Java version and flags are not stated, and each JMH row used only 3 iterations. The JTransforms README itself shows no FFTW numbers.
found_via: WebSearch 'JTransforms github Java FFT benchmark compared to FFTW multithreaded speed' result page for hageldave/FFTBench

name: juFFTe
baseline: FFTW3
workload: 1-D/2-D/3-D complex and real FFTs (double precision in the benchmark) on RISC-V RVV 1.0 CPUs; repo fftbench prints time and MFLOPS and, with WITHFFTW=1, FFTW time.
claimed_speedup: Repo README and docs contain no numbers. The accompanying preprint (arXiv 2608.28076, 'Performance Evaluation of Fast Fourier Transforms on Emerging RISC-V Hardware with Vector Extension Support', seen only as a WebSearch snippet because arxiv.org is blocked) says juFFTe 'can yield average performance improvements of up to a factor of three depending on hardware' over FFTW3 on the SiFive X280, the X100 core of the SpacemiT K3 and the C920v2 core of the Sophon SG2044.
compiler_and_flags: Repo defaults in benchmark/Makefile: gfortran -g -O3 -fopenmp; ifx/ifort -g -O3 -qopt-zmm-usage=high -qopenmp; flang -g -O3 plus -ffast-math -mepi; nvfortran -g -O3. Flags used for the paper runs not seen.
hardware: Not stated in the repo. Per the preprint snippet: SiFive X280, SpacemiT K3 (X100 core), Sophon SG2044 (C920v2 core).
tradeoffs: Modern Fortran (2003) library with an FFTW-compatible C/Fortran API (fftw_plan_dft_1d, fftw_execute_dft, fftw_malloc), a C header (src/juffte.h) and OpenMP; link needs the Fortran runtime (-lgfortran) from C/C++. Only RVV kernels are generated so far (Spiral backend; the SVE and plain Spiral options stop at configure time). Inspired by FFTE; FFTE's own license terms were not checked.
caveats: No result tables in the repo; benchmark/sc.sh listed in its README returns 404. The 3x figure is from a preprint abstract (first-party, unreviewed as far as I could see) that I could not open, and the CPU, compiler and flags in it are unverified, so it is tier C; the benchmark code is public, so a verifier with arXiv access could reach tier A if the paper states compiler and flags. Upstream FFTW has no merged RVV kernels as far as I can tell (search results show only an open RVV pull request and issue), so the win may be vectorized code against scalar FFTW rather than an algorithmic win; check how the paper built FFTW. The repo is young (its ten most recent commits are all from September 2026) and benchmark/README.md lists segmentation faults in some environments (raise stack size).

name: matchedfilter (formerly peak-fft)
language: C core with Python bindings; GPU kernels in Slang (Vulkan/Metal)
baseline: FFTW (inverse transform only, timed through pyFFTW); on GPU rocFFT / MLX FFT inverse-only references
workload: Batched matched filtering (frequency-domain product, inverse FFT and peak scan) of 16 data spectra x 512 templates x 4096-point complex64 transforms, one CPU thread, timed against FFTW doing only the inverse FFT of the same batch.
claimed_speedup: Milliseconds per batch, FFTW inverse-only vs matchedfilter peak-only: Ryzen 9 5950X 63.63 vs 34.27; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 69.54 vs 20.68; Apple M2 252.55 vs 57.84; Core i5-13500H 44.96 vs 35.49. Full-output mode: 52.23, 35.12, 68.75 and 56.24 ms respectively (slower than FFTW on the i5-13500H). Hierarchical screening: 3.95, 3.12, 6.28 and 4.69 ms at fd=0.01. Peak-only is 1.86x, 3.36x, 4.37x and 1.27x faster than FFTW's inverse-only time on those four CPUs (derived from page data). GPU (Radeon 8060S): FFT-only reference 2.58 ms vs peak-only 0.71 ms.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Radeon 8060S); Ryzen 5 5500U; Intel Core i5-13500H; Apple M2; Xeon Platinum 8260 (VM); Xeon E5-2698 v3 (shared, contended node)
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose FFT. It fuses the spectral product, inverse FFT and peak search for matched-filter searches. Peak-only sizes are powers of two from 64 to 1,048,576 on CPU; full-output sizes are powers of two from 1,024 to 4,194,304. Single precision (complex64) only, one CPU thread per filter. The main interface is a pip-installable Python package over a C core, so use from C++ means linking the C code directly. Hierarchical mode needs calibration files and trades a false-dismissal budget for speed. The README calls it alpha software with an unstable API.
caveats: First-party numbers from a very young repo. FFTW and the GPU FFT references time only the inverse transform, so the comparison is between unequal amounts of work (the page says so itself); the gain comes from fusion and peak-only output, not from a faster FFT kernel. Full-output mode is slower than FFTW on the Core i5-13500H and on the Haswell node. The page flags the Haswell node as contended (its full-output and hierarchical rows are indicative only) and the Xeon VM as least stable. FFTW version, planner flags and thread count, and the compile flags used for matchedfilter, are not stated, so tier C. The interactive benchmark pages at ahnitz.github.io are not reachable from this environment; numbers come from the repo's own measurement document and README. The repo was renamed from peak-fft, and its docs mention agent handoffs and plan files, so treat claims as unreviewed.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch restricted to code hosts for 'FFT library README "faster than FFTW" benchmark AVX2 radix-4 split-radix single header' returned ahnitz/peak-fft, which redirects to ahnitz/matchedfilter

name: minfft
baseline: KissFFT (the README also plots PocketFFT and FFTW with SSE2 for reference)
workload: One-dimensional double-precision in-place forward complex DFT of power-of-two size N = 2^1 to 2^20, speed in Mflops (plot docs/speed.svg).
claimed_speedup: README: 'It achieves high performance by simple means' with speed plots against KissFFT and PocketFFT. Values digitised from the plot (derived from page data, approximate): minfft is above KissFFT at every size, roughly 1.4x to 4.8x and about 2x typical (about 8,400 vs 4,700 Mflops at N=2^8, 6,400 vs 3,700 at N=2^16, 1,700 vs 850 at N=2^20). minfft is faster than PocketFFT only up to about N=2^6 and slower than PocketFFT from 2^7 to 2^16; FFTW SSE2 is faster than minfft at every size.
tradeoffs: Power-of-two sizes only; double precision by default (MINFFT_SINGLE for float); scalar C99 code with split-radix kernels, no explicit SIMD; also provides real DFT and DCT/DST types 2-4, multi-dimensional transforms, a Fortran 2003 interface; very small (two source files).
caveats: First-party plot only; no CPU model, compiler or flags, and no benchmark program is documented in the README, so numbers are read off an SVG and approximate. It loses to FFTW (SSE2) at all sizes and to PocketFFT at mid sizes, so the real claim is 'small and faster than KissFFT'.

name: MPSFT (Matrix Pencil Sparse Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (FFTW_ESTIMATE and FFTW_MEASURE plans)
workload: Sparse Fourier transform of an N=2^22 signal with S nonzero frequencies, single core, Google Benchmark, FFTW built from source on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: 'For N=2^22, we are faster than FFTW when S is less than around 1800.' README timings: MPSFT at N=4,194,301 S=64 19.38 ms, S=1024 140.8 ms, S=4096 502.3 ms; FFTW at N=4,194,304 225.3 ms (FFTW_ESTIMATE) and 102.3 ms (FFTW_MEASURE). So S=64 is about 5.3x faster than FFTW_MEASURE (derived from page data) while the README itself notes 'the sparsity has to be around 1000 in order for MPSFT to be faster than FFTW'.
compiler_and_flags: Bazel --config=opt, FFTW built from source (--enable-shared --enable-threads --enable-openmp), Google Benchmark release mode; compiler version not stated
hardware: Not stated (CPU frequency scaling disabled, single core)
tradeoffs: Only useful for signals that are exactly or nearly sparse in frequency; approximate output; depends on FFTW, Eigen and Boost.SIMD.
caveats: Abandoned since 2017. README says 'For now, we will use the GPL license' because of FFTW, but the repo has no LICENSE file, so treat as reference. Hardware and compiler not stated; benchmark sizes differ slightly (N=4,194,301 vs 4,194,304). The win applies only to sparse inputs (S below roughly 1000-1800 of 4 million bins) and README says SFFT1/SFFT2 (other sparse algorithms) are faster at larger S.

name: OFFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.5 (FFTW_ESTIMATE, with and without SIMD) and Intel oneMKL
workload: Complex FFT at powers of two (1024 to 2^24), powers of ten and 30 non-power-of-two lengths (1023 to 16777217); numbers are nanoseconds per n*ln(n), single table per size.
claimed_speedup: Author claim: for arbitrary sizes OFFT is often faster than FFTW, even the SIMD version. From the table, OFFT beats FFTW_ESTIMATE-with-SIMD at 10 of 30 non-power-of-two lengths (e.g. 1025: 6.7 vs 8.0; 4097: 6.0 vs 7.4; 262145: 9.0 vs 11.6; 16777217: 8.7 vs 12.3, i.e. 1.41x derived from page data) and is slower at powers of two (1024: 2.1 vs 0.5) and than MKL.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.2.0 (MSYS2) on Windows; optimization flags not stated
hardware: Intel i5-2450M 2.5 GHz laptop, SSE4 only, Windows 10
tradeoffs: C++11 header-style library for arbitrary-length transforms, no SIMD yet, code-generated kernels, keeps code size small.
caveats: Mixed result that the author's wording overstates: slower than FFTW_ESTIMATE at powers of two and at 19 of 30 non-power-of-two sizes (one tie), and slower than MKL; FFTW_MEASURE was deliberately not used. Old CPU, no SIMD in OFFT, optimization flags not stated, FFTW 3.3.5 Windows binaries. Author says numbers are noisy.

name: pocketfft-tuned (benchmark-driven PocketFFT fork)
baseline: FFTW3 FFTW_ESTIMATE, upstream PocketFFT (ref 32424d2) and KissFFT; the fork is slower than FFTW_MEASURE and KFR
workload: Randomized interleaved Google Benchmark sweep, 90 iterations per scenario, taskset -c 2: 14 mixed 1-D sizes (4096 to 1048576 including primes and near-primes), five 2-D shapes (256x256 to 1024x1024) and four 3-D shapes (64^3 to 128x128x64); c2c, r2c and c2r. Ratio is other implementation CPU ns over tuned fork CPU ns.
claimed_speedup: SIMD build, median ratio (tuned wins/ratios): 1-D c2c 2.40x vs upstream PocketFFT (1258/1260), 1.35x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE (813/1260), 4.63x vs KissFFT (952/990), 3.25x vs meow_fft; 1-D r2c 2.50x and c2r 2.75x vs upstream, 1.45x and 1.44x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE; 2-D c2c 6.43x vs FFTW_ESTIMATE. Slower than FFTW_MEASURE (0.71x for 1-D c2c) and KFR (0.49x). 2-D and 3-D versus upstream PocketFFT are about 1.0x.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the READMEs: benchmarks use CXX/CXXFLAGS from the Makefile environment; FFTW 3.3.10 built from the release tarball; KFR 7 built with clang++ C++20; SIMD and no-SIMD builds
tradeoffs: Header-only C++11 like PocketFFT; the tuning targets hot 1-D paths (large power-of-two c2c terminal stages, fused pass4x4, split8 buffering, measured dispatch for selected mixed radix). Keeps PocketFFT features (float/double/long double, multi-dimensional, DCT/DST, Bluestein).
caveats: First-party benchmark by the fork author. CPU model is not stated; the workstation was not quiet (ASLR on, load average often above idle) and the author calls the numbers a local snapshot. The fork loses to FFTW_MEASURE and KFR on most 1-D cases and to upstream on some 2-D/3-D cases. MKL is not in the harness. Fork changes performance-relevant code, so it is reported here, but the orchestrator may fold it under PocketFFT. Floating-point precision of the runs is not stated in the README.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_repositories query 'pocketfft' (sorted by stars) listed Dimandragon/pocketfft-tuned 'benchmark-driven optimized fork of pocketfft'

name: SFFT3 (3-D FFT built from FFTW 1-D transforms)
baseline: FFTW3 own 3-D routines (FFTW_PATIENT on the Ryzen table, FFTW_MEASURE on the i7 table)
workload: Average time of a forward plus reverse 3-D real FFT from 64^3 to 2100x2100x121 (and 2048x2048x1024), one OpenMP thread per physical core, padding and planning time excluded; SFFT3 uses FFTW's 1-D routines with cache-blocked transposes and a per-thread workspace.
claimed_speedup: 8-core Ryzen 3700X: 512^3 8.428e-2 s vs FFTW3-P 1.009e-1 s (1.20x, derived from page data); 1024^3 7.733e-1 s vs 1.011 s (1.31x, derived); 256^3 1.112e-2 vs 1.213e-2 s; slower at 64^3 (1.821e-4 vs 1.185e-4 s) and 128^3. 4-core i7-6700K vs FFTW_MEASURE: 512^3 0.182 vs 0.196 s (1.08x, derived), 1024^3 1.640 vs 1.705 s (1.04x, derived), slower at 128^3 and 2100x2100x121.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version and optimization flags not stated in the README); i7 run built with CFLAGS=-DSFFT3_L2=256000
hardware: 8-core AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (Ubuntu 24.04.2); 4-core Intel i7-6700K (Ubuntu 22.04.5)
tradeoffs: Not an independent FFT: it calls FFTW3 for every 1-D transform (GPL). Uses a larger workspace than FFTW's 3-D plans (author says timings are not directly comparable). No explicit vectorization, no auto-tuning; L1/L2 sizes are compile-time constants.
caveats: Author calls it an untested proof-of-concept run on two similar machines and expects the results not to generalize; wins are 4-31% on large cubes and it loses at small sizes. Compiler version, flags and FFTW version are not stated.
found_via: GitHub: mcp github search_code query '"vs FFTW" filename:README.md' followed by a 'faster than FFTW' README search surfaced elgw/sfft3

name: SYLT-FFT (fixed-point FFT for Cortex-M4)

name: SFFT library (ETH Zurich optimized sparse FFT, versions 1-3)
baseline: FFTW
workload: Discrete Fourier transform of a signal whose spectrum has only k non-zero frequencies out of n (sparse spectrum), compared in the underlying sFFT work against a full dense FFT such as FFTW; this repository itself contains no benchmark.
claimed_speedup: No numbers anywhere in the repository or its docs. The docs call it a 'high-performance C++ implementation' of sFFT v1, v2 and v3 with SSE kernels. The underlying MIT sFFT algorithm is billed as faster than FFTW for sparse spectra (Hacker News thread 'The faster-than-fast Fourier transform'), but those figures were not opened this session.
tradeoffs: Only helps when the spectrum is sparse; it is not a general dense FFT. README states it is experimental and 'NOT intended to be used as a drop-in replacement for the FFT library of your choice'. Docs say v1 and v2 work only with a few specific input parameters and v3 cannot handle noisy signals. Targets x86 with SSE; Intel IPP is required by default (configure --without-ipp disables it). It calls FFTW internally for its sub-transforms (FFTW plan flags are a plan parameter), so FFTW is a dependency as well as the baseline. GPL-2.0-or-later (strong copyleft).
caveats: Tier D: I found no benchmark numbers in the README, CHANGELOG or doc/*.rst (all read via raw.githubusercontent.com). The speedups presumably live in the ETH master thesis by J. Schumacher (2013, supervised by M. Pueschel) and the MIT sFFT papers; spiral.net, groups.csail.mit.edu and arXiv are egress-blocked, so none were opened. The claim concerns sparse versus dense transforms, so it is valid only for sparse signals. Notability is modest by stars (69) but the sFFT algorithm is widely cited; included as the single tier D for this run. Repository last updated 2015-06-03; its first commit imports 'Official download of version 0.1.0' from spiral.net, so it is not a GitHub fork. Related sparse-FFT repos mpsft and Auto-MPFT are already catalogued. The MIT original code (groups.csail.mit.edu/netmit/sFFT) was not reachable and has no GitHub canonical repo that I opened.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN faster FFT library than FFTW' surfaced the thread 'The faster-than-fast Fourier transform' (item 3480016); the repo came from WebSearch 'sFFT sparse Fourier transform MIT code github faster than FFTW'. The HN thread itself could not be opened (egress-blocked).

name: SpFFT (sparse-input 3D FFT)
baseline: FFTW (dense 3D FFT) and cuFFT (implied; no comparison is published)
workload: No benchmarked workload. Design target: 3D FFT of sparse frequency-domain data with spherical cutoff, as in plane-wave electronic-structure codes, with MPI slab and pencil decomposition and CUDA or ROCm backends.
claimed_speedup: none: no numbers or speedup claim appear in the README, docs/source details.rst, index.rst, examples.rst or tests/programs/benchmark.cpp
stars_or_usage: 56 stars, 16 forks; conda-forge package; README says it was written for computational materials-science codes with spherical cutoff data (lead names SIRIUS, not verified here)
tradeoffs: Not a new FFT kernel: the 1D transforms are done by FFTW, MKL or cuFFT underneath, and the gain comes from skipping z-columns that are all zero in frequency space and exploiting Hermitian symmetry for R2C and C2R. Needs a precomputed list of non-zero columns, sizes best of the form 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d, optional MPI, OpenMP, CUDA 11+ or ROCm 5+; C++17, with C and Fortran interfaces; pre-allocated Grid objects are reused between transforms.
caveats: Tier D: I found no numeric comparison against any recognizable baseline. tests/programs/benchmark.cpp (CLI11 plus rt_graph timing, runs only SpFFT transforms with JSON output) contains no FFTW, cuFFT or dense reference, and docs/source/details.rst and README.md state no speed numbers. Published performance data for SpFFT, if any (for example in the SIRIUS or material-science code papers), is behind egress-blocked hosts (readthedocs, doi.org, arXiv) and was not checked. Notability is limited (56 stars) but the project is a dependency of plane-wave DFT codes per its own description. Last commit date was read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch (latest tag mentioned there: release v1.1.1, 2025-01-19).

name: detria
baseline: CDT (artem-ogre/CDT) and poly2tri; Triangle (CMU) is also in the comparison but is faster on random point sets
workload: Constrained Delaunay triangulation timing (set-up and result retrieval excluded) on Natural Earth country outlines, poly2tri test files, a cocircular fractal, and 1,000 to 1,000,000 random points inside a square; box plots of repeated runs.
claimed_speedup: Medians printed in the per-case SVG result files (images/benchmark/*.svg, embedded in BENCHMARKS.md; detria vs CDT vs Triangle, ms): world land outline (407,072 vertices) 502 vs 1431 vs 441; United States outline 24.4 vs 58.8 vs 27.2; Afghanistan (1,532 vertices) 0.74 vs 2.17 vs 0.87; 10,000-vertex debug2.dat 11.6 vs 28.7 vs 12.5. Tallied over the 23 result files: faster than CDT in 21 of 23 cases (about 1.5x to 3.2x), faster than poly2tri in all 14 cases it supports, faster than Triangle in 16 of 23 (country outlines, city.dat, debug2.dat). Slower than Triangle on random points (1,000,000 points: 1798 vs 946 ms) and the world land outline (502 vs 441 ms), and slower than both Triangle and CDT on the cocircular fractals of depth 6 and 8 (depth 8: 3091 vs 1407 CDT vs 857 Triangle).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17.0.3 (MSVC-like command line), release build with default compiler flags
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Single-header CDT with a C# port; no point insertion after triangulation, no Steiner or refinement (stated non-goal). CDT and poly2tri versions are not stated. Triangle is still faster for generic point sets.
caveats: Mixed result: the library wins against CDT and poly2tri on most inputs, wins against Triangle only on country-outline style inputs, and loses to Triangle on random points and fractals and to CDT on the deep fractals. The A tier rests on 'default compiler flags' of a release build, which is vague. Baseline versions are not stated, the machine is a 2019 desktop on Windows, and neither CDT nor poly2tri is the category's incumbent (CGAL, Boost.Geometry, GEOS are not compared).

name: geo-utils-cpp
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 (spherical_equatorial strategy: bg::within and bg::area); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7
workload: Google Benchmark on seeded random lat/lng data: spherical point-in-polygon (polygons of 10, 100 and 1000 vertices, 1000 query points per iteration) and spherical polygon area (10/100/1000 vertices); native library types are built outside the timed loop.
claimed_speedup: contains (M queries/s, geo-utils-cpp vs Boost.Geometry): 16.2 vs 1.91 at N=10, 2.87 vs 0.234 at N=100, 0.329 vs 0.024 at N=1000 (about 8.5x, 12x and 14x, derived from page data). area (M polygons/s): 69.9 vs 45.0 at N=10, 67.2 vs 36.2 at N=100, 67.7 vs 36.6 at N=1000 (about 1.5-1.9x, derived from page data). distance_between and heading tie Boost.Geometry within noise.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Release, Google Benchmark 1.8.4, Boost 1.90.0
hardware: Apple M1, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, macOS 15.7
tradeoffs: Header-only, no dependencies, lat/lng-native API. Spherical Earth only (mean radius 6371009 m), not WGS84 ellipsoidal; accuracy degrades near the poles and for antipodal pairs. Far smaller feature set than Boost.Geometry (no generic geometry types, no spatial index).
caveats: The contains comparison is not like for like: geo-utils-cpp uses an O(N) ray cast over rhumb-line edges while bg::within with the spherical CS picks a great-circle winding strategy, so the 8-14x gap partly reflects algorithm choice (the docs say so). S2 beats it by a wide margin on contains (18.0 M/s at N=100) and on distance at small N. Single machine (Apple M1, clang) only, no GCC/MSVC or x86 numbers. Young repo (commits visible from May 2026).

name: GeoRepair (geo-repair)
baseline: GEOS 3.14.1 (conda-forge libgeos, MSVC build) makeValid / UnaryUnion
workload: Validation and repair (ST_MakeValid equivalent) of 1,579,030 polygon parts from a production GeoPackage, plus synthetic cases (valid polygons, bowties, collapsed rings, near-collinear, large coordinates, linestrings) of 4 to 10,000 vertices; parallel batch.
claimed_speedup: Real-world dataset (README): validation 2.1 s (1.3 us/poly) vs GEOS 3.0 s (1.9 us/poly), 1.4x; full pass 3.6 s vs 3.0 s (0.83x, GEOS faster). docs/BENCHMARKS.md table: validation 2.47 s vs 3.46 s (1.40x), full pass 4.05 s vs 3.49 s (0.86x). Synthetic: valid polygon 4v 4.8x, invalid bowtie 4v 25x, bowtie 1000v 8.0x, collapsed 1000v 5.5x, zero-length line 45x. GEOS faster on large valid polygons (10000v 0.37x), spaghetti (0.56x) and large coordinates 1e12 (0.08x at 1000v).
compiler_and_flags: Rust release profile: lto=fat, codegen-units=1, mimalloc, Rust edition 2024 (rust-version 1.88); GEOS conda-forge 3.14.1 MSVC, no LTO
hardware: Intel i5-12400F (6C/12T), Windows 10
tradeoffs: Specialised to geometry validation and repair, not a general GEOS replacement. Rayon parallel batch API; Structure strategy mirrors GEOS ST_MakeValid, Arrange strategy is a CDT fallback. Built-in WKB/WKT/batch I/O. Passes the GEOS XML validation suite per README.
caveats: Mixed results: GeoRepair loses on large valid polygons, spaghetti geometry, large coordinates and on the full real-world pass. GeoRepair column is a 12-thread Rayon batch while GEOS is serial per call driven concurrently via Rayon in the same process. README history note: earlier GEOS columns went through a WKT round trip that inflated wins 30-500x; the current harness builds geometry directly. First-party benchmark. Sub-microsecond rows are dispatch noise per the authors.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Rust OR C++ geometry library "faster than GEOS" OR "outperforms GEOS" benchmark'

name: kigumi
baseline: CGAL Polygon_mesh_processing corefinement ('coref.'); also libigl igl::copyleft::cgal::mesh_boolean (CGAL exact), geogram, Manifold, MCUT
workload: Boolean intersection of two triangle meshes, excluding I/O, on four generated mesh pairs (open, open and closed, closed, non-manifold); wall-clock seconds.
claimed_speedup: README table (seconds): Closed: CGAL coref. 27.2 vs kigumi 4.6 sequential (about 5.9x, derived) and 1.1 parallel; libigl (CGAL exact) 39.3. Open: coref. 3.2 vs kigumi 2.4 sequential (about 1.3x, derived) and 0.6 parallel. Open and closed, and non-manifold: CGAL coref. FAILED, kigumi 1.0/0.4 and 0.5/0.1 s. Manifold is faster on closed meshes (1.3 s sequential, 0.2 s parallel) but approximate.
compiler_and_flags: Homebrew Clang 22.1.1, CMake Release build (./run configure uses -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; explicit -O flags not stated); benchmark programs in benches/, driven by tools/run_benches.sh and tools/gen_bench_meshes.sh
hardware: MacBook Pro 14-inch (M4, 2024), 16-core CPU
tradeoffs: Header-only; needs a CGAL-compatible kernel and 2D triangulation (LGPL and GPL-or-commercial CGAL packages), so using it brings CGAL's license terms. Exact predicates and constructions, open/closed/non-manifold meshes, nested regions, per-face data. Inputs must be free of degenerate faces and self-intersections. Based on Barki et al. 2015 with optimizations.
caveats: Mesh sizes, CGAL and libigl versions and the exact meshes are not stated in the README (meshes are generated by a script in the repo), and the build flags are only implicit in CMake Release, so the A tier is borderline. The 'Open' sequential gain over CGAL is only 1.3x. Manifold beats kigumi on the closed case but is approximate. Single machine (Apple M4). MIT code, but the CGAL dependency makes the combined work LGPL/GPL.

name: GeometryOps.jl
baseline: GEOS (through GeoPandas/Shapely in Python and the 'geos' package in R)
workload: kadyb/vector-benchmark: 500,000 synthetic planar points and derived geometries; tasks are buffer, distance between points, intersects, sampling points in a polygon, CRS transform, and GeoPackage load/write; median seconds per task.
claimed_speedup: Median seconds, GeometryOps.jl vs GEOS-backed packages: distance 0.11 vs 5.37 (R geos) and 0.90 (GeoPandas); intersects 0.04 vs 0.08 (R geos) and 0.12 (GeoPandas); sample 0.04 vs 0.90 (GeoPandas); transform 0.08 vs 0.23 (GeoPandas); load 0.36 vs 0.45 (GeoPandas). Not faster: buffer 5.75 vs 4.07 (GeoPandas) and 5.65 (R geos); write 1.38 vs 1.28 (GeoPandas). Derived ratios (derived from page data): distance about 8x vs GeoPandas and 49x vs R geos, intersects 2x vs R geos and 3x vs GeoPandas, sample about 22x vs GeoPandas.
compiler_and_flags: Interpreted/JIT packages (Julia, Python, R); no compiler flags and no package versions are stated in the repo README
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X @ 3.7 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS

caveats: GEOS is measured through wrappers (GeoPandas/Shapely, R 'geos'), so wrapper and marshalling overhead is part of the baseline times; the 5.37 s R geos distance time looks like such an artifact. Buffer and write are not faster. Numbers are one run set from a third-party suite repo (kadyb/vector-benchmark, 23 stars, MIT) with no package versions; the Julia scripts there were added by GeometryOps contributors (commit history shows PR #12 and later Julia commits), so the suite is not fully independent of the library. The suite's detailed report page is on github.io and was not reachable; numbers come from timings.csv and the comparison.png in the repo (the two agree). GeometryOps' own README only points at this suite and says more benchmarks are coming. Julia is outside the 'usable from C++' scope.

name: Pkd-tree (parallel kd-tree with batch updates)
baseline: CGAL kd-tree (Spatial_searching) and Boost.Geometry R-tree (also BHL-tree and Log-tree)
workload: Parallel kd-tree construction, batch insertion and deletion, k-nearest-neighbor, range query and range count on large point sets, compared with CGAL, Boost's sequential R-tree and other parallel kd-tree baselines (SIGMOD 2025 paper).
claimed_speedup: Paper text seen only as a search-result summary: 'orders of magnitude faster' than CGAL and BHL-tree on batch updates because those rebuild the whole tree after every update; 17.4-40.7x faster insertions and 3.27-21.7x faster deletions than the fastest baseline (Log-tree); 59.3x self-relative speedup for batch insertion and 52.4x for deletion on 96 cores; also compared against Boost's sequential R-tree for construction, kNN and range report (ratios not seen).
hardware: 96 cores (CPU model not seen)
tradeoffs: Built on ParlayLib (git submodule) for shared-memory parallelism, so wins need many cores; low-dimensional point sets (kNN, range, count queries), not general geometry or polygons. The repo README says Pkd-tree is now integrated into PSI-Lib (github.com/ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib, MIT, PPoPP 2026 'Parallel Dynamic Spatial Indexes') which adds orth-trees and space-filling-curve indexes.
caveats: The SIGMOD 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3709712, arXiv 2411.09275) could not be opened in this session (arxiv.org, dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu and mirrors blocked), so every number comes from a WebSearch summary of the paper and was not checked against the page. The headline wins over CGAL are for batch updates where CGAL rebuilds the tree, not for static construction or single queries; the largest ratios are against Log-tree, which is not a named incumbent. The opened repo README confirms that a CGAL baseline can be built with -DCGAL=ON (a 'cgal' binary takes the same arguments) and a ParGeo branch exists, but gives no numbers, compiler, flags or CPU.
found_via: WebSearch: '"Parallel kd-tree with Batch Updates" Men Shen Gu Sun Pkd-tree compared CGAL Boost R-tree speedup'; repo page github.com/ucrparlay/Pkd-tree; lead from github.com/topics (SpaceTreeLib, spatial-index C++ topic page)

name: PSI-Lib / SpaceTreeLib (P-Orth tree, SPaC-tree; also contains the Pkd-tree)
baseline: Boost.Geometry bgi::rtree (quadratic, sequential); the repo also benchmarks CPAM and Zd-tree, and has a CGAL kd-tree harness (tests/cgal.cpp)
workload: Real-world point sets GeoLife (3-D), Cosmo50 (3-D) and OSM (2-D): batch build/insert/delete, k-NN (k=1,10,100) and range count/report, parallel PSI trees against a sequential Boost R-tree (script/data/real_world/real_world.csv, from the PPoPP '26 paper's scripts).
claimed_speedup: All ratios derived from page data (real_world.csv, 'tot' column, seconds presumably). Build/insert whole set (ratio 1.0): Cosmo50 Boost 414.38 vs P-Orth (OrthTree) 1.899 and SPaC-Z (PTree-Z) 0.8365 (about 218x and 495x); OSM Boost 666.0 vs OrthTree 4.960 and PTree-Z 2.122 (about 134x and 314x); GeoLife Boost 0.2132 vs OrthTree 0.00639 and PTree-H 0.00150 (about 33x and 142x). Batches of 0.01% of n deleted: Cosmo50 Boost 1482.7 vs OrthTree 17.85 and PTree-Z 8.463 (about 83x and 175x); OSM 264.2 vs 14.93 and 7.368 (about 18x and 36x). Range report (RRL): Cosmo50 Boost 19.25 vs OrthTree 1.738, OSM 8.347 vs 1.128, GeoLife 7.829 vs 0.4466 (about 7-18x). Not uniformly faster: GeoLife batch insert/delete at 0.01% is about equal (Boost 0.0871 vs OrthTree 0.0790), and k=10 in-distribution uniform k-NN is on par for kd/orth trees (Cosmo50 Boost 0.276 vs OrthTree 0.244) and slower for SPaC trees (Cosmo50 PTree-H 1.869, PTree-Z 11.55). Paper (PPoPP '26, per search snippet) says the P-Orth and SPaC trees beat existing parallel kd-trees and orth-trees on batch updates with competitive queries.
compiler_and_flags: Clang >= 19 or g++ >= 14 (CMakeLists check); Release -O3; docs/ARTIFACT_EVALUATION.md says the paper numbers were measured with -march=native -mcx16 (PSI_NATIVE_ARCH=ON). The compiler used for the paper runs is not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated in the repo; artifact doc asks for at least 512 GB RAM and preferably more than 128 cores; run scripts use numactl -i all.
stars_or_usage: 10 stars, 734 commits; PPoPP 2026 (doi 10.1145/3774934.3786412) and SIGMOD 2025 artifacts; successor repo of ucrparlay/Pkd-tree
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 on ParlayLib (submodule) and libmorton; needs many cores to win; points only (2-D to 16-D data generator), kd/orth/SPaC trees chosen per update-heavy vs query-heavy use. SPaC trees are built on a permanent fork of CPAM; vendored Hilbert code carries a Rice University notice requirement (THIRD_PARTY.md). A migration table from bgi::rtree is in docs/MANUAL.md. README notes the code was recently refactored with AI help and gives commit af67b82 for the original design.
caveats: Boost baseline is a single-threaded bgi::rtree, PSI is parallel, so the ratios mostly measure parallelism and batch updates; Boost is competitive or better on small data (GeoLife) and on some k-NN rows. The column meaning of 'tot' is inferred from script/merge_real_world.py. The paper itself (dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu, arXiv 2601.05347) was blocked, so peer review is confirmed only from the README citation and a search snippet; CPU model missing keeps this at B, not A. The other CSVs (summary.csv, knn_3.csv) compare PSI's own trees (solver 'cpam' there is PSI's SPaC build on the CPAM fork, not an external baseline) and contain no CGAL or Zd-tree rows. Fold question: the kd_tree.h tree is the Pkd-tree and the Pkd-tree repo is archived with a pointer to this repo, so Pkd-tree should be treated as a component of PSI-Lib (CGAL and Boost numbers for it are already in the Pkd-tree record); keep this record for P-Orth/SPaC and the Boost R-tree evidence, link both, and prefer this URL as the canonical repo.

caveats: The baseline is GeoPandas, a Python wrapper over GEOS, so much of the gain is probably multi-threading and removing per-geometry Python overhead rather than a faster geometry algorithm; I did not verify what geometry engine Arctern's C++ core uses. Dataset, hardware, compiler and flags are not stated, and per-operation numbers exist only in an image. No comparison with GEOS called directly from C++. Dormant since 2020.

Shapely STRtree row uses numpy points and returns. Rust compiler flags not stated. Query count is only 500. Workload is point data, not extended geometries.

name: geo-index (packed immutable R-tree and k-d tree)
baseline: rstar (georust dynamic R-tree, bulk_load)
workload: Criterion benchmark on one bounding-box dataset (benches/bounds.raw): bulk construction of an R-tree from boxes, and a bounding-box search, geo-index (Hilbert-sorted packed tree) vs rstar::RTree::bulk_load.
claimed_speedup: README: construction is ~2x faster than rstar and search is ~33% faster. Numbers: construction geo-index hilbert 80.891 ms vs rstar bulk 159.34 ms; STRTree 116.52 ms; search 116.41 us (flatbush-style) vs rstar 153.62 us; with the rayon feature STRTree construction drops to 72.099 ms.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench rtree (Criterion); rustc version, profile and flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 200 stars; used under the hood in geoarrow-rs
tradeoffs: Trees are immutable (no insert or delete after build), fully packed single-buffer layout with ABI-stable memory shared with Python and the flatbush/kdbush JavaScript libraries. Hilbert and STR sort methods. Also ships a k-d tree.
caveats: Author says it is just one benchmark and recommends benchmarking on your own data. Hardware, dataset size and compiler settings are not stated. Comparing a static packed index against a dynamic R-tree's bulk load is not like-for-like on features (rstar supports updates). Search is a single fixed bounding-box query on one dataset (the bench labels geo-index runs 'flatbush' because the tree is a Rust port of the flatbush packed Hilbert R-tree), so the 33% figure rests on one query.

name: ikd-Tree (incremental k-d tree)

claimed_speedup: README: ikd-Tree 'incrementally updates a k-d tree with new coming points only, leading to much lower computation time than existing static k-d trees' (no numbers on the page). Paper numbers (arXiv 2102.10808, seen only in WebSearch snippets because arxiv.org is blocked): about 1.6 ms nearly constant update time against more than 10 ms and growing for PCL's static k-d tree on SLAM data; overall about 4% of the computation time of state-of-the-art static implementations; against nanoflann, insertion is often slightly faster for nanoflann but with huge spikes on large maps, while nanoflann's k-NN is slightly slower than ikd-Tree's.

stars_or_usage: 810 stars, 219 forks; used inside FAST-LIO2 (IEEE T-RO 2022)
tradeoffs: GPLv2 (README: contact the authors for commercial use). Dynamic deletion is lazy: points are flagged deleted and removed during a background rebuild, so memory and k-NN cost depend on rebuild timing; threaded rebuild (-pthread). Supports box delete, box/radius search and on-tree downsampling; written for 3-D LiDAR points and later templated (README thanks a contributor for templating it). Demo build requires PCL.
caveats: The repo has a speed demo (examples/ikd_Tree_demo.cpp) that times only ikd-Tree operations; it contains no baseline code, no results and no hardware, so tier C (first-party preprint, unreviewed, could not be opened). FAST-LIO2 (peer-reviewed) uses ikd-Tree but I could not open it. Baselines are not on the category list (PCL kd-tree, nanoflann); the gap against PCL is against a tree that is rebuilt each scan, so it measures incremental vs rebuild. Last commit March 2022; README says GPLv2 without 'or later', so SPDX GPL-2.0-only is an assumption.

ERational vs EPECK: segment intersection 0.55x (0.19-1.8), regularized union of triangles 0.23x (0.20-0.59), arrangement point-location query 0.46x (0.32-0.84), segment search count in Rectangle 0.68x, nearest neighbor query 0.82x. int vs EPICK: segment search count in Triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x, count in Rectangle 0.51x, convex hull 0.51x. CGAL is faster on Delaunay triangulation (pgl 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK, 1.7x slower int/EPICK), triangulation point location, Minkowski sum and kd-tree build. Overall ERational/EPECK spans CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; int/EPICK spans CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++23 -O2 -DNDEBUG, CGAL 6.1.2
hardware: Two machines, one run each; CPU models not stated in doc/cgal.md
tradeoffs: Plane-only (2D) library; no higher dimensions, curved geometry, straight skeletons/offsets, alpha shapes or file formats. Header-only, needs C++20 or newer (tested GCC 13, Clang 18, MSVC). Fixed short list of number types, no filtered-kernel layer.
caveats: First-party comparison with partial methodology (CPU model not stated), so tier C. The README itself says pgl is tuned against this benchmark. Mixed result: CGAL wins Delaunay triangulation, convex hull (ERational), Minkowski sum and some builds. Some rows favor pgl by construction (CGAL Kd_tree has no triangle query, so the benchmark wrote one). Ratios are averaged over two machines. Only a small number of the rows are clear pgl wins; do not read it as a blanket CGAL replacement.

name: qdgeo
baseline: GEOS 3.13.1 (via Shapely 2.1.2): union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and buffer
workload: 26 boolean/buffer workloads over a 4,040-parcel, 135,080-coordinate public county parcel dataset (GeoMoose demo data); each figure is median of three suite runs of 11 repeats.
claimed_speedup: README: full-dataset parcel union is 3.1x native GEOS (qdgeo wasm 160 ms, qdgeo native 130 ms vs GEOS 426 ms for 4,040 parcels; 1,000 parcels 20.3 / 16.8 ms vs 65.7 ms). Geometric mean over the 26 workloads: GEOS native 1.5x slower than qdgeo wasm (range across runs 1.36-1.62). Buffer of 100 parcels +2 m: 1.30 ms vs GEOS 4.54 ms. GEOS is faster on a single 19,208-coordinate parcel buffer (8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe (shipped build keeps safety checks); WASM build run in Node 22+
hardware: One idle machine; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Only five operations (four booleans and rounded buffer). Rejects invalid geometry instead of repairing it, and valid input can occasionally fail (4 of 3,946 cluster unions) because it declines to snap coordinates. WASM artifact 135 KB raw, 50.8 KB gzipped, no C or C++ dependency; Zig native build has a C-compatible ABI.
caveats: Application-level comparison: the README admits boundaries are not equal. GEOS runs on already-built geometry objects via shapely.union_all (no parse/encode) while qdgeo rows include WKB codec cost, which favors GEOS; but GEOS is native and qdgeo also reports a native column. The README says to treat gaps under 20% as unresolved. GEOS is faster on very large single polygons. Project is days old. Not a general GEOS replacement. CPU model missing so tier C.

name: EigenRand
baseline: C++ <random> distributions (std::normal_distribution, std::uniform_real_distribution, std::uniform_int_distribution, etc.) and Eigen::DenseBase::Random

claimed_speedup: README: '5~10 times faster than non-vectorized functions' and 'You can get 5~10 times speed by just replacing old Eigen's Random or unvectorizable c++11 random number generators with EigenRand'. Ubuntu/gcc 7.5/AVX2 chart (values read off the bar chart, approximate): normal(0,1) about 8x, uniformReal about 22x, uniformInt(0..63) about 10x, discrete about 32x, binomial(20,0.5) about 24x, but only about 1.6-1.7x for chiSquared, gamma(10.5,1) and uniformInt(0..100k).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.5.0 on Ubuntu 18.04; MSVC 19.29.30147 on Windows 2019; clang 13.1.6 on macOS 12.2.1; Eigen 3.4.0; CMake Release flags -O3 (gcc/clang) and -O2 -Oi -Gy (MSVC)

compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K (Kaby Lake, 4.51 GHz measured); second machine Intel Core i5-8250U laptop

name: ra_prng (ra_core singleblock)
baseline: xoshiro256** (also Philox4x32-10, ChaCha20 and /dev/urandom)
workload: Wall-clock generation of batches of up to 255 words (K=255) and single-word reinitialise-per-call use (K=1), plus long streams, comparing the array-permutation generator ra_core_singleblock/orbit against xoshiro256** and Philox4x32-10 with the code inlined the same way.
claimed_speedup: README table (2026-09-12): ra_core_singleblock K=255 real throughput 20018.1 MB/s vs Xoshiro256** K=255 2937.2 MB/s and Philox4x32-10 K=255 1007.9 MB/s ('~19.9x faster than Philox and ~6.8x faster than Xoshiro256**'); at K=1, 307.3 MB/s vs xoshiro 544.8 MB/s, i.e. slower.

Statistical testing is thin (PractRand clean to 8 GB for K=1/K=255, to 128 GB for ra_prng2; BigCrush for ra_prng2). workload: Criterion benchmark that generates and accumulates batches of u64x8 values (64 u64 values per iteration according to the page's Gelem/s figures) with scalar versus portable-SIMD and AVX-512 vectorised generators.
claimed_speedup: Scalar rand Xoshiro256+ 33.10 ns per batch (1.93 Gelem/s) versus portable Xoshiro256+X8 7.51 ns (8.52 Gelem/s) and AVX-512 specific Xoshiro256+X8 7.08 ns (9.04 Gelem/s): about 4.4x and 4.7x (derived from page data). The author's simpler 'frand' X8 generator runs 2.53 ns per batch, about 13x the scalar Xoshiro256+ (derived from page data). README text: vectorised PRNGs 'may perform anywhere from 4-6 times faster'.

tradeoffs: Rust crate (not callable from C++ without FFI work); the 8-lane generators produce eight independent streams per call, so the sequence differs from the scalar generator; lane jumps are not implemented (TODO in README); AVX-512 specific paths need avx512f and avx512dq, and the portable module needs nightly Rust.
caveats: The speedup compares the same algorithm scalar versus lane-parallel, so it measures vectorisation, not a better algorithm. Benchmarks keep the work observable by accumulating batches, which favours wide registers. The 'frand' generator is the author's own and the README says he is no expert in statistical testing; the latest commit is titled 'fix frand implementation (#34)', so frand numbers deserve a re-check. name: VMT19937 (V-family and X-family vectorized Mersenne Twister)
baseline: std::mt19937_64 (the 'STL-MT19937-64' rows); also the original reference MT19937 / SFMT19937 and Intel MKL MT/SFMT
workload: Throughput in million samples/s of 32-bit (MT19937, SFMT19937) and 64-bit (MT19937-64) random numbers, about 1.6e10 numbers per CPU (30 runs of 8.19e6 samples), in scalar (one value per call) and vectorial (block of 10,240) query modes, on five CPU targets (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE256).
claimed_speedup: README table, M samples/s, vectorial mode: V-MT19937-64 2865 (AVX-512) / 1161 (AVX2) vs STL-MT19937-64 590 / 317 (about 4.9x and 3.7x, derived from page data); V-MT19937 2392 (AVX2) vs ORIG-MT19937 259 (about 9.2x, derived from page data); V-SFMT19937 10943 (AVX-512) vs ORIG-SFMT19937 4445 (about 2.5x, derived from page data). Scalar mode: X-MT19937-64 1095 (AVX-512) vs STL 590 (about 1.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16 per doc/main.tex; Makefile default is -O3 -std=c++20 with -march=native on x86 (-march=armv8-a+simd on NEON, -march=armv8-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=256 on SVE); the bench harness is perf.exe built by the repo Makefile.
hardware: Intel Celeron J4125 2.0 GHz (SSE4.2), Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (AVX2), Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C 2.9 GHz (AVX-512), Neoverse-N1 2.5 GHz (NEON), Neoverse-V1 2.6 GHz (SVE256) (from doc/main.tex).
tradeoffs: The V-family changes the output sequence: it interleaves several MT19937 states de-phased by polynomial jump-ahead, and the sequence depends on the chosen register width (VRegBitLen). The X-family is bit-identical to the original MT19937/MT19937-64/SFMT sequences. Needs jump-polynomial data files (dat/poly) for the V-family, C++20, and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON/SVE hardware for the large gains. Large block-fill API (block of 16 or state-size blocks) is where the speedup is.
caveats: Big speedups are in vectorial (block fill) mode; scalar single-value V-MT19937 is only about 1.7-2.1x the original reference. Intel MKL-MT is faster than V-MT19937 at AVX-512 vectorial (6479 vs 5742 M/s). The STL row exists only in the MT19937-64 table, so 32-bit std::mt19937 is not measured directly (the ORIG-MT19937 reference is the baseline there); on SVE256 STL-MT19937-64 (573) beats V-MT19937-64 scalar (513). Which standard library built the STL rows is not stated. First-party results from a single author; paper arXiv 2309.16682 could not be opened (egress blocked). CPU models and 'GCC 16' were read from the LaTeX source doc/main.tex, not the README. All ratios are derived from page data.

baseline: Go math/rand (rand.NewSource Int63 source, and rand.New(source).ExpFloat64())
workload: go test -bench: nanoseconds per call of a raw Uint64 from each source versus rand.NewSource(...).Int63, and per rand.New(source).ExpFloat64() call for the wrapped variants.
claimed_speedup: Raw source ns/op: math/rand BenchmarkRandSource 4.93 versus XorShift128Plus 2.42, XorShift1024Star 2.40, Xoroshiro128Plus 2.66, Xoroshiro256PlusPlus 3.86, Xoroshiro256StarStar 3.93, SplitMix64 1.61. Wrapped in rand.Rand (ExpFloat64): BenchmarkRand 10.2 versus XorShift128Plus 8.42, Xoroshiro128Plus 8.10, SplitMix64 8.66. About 2.0x faster raw for XorShift128Plus and 3.1x for SplitMix64, but only 1.2x once wrapped in rand.Rand (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.14, go test -bench=. with default flags; benchmark code is xorshift_test.go in the repo (includes the math/rand baseline)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3840QM, Fedora 31, Linux 5.6.9
tradeoffs: Generators are not concurrency-safe (README says to wrap with a monitor goroutine). Generators with state larger than 64 bits are seeded via SplitMix64 as Vigna suggests. Implements Vigna's generators, so it carries their known linearity weaknesses in low bits for the + scramblers.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. Numbers are from 2020 on a 2012-era laptop CPU with Go 1.14, run by the repo author. The baseline is Go's default math/rand source, not a C++ standard facility. The wrapped rows call ExpFloat64 on both sides, so most of the raw gain is hidden by the distribution code. Go's standard library has since added math/rand/v2 (PCG, ChaCha8), so the gap against current Go is likely smaller (background knowledge, not tested).

name: FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers)
baseline: std::shuffle (same underlying PRNG), plus OpenBSD-style and Java-style bounded-integer generation
workload: Random shuffles of arrays of 5 to 10^9 elements, ns per element, with 32-bit and 64-bit random words, comparing Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded-integer method against OpenBSD-like, Java-like, floating-point and std::shuffle approaches.
claimed_speedup: README sample output (arrays of 1000 elements, ns per element): nearly divisionless 1.88 (32-bit) and 1.86 (64-bit) vs std::shuffle 18.66 and 15.28, vs OpenBSD-like 5.40 and 14.36, vs Java-like 3.08 and 7.96 (about 10x and 8x faster than std::shuffle, derived from page data); the README notes 'the exact numbers will vary'.
compiler_and_flags: g++ or clang++ with -std=c++11 -O3 (from cpp/Makefile)
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; technique adopted by libstdc++ std::uniform_int_distribution, Abseil, Swift, Go, Julia, Zig, NumPy per README
tradeoffs: Needs 128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t) for 64-bit words; the buffered/precomputed variants trade memory for speed; unbiased, nearly divisionless rejection method.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (D. Lemire, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval', ACM TOMACS 29(1), 2019) with an RCR artifact, but the paper itself could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked); the CPU model is not stated in the README and the sample numbers are illustrative. libstdc++ has since adopted the same technique, so std::shuffle in current GCC is much closer to this result than the README sample suggests. Related repo lemire/cpp_batched_random is already catalogued.

name: MELG-64 (MELG19937-64)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference C code (algorithmically std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 10^9 64-bit unsigned integers with MELG19937-64, MT19937-64, MT19937-64 (ID3), SFMT19937-64 without SIMD and SFMT19937-64 with SIMD.
claimed_speedup: README table: MELG19937-64 4.2123 s (Intel) / 6.2920 s (AMD) vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s / 6.6490 s (about 1.21x and 1.06x faster, derived from page data); SFMT19937-64 with SIMD is faster at 1.8457 s / 2.8806 s. The paper's main claim is maximal equidistribution (Delta 0 vs 7820 for MT19937-64) at MT-like speed.
compiler_and_flags: Linux gcc -O3
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3.40GHz) and AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (2.70 GHz)
tradeoffs: Plain C, 312-word state like MT19937-64; jump-ahead for disjoint streams; recommends using most significant bits; no SIMD path.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) but the timing harness is not in the repo (the C file's main does not time) and the baseline is the reference MT19937-64 C code, not std::mt19937_64; the speedup over MT is modest (6-21%) and SFMT with SIMD beats MELG. Licensing is inconsistent: LICENSE.md is MIT (2021) while the source file header says free for personal, academic or non-commercial use and to contact the author for commercial use, hence usability mixed. name: Romu family PRNGs (RomuDuoJr, RomuTrio, RomuQuad; C++ code and benchmark in t-mat gist)
baseline: PCG32 and xoroshiro128+ (same table also lists Wyrand, Shioi128, Sfc64, Stc64 and an Mmix control)
workload: Synthetic loop (as extracted from the gist): 1024 tests of 2,097,152 loop iterations each, five random values consumed and combined with arithmetic per iteration; throughput reported in GiB/s of generated random bits.
claimed_speedup: GCC 11.2.0 on Ubuntu: RomuDuoJr 11.40 GiB/s, RomuQuad 9.68, RomuTrio 9.29, RomuDuo 8.67 (64-bit outputs) versus Xoroshiro128p 8.02 GiB/s and Pcg32 3.71 GiB/s (32-bit outputs); Wyrand 8.85, Shioi128 10.15, Sfc64 9.22, Stc64 11.09, Mmix control 7.22. RomuDuoJr is about 1.42x Xoroshiro128p (derived from page data: 11.40/8.02).
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -fno-unroll-loops -fno-move-loop-invariants, GCC 11.2.0 on Ubuntu; an MSVC 19.32.31329 (x86) table is also in the gist, flags not extracted
tradeoffs: Romu is a non-linear generator: the period is seed dependent and probabilistic (the hasenbanck/romu README quotes the author's formula for the chance of a too-short cycle), there is no jump-ahead or stream support, and the rhet_RNG README notes the first 12 to 18 outputs of chaotic generators are low quality until warmed up. Not cryptographic.
caveats: Independent but casual single-author benchmark: code, compiler and flags are public, but no CPU model is stated, so it falls short of tier A. Pcg32 returns 32 bits per call while the Romu variants return 64, so GiB/s mixes output widths. No std::mt19937 row. The gist carries no license of its own: the Romu header credits Mark A. Overton (license not confirmed, romu-random.org and the paper arXiv 2002.11331 are unreachable here), the Wyrand code is marked Unlicense and the xoroshiro code credits Blackman and Vigna, so treat as reference. Last gist activity 2022-11-24. Related, not used for the tier: Almightygir/rhet_RNG (https://github.com/Almightygir/rhet_RNG) reproduces a 47 PRNG by 9 console 'Battle Royale' in which Romu2jr won, but the benchmark code is private and results are chart images only.

name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers, SFMT19937-64 (with SIMD) vs MT19937-64, measured by a third party (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) in the README of sharase/melg-64.
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s per 1e9 numbers (about 2.8x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s (about 2.3x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD: 4.2654 s and 5.6123 s (about 1.2x on both, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the melg-64 README)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; widely used reference generator (also dSFMT for doubles in the same org)
tradeoffs: Produces a different sequence from MT19937, so it is not a drop-in for std::mt19937 output. Designed for 32-bit output; for 64-bit output the high-dimensional equidistribution is worse (Harase's table gives Delta=14095 vs 0 for MELG), and dSFMT is the variant meant for doubles. 128-bit SIMD blocks with SSE2, AVX2/AVX512 (added in 1.5.2), NEON (1.5.3) and Altivec backends; README warns big-endian and Altivec are not tested. C API with the state in a struct.
caveats: The SFMT repo README has no numbers; the authors' 'about twice as fast as MT19937' claim and the MCQMC 2006 paper live on pages that could not be opened (egress blocked), so this entry rests on a third-party table from the melg-64 README, measured on 2012-era CPUs with an older gcc. The baseline is the original mt19937-64.c, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64. I did not verify that the timing harness is in the melg-64 repo.

name: AVX512-VAES2-PRNG (AVX-512/VAES/GFNI 8-way hybrid PRNG, proof of concept)
baseline: Mersenne Twister (mt19937), PCG32 / XorShift128+, ChaCha8 and ChaCha20 AVX-512 (rows in the README table)
workload: Cycles per byte of bulk output on an AMD EPYC machine with AVX-512, VAES and GFNI, generating 64-byte outputs from an 8-way pipeline with non-temporal stores.
claimed_speedup: This implementation 0.0932 cpb (5.964 cycles per 64-byte output; best about 0.093) versus table rows ChaCha8 AVX-512 about 0.08-0.18 cpb, VAES about 0.16-0.20, ChaCha20 about 0.35-0.50, PCG32/XorShift128+ about 0.60-1.00, mt19937 about 4.00-6.00 cpb: roughly 43-64x versus mt19937 and 6-11x versus PCG32/XorShift128+ (derived from page data).
hardware: AMD EPYC (model not stated) with AVX-512, VAES and GFNI, shared server environment
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 plus VAES and GFNI (recent Intel server or AMD Zen 4+ cores); outputs 64 bytes at a time; the author states it is not proven as a CSPRNG; the code is a single header.
caveats: Baseline rows are given as approximate ranges and are not shown as measured in the same run, no benchmark source or compiler flags are stated, and the more-than-50x gap versus mt19937 is implausible without flags, so the tier is capped at C. Statistical testing is thin: a SmallCrush-equivalent plus about 0.96 GiB of PractRand, and the author invites cryptanalysis and bare-metal benchmark contributions. Keep as a flagged proof-of-concept.

name: cauldron random.h (ziggurat normal distribution)
baseline: std::normal_distribution (driven by std::minstd_rand in the benchmark's cpp11random entry)
workload: Generating 1,000,000 standard-normal float or double samples per trial (minimum over 10 trials) in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark, camel-cdr's 128-block ziggurat with a single condensed lookup table and an LCG as the uniform source versus the benchmark's other implementations.
claimed_speedup: Issue #3 in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark (author camel-cdr), ns per sample, float: ziggurat_new 4.018, cpp11random (std::normal_distribution) 8.852, existing ziggurat 7.289, marsagliapolar 6.133, inverse 6.017, boxmuller 7.484; double: ziggurat_new 4.081, cpp11random 17.009, existing ziggurat 7.817, marsagliapolar 8.711, inverse 7.222, boxmuller 16.546. Derived from page data: 2.2x faster than std::normal_distribution for float and 4.2x for double; 1.8x and 1.9x faster than the benchmark's existing ziggurat. The issue says its implementation is 60% faster than the existing ziggurat.
tradeoffs: Single-file C header (usable from C++) with the ziggurat entry points dist_normalf_zig and dist_normal_zig that need an init call and a lookup table (128 entries, float or double) and a caller-supplied RNG function; the slow path uses log and exp. The library also offers a lower-accuracy dist_normalf_fast that was not part of this evidence. Output quality of the issue's code was not verified here (the benchmark harness has a correctness check, but the issue does not report its result).
caveats: First-party claim in a GitHub issue comment with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier C. The std::normal_distribution baseline is driven by std::minstd_rand, not std::mt19937, and the standard library implementation is not stated; the ziggurat uses a cheap LCG, so the gap partly reflects RNG cost (the benchmark's null entry is about 1.05 ns). The code in the issue is the author's proposed template, not literally the current cauldron function: random.h's dist_normal(f)_zig is described as based on Doorki's implementation with the same one-table idea and later changes, so the link is by author and design, not identical code. The double version builds a 64-bit value from two 32-bit LCG outputs per the issue. The cauldron repo has tools/random/bench.c (dist_normal versus dist_normal_zig, PRNGs) but publishes no results. Issue dated 2020-12-19; last repo commit 2025-02-01. The lead's '4.0 ns versus 7.3-7.8 ns' compares against the benchmark's existing ziggurat, while the std::normal_distribution figures are 8.9 ns and 17.0 ns.

baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::minstd_rand, std::default_random_engine and C rand())
workload: Quick Bench runs of raw engine next() throughput, bounded integers and bounded floats comparing the library's engines (PCG32, Xoshiro256SS, RomuDuoJr, QuarkBurst64, Konadare192, SmallFast*) against standard-library generators.
claimed_speedup: README: 'All of the included engines substantially outperform the standard-library generators in this benchmark.' Engine-throughput chart (CPU time / no-op time, lower is faster; values read off the bar chart, approximate): std::mt19937 about 13,000; PCG32 about 5,000; Xoshiro256SS about 4,000; QuarkBurst64 and RomuDuoJr about 2,500 (roughly 5x faster than std::mt19937, derived from chart).

The baseline is std::mt19937 directly, but the stronger baselines (PCG, xoshiro) are the same algorithms the library wraps.
