claimed_speedup: rnorm(1e4) median 654.7 us vs dqrnorm 85.9 us (7.6x, derived from page data); sample.int(1e7, 1e5, replace=TRUE) 7.07 ms vs dqsample.int 296.86 us (24x, derived); sample.int(1e7, 1e5) without replacement 42.8 ms vs dqsample.int 679.1 us (63x, derived).
tradeoffs: The RNG and distribution code is a C++ header-only library usable from C++ (xoshiro.h is CC0, pcg_* headers are Apache-2.0 or MIT per LICENSE.note), but the package as a whole is AGPL-3.0 strong copyleft. R-centric API (registers as a user-supplied R RNG).
caveats: Baseline is R's generators, not std::mt19937 or xoshiro/PCG. No hardware or compiler stated. The speedups combine different engines and different distribution algorithms, not just the generator. Timings are median R microbenchmarks from the README.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic pages github.com/topics/rng (C++) and github.com/topics/random (C++) listed daqana/dqrng; README opened.

name: DualMix128 (128-bit-state PRNG; superseded by LoopMix128)
baseline: xoroshiro128++ (also wyrand, Java xoroshiro128++ and java.util.Random)
workload: ns per call of the generator in a 10-billion-iteration loop, built with gcc and run by benchmark.c.
claimed_speedup: benchmark.out: DualMix128 0.401 ns/call versus xoroshiro128++ 0.829 ns/call (about 2.07x, derived from page data) and wyrand 0.401 ns/call (parity). README: '107% faster than C xoroshiro128++, 27% faster than Java xoroshiro128++, 8.82x Java random'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.4.0 (Ubuntu 22.04): gcc -o benchmark benchmark.c -O3 -march=native
tradeoffs: Two 64-bit state words; period not guaranteed (README replaced the injectivity claim and points users to LoopMix128, which has a guaranteed 2^128 period); not cryptographic.
caveats: First-party; the benchmark output gives gcc version and flags but no CPU model. The repo is marked as replaced by LoopMix128, whose repository (danielcota/LoopMix128) now serves the biski64 README, and biski64 is already catalogued. Statistical claims: PractRand 256MB to 8TB with zero anomalies and BigCrush pass, per the README. Speed ties wyrand.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'fast PRNG library benchmark vs std::mt19937 header-only C++ xoshiro wyrand sfc64' (github.com only); README and benchmark.out opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: fast_prng (cd-mcfarland modified ziggurat)
baseline: Doornik ziggurat normal and Marsaglia-Tsang ziggurat exponential (other ziggurat generators profiled in the repo); not std::normal_distribution or Boost
workload: Mean time per generated standard normal (and exponential) variate over 1e9 draws, uniform source is SFMT-based MT19937.h.
claimed_speedup: README example output: 'Mean execution time (per PRN): 7.987 (ns)' for 1e9 standard normal draws. The README page gives no baseline timing; benchmarks/ holds profile.c variants for Doornik normal and Marsaglia-Tsang/double Marsaglia exponential but no committed results file was found.
compiler_and_flags: README: gcc -O2 -DNORMAL profile.c -lm. benchmarks/profile_all.py default config: gcc-4.8 -O2, 5 trials, median.
hardware: README run: not stated. benchmarks/profile_all.py default CPU string: Intel Core i7-3770K @ 3.50GHz (other CPUs commented out).
stars_or_usage: 13 stars; algorithm ported to Apache Commons RNG (ZigguratSampler), USGS BiF Fortran lib, and cited by a pedrobtz/zurand method request
tradeoffs: Header-only C (normal.h, exponential.h, shared.h) with its own SFMT-derived MT19937.h as the uniform source; also Python (pip fast_prng), MATLAB/Octave bindings. Table-based ziggurat with global generator state; the README describes bug fixes by a contributor (rejection sampling and overhang indexing off by one) that moment tests did not detect.
caveats: The listed baselines (std::mt19937, PCG, xoshiro) are uniform generators, not normal samplers, so they do not fit this project; the real comparison is against other ziggurat implementations. No head-to-head against std::normal_distribution or Boost was found on pages opened. Paper (J. Stat. Comput. Simul. 86(7), 2016; arXiv 1403.6870) abstract says median runtimes of the new algorithm for exponential and normal variates are reduced to 58% and 53% (range 41-93%); this was seen only in a WebSearch result snippet because arxiv.org and tandfonline.com are blocked here (snippet only, not opened). The last commit only added a LICENSE file. Third-party PR pedrobtz/zurand#45 (opened) reports McFarland's method 1.02-1.25x faster than that package's default normal method and 'transform alone 21-39% faster per value on eight CPUs', which is a different baseline and not a std comparison. A timings.csv referenced by benchmarks/profile_all.py returned 404 at HEAD.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/cd-mcfarland/fast_prng README and benchmarks/profile.c, profile_all.py

name: fastrand (PCG32 and xorshift128+ with nearly-divisionless bounded integers for Python)
baseline: CPython random.randint (Mersenne Twister)
workload: python3 -m timeit of a single bounded integer draw in [0,1001) or [100,1000] with fastrand versus random.randint(0,1000) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000).
claimed_speedup: fastrand.pcg32bounded(1001) 23.6 ns and fastrand.pcg32randint(100,1000) 24.6 ns versus random.randint(0,1000) 216 ns (about 9.2x and 8.8x, derived from page data) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000) 955 ns (about 40x, derived). README headline: 'up to 10x faster than random.randint'.
tradeoffs: Python extension with module-level generator state; pcg32 gives 32-bit output only and xorshift128+ is available only on some 64-bit platforms; not cryptographically secure; the C core (PCG32 plus Lemire's multiply-shift bounded draw) is small enough to reuse in C/C++.
caveats: One-line timeit measurements with no CPU, Python version or compiler stated; the gap is dominated by Python-level call overhead in random.randint and by its slower bounded-integer path rather than by raw generator speed. Baseline is CPython, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/prng topic page (lemire/fastrand, 124 stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: frand (lukechampine/frand, Go userspace CSPRNG)
baseline: Go crypto/rand (and math/rand in parallel benchmarks)
workload: Generating large amounts of random data, sequentially and in parallel.
claimed_speedup: README prose: 20x faster than crypto/rand when generating large amounts of random data, and over 100x faster when generating data in parallel; as fast and convenient as math/rand. No table or numbers beyond these ratios.
tradeoffs: Userspace CSPRNG seeded once from the kernel CSPRNG with no new entropy mixed in afterwards (README); the state lives in process memory, which the README acknowledges is easier for an attacker with memory access to read. Scales across cores through a sync.Pool of derived generators.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. First-party prose with no benchmark code in the repo listing and no hardware or Go version. Since commit 'switch to stdlib ChaCha8 generator' (2024-10-07) it is a thin wrapper over Go's math/rand/v2 ChaCha8, so the speedup really belongs to Go's stdlib ChaCha8 over crypto/rand rather than to this package's own code. Not a like-for-like comparison with PCG or xoshiro.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search (HN item 40087206 'Modern CSPRNGs can generate numbers at GB/s...' appeared in the results of the 'fast PRNG faster than xoshiro PCG benchmark' search and motivated looking at userspace CSPRNGs; thread not openable); recalled from prior knowledge. Opened repo page, README and commits page on github.com.

name: libchaos (KISS, Xoroshiro128Plus, Xorshf96 and other PRNGs)
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (also std::minstd_rand, ranlux24/48, knuth_b)
workload: Google Benchmark items/s for 'Next' calls of libchaos PRNGs vs STL engines, run on Travis CI.
claimed_speedup: README: CHAOS_PRNG_XOROSHIRO128PLUS 178.426M items/s, CHAOS_PRNG_XORSHF96 185.148M, CHAOS_PRNG_ABYSSINIAN 165.754M, CHAOS_PRNG_KISS 99.9175M vs STL mt19937 68.239M and mt19937_64 60.0674M items/s (Xoroshiro128Plus about 2.6x mt19937, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.7 or newer required; flags not stated
hardware: Travis CI (CPU not stated)
tradeoffs: Library built around 'chaos machines' (hashes and PRNGs) with its own push/pull API; the PRNG classes are listed with seed, output and period; whether they satisfy the C++ UniformRandomBitGenerator interface was not checked. Several generators (Xoroshiro128+, KISS, Xorshf96) are ports of existing algorithms.
caveats: 2016-2017 numbers measured on a shared Travis VM with no stated compiler flags or CPU; the libchaos xoroshiro128+ code was not inspected, and the speed edge is essentially what any xorshift-family generator gives over MT19937. The benchmark source tests/b_generators.cc was not opened. Most of the library is not about speed.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/random?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars; opened the repo page, README.md, LICENSE and commits page.

name: mir-random (libmir/mir-random, D random number generators)
baseline: D Phobos std.random (Mt19937 generation and initialization, modulo-reduction bounded integers)
workload: README 'Comparison with Phobos' bullets: Mt19937 generation and initialization speed, and randIndex bounded-integer throughput using Lemire's fast alternative to modulo reduction.
claimed_speedup: Mt19937: +100% performance for initialization and +54% for generation versus Phobos (merged back to Phobos). randIndex with Lemire's method on x86-64 with LDC 1.6.0: 1.40x for uint with Mt19937_64, 1.73x for uint with Xoroshiro128Plus, 2.36x for ulong with Mt19937_64, 4.25x for ulong with Xoroshiro128Plus.
compiler_and_flags: LDC 1.6.0 (flags not stated)
hardware: an x86-64 processor (model not stated)
tradeoffs: D language with a Better C mode and no DRuntime dependency; provides Mt19937, PCG (Apache-2.0), SplitMix, XorshiftStar, Xoroshiro128Plus and Xoshiro256** engines plus ndslice-based random arrays and distributions; the new API uses opCall rather than a range interface. Not for cryptography.
caveats: D only, not callable from C++ without bindings. First-party bullets without a benchmark source or CPU, from the LDC 1.6.0 era (about 2017-2018). The Mt19937 improvements were merged back into Phobos, so that gap has probably closed. The 1.40x to 4.25x figures compare Lemire's reduction against modulo reduction on the same engine, not mir-random against another library. License per dub.sdl: BSL-1.0 by default, Apache-2.0 for PCG.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of non-C++ RNG libraries. Opened README, repo page and commits page on github.com, and read dub.sdl via raw.githubusercontent.com for the license.

name: miranda (coolbutuseless/miranda, R package with C PRNGs: romu trio, xoshiro256+, lehmer64, splitmix64)
baseline: R base runif()
workload: bench::mark of generating 1 million uniform random numbers with each package function versus runif(N).
claimed_speedup: README text: these PRNGs are up to 20x faster than the built-in PRNGs in R, about 20x at best versus runif(); the timing chart is an image and the page text has no ns or ms values.
tradeoffs: R package with C source in src/, lifecycle marked experimental; includes jump-ahead for xoshiro256+; romu trio has a probabilistic period and xoshiro256+ has weak low bits; all four generators are listed as passing or having no systematic failures in BigCrush.
caveats: R package, usable from C++ only by reusing its small C sources. Chart image not readable, so the 20x figure is first-party text without per-generator numbers; no CPU, R version or compiler stated. The speedup includes R call and vector-allocation overhead of runif, so it is not a generator-only comparison, and the baseline is not std::mt19937 or PCG.
found_via: Lead from a README saved in the scratchpad by an earlier attempt at this assignment (not found by me through an HN search); I then opened the repo page and commits page on github.com.

name: MRG32k3a branchless implementation (Vigna)
baseline: L'Ecuyer's reference double-based MRG32k3a.c (also the equivalent 64-bit integer implementation)
workload: Time to emit one double in (0,1) from MRG32k3a using the author's standard PRNG timing harness; output stream is identical to the original when seeded through MRG32k3a_init6().
claimed_speedup: Header comment: double-based reference about 17.5 ns per double, equivalent 64-bit integer implementation about 7.9 ns, this implementation about 4.1 ns (about 4.3x and 1.9x faster, derived from page data). README: 'roughly four times faster than the double-based implementation and two times faster than the trivial 64-bit integer implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1 with the author's standard harness; optimisation flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz
tradeoffs: Single stream only (no stream or jump support yet); returns doubles in (0,1); emits the output from the current state, so one value must be discarded to line up with L'Ecuyer's original stream; state is six 64-bit integers.
caveats: First-party header comment with CPU and gcc version but no flags and no separate benchmark code (the harness is the author's external one, not opened here). The README itself notes that for batch generation nothing beats Intel MKL's vectorised MRG32k3a. Baseline is the reference MRG32k3a, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/pseudorandom-number-generator topic page (vigna/MRG32k3a); README, MRG32k3a.h and MRG32k3a.c opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: nanorand-rs (WyRand, Pcg64 and ChaCha for Rust)
baseline: Pcg64 as implemented in the same crate (port of rkern/pcg64); README also contrasts with PCG32 crates fastrand, oorandom, random-fast-rng and randomize
workload: Table of generator output speed in GB/s for each RNG shipped by the crate, footnoted as benchmarked on an M1 MacBook Air.
claimed_speedup: WyRand 14 GB/s versus Pcg64 1.6 GB/s (about 8.8x, derived from page data); ChaCha8 980 MB/s, ChaCha12 749 MB/s, ChaCha20 505 MB/s. README text: PCG32 crates are 'much slower than wyrand'.
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Air
tradeoffs: Rust-only; WyRand is not cryptographically secure and has a single 64-bit state; ChaCha variants provide the CSPRNG option; minimal dependencies and fast compile time are the stated goals.
caveats: First-party table with one footnote, no benchmark code, compiler version or flags. The Pcg64 figure of 1.6 GB/s (about 5 ns per u64) is far slower than PCG64 timings seen elsewhere (for example about 1.3 ns per value for pcg64_fast in the zeFresk/cpp-random-benchmarks README), so the gap mainly reflects this crate's Pcg64 port rather than PCG itself. The WyRand algorithm is the same as in wyhash (already catalogued).
found_via: GitHub: probed README of Absolucy/nanorand-rs as a Rust PRNG crate with a stated speed table; opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: NumPy numpy.random Generator (PCG64, PCG64DXSM, SFC64 bit generators)
baseline: MT19937 (legacy RandomState and MT19937 under Generator)
workload: Time in ns to produce one random value (32-bit and 64-bit unsigned ints, uniforms, normals, exponentials, gammas, binomials, laplaces, poissons) per bit generator, on Linux with an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X; plus relative tables for 64-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows and 32-bit Windows.
claimed_speedup: Uniforms: PCG64 3.1 ns, PCG64DXSM 2.9, SFC64 2.6 versus MT19937 5.9 and legacy RandomState 6.0; 64-bit unsigned ints: PCG64 3.2, SFC64 2.5 versus MT19937 5.6. Overall geometric mean relative to RandomState: PCG64 219%, PCG64DXSM 225%, SFC64 251%, MT19937 under Generator 159%. 64-bit Linux table normalised to MT19937=100: PCG64 161, PCG64DXSM 168, SFC64 192 overall.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Linux (main timing table); hardware of the Windows tables not stated
tradeoffs: Python-first API; using the generators from plain C++ means embedding Python/NumPy or copying the C sources. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the same page); PCG64DXSM is recommended for heavily parallel use.
caveats: First-party docs: CPU stated for the main table, compiler and flags not stated. The same page shows the new generators are slower than MT19937 on 32-bit Windows (PCG64 25, PCG64DXSM 39, SFC64 77 versus 100) and Philox is 28 on 64-bit Windows, so the win is platform dependent. Much of the normals and exponentials gap versus RandomState comes from the algorithm (ziggurat versus Box-Muller or log inversion), not only the bit generator. The page does not say whether values were drawn in bulk or one call at a time. PCG64 is the PCG family already catalogued as pcg-cpp, so the PCG64 rows are evidence for that project as much as for NumPy.
found_via: GitHub: randomgen docs referenced NumPy's bit generators; opened numpy/numpy repo page and doc/source/reference/random/performance.rst via raw.githubusercontent.com (numpy.org itself was blocked)

name: OpenRAND (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche counter-based generators)
baseline: std::mt19937 (libstdc++) on CPU and NVIDIA cuRAND on GPU
workload: Raw generation speed of the four OpenRAND generators on CPU (Google Benchmark, 10 to 100000 draws per generator instance) and GPU (GB/s of 32-bit integers produced into 1 GB), plus Brownian-walk style simulations in the paper.
claimed_speedup: README: 'as fast and often faster than native libraries like libstdc++ or Nvidia's Curand, with minimal memory overhead'; no numbers on the page. The repo benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp includes std::mt19937 as the CPU baseline.
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17, works on CPU and GPU (CUDA) device code; counter-based design needs a (seed, counter) pair per work unit and gives reproducibility independent of thread count; the std-compatible engine interface lets it drive standard distributions.
caveats: The numbers (a 1.8x gain over cuRAND in a Brownian-walk test, per search results) are in the SoftwareX paper, which could not be opened, so only a qualitative first-party claim is recorded; a verifier with paper access may be able to raise the tier. The CUDA benchmark in the repo only times OpenRAND generators, so the cuRAND comparison lives in the paper. Compiler, flags and hardware are not stated on the opened pages.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github OpenRAND counter-based random number generation library Philox Tyche Squares CUDA C++ performance vs curand'; opened the repo page, README.md, benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp, benchmarks/raw_speed_cuda.cu and commits page.

name: pgregory.net/rand (sfc64-based replacement for Go math/rand)
baseline: Go math/rand/v2 (PCG source and top-level functions), math/rand, golang.org/x/exp/rand
workload: Go benchmark suite (benchstat output) of Float64, Intn, Uint64, Shuffle, Perm, NormFloat64, ExpFloat64 and constructor cost, versus math/rand/v2 on a laptop and versus math/rand and x/exp/rand on a 48-thread Xeon.
claimed_speedup: Versus math/rand/v2 on i7-10510U: Rand_Float32 7.67 ns to 3.61 ns (-52.93%), Rand_Int31n 10.2 to 4.2 ns (-59.15%), Rand_Uint64 6.86 to 3.93 ns (-42.64%), Rand_Shuffle 711 to 412 ns (-42.12%), but top-level Uint64 3.06 to 3.20 ns (+4.75%, slower) and Float64 3.29 to 3.55 ns (+7.92%, slower). Versus math/rand on Xeon E5-2680 v3 with 48 threads: top-level Uint64 193 ns to 1 ns (-99.72%), Rand_Uint32 7.82 to 1.72 ns (-77.98%).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, linux/amd64; Go version and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U @ 1.80GHz (versus math/rand/v2) and Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 @ 2.50GHz (versus math/rand and x/exp/rand)
tradeoffs: Go-only; deliberately omits the Source interface and top-level Seed(); generator is sfc64; Rand_New costs 48 bytes and seeding (Rand_Seed 46.09 ns versus 0.57 ns) is much slower than in math/rand/v2.
caveats: README author-run benchmarks without Go version or flags. The win over math/rand/v2 is mixed: raw top-level Uint64, Float64 and Intn are slightly slower than v2, and the headline gains are in float conversion, bounded ints, shuffle and the legacy math/rand package. The huge 99% gains versus math/rand are lock-contention effects of the global source on 48 threads. Go's own PCG source in math/rand/v2 is the closest named baseline.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/prng topic page (flyingmutant/rand, 240 stars); README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: prng-test-bench (aes_ctr_128 and clmulrand PRNG headers)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::mt19937_64, pcg64, xoshiro256**, wyrand in the same table)
workload: Google Benchmark loop calling next() once per iteration on a randomly seeded generator, 7 threads, per-thread average, 5 repetitions, reported as GiB/s of generator output.
claimed_speedup: Results file prng-next-benchmark.txt: aes_ctr_128 37.22 GiB/s, aes_compress_ctr2_128 28.60 GiB/s, clmulrand 21.03 GiB/s, wyrand 16.88 GiB/s, xoshiro256starstar 8.53 GiB/s, xoshiro256plusplus 8.10 GiB/s, std::mt19937_64 5.24 GiB/s, pcg64 5.17 GiB/s, std::mt19937 4.67 GiB/s, pcg32 3.73 GiB/s. aes_ctr_128 vs std::mt19937 is about 8.0x in GiB/s (derived from page data), but aes_ctr_128 returns a 128-bit value per call (__uint128_t in include/aes_ctr_128.hpp) and mt19937 returns 32 bits, so the per-call rate ratio is only about 2.0x (derived from page data and header).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile defaults: g++ -std=c++26 -O3 -flto=auto -march=native with Google Benchmark 1.9.5 (release build); g++ version not recorded in the results.
hardware: CPU model not stated in the results JSON (8 CPUs at 2419 MHz, L3 36 MiB, host arch-vm, run dated 2026-09-18); the same author's randp README names an i9-13980HX, which is consistent but not confirmed for this run.
tradeoffs: AES-based generators need AES-NI (and __int128) and g++ (clang++ unsupported per README). The headers expose each generator as a std::uniform_random_bit_generator. aes_ctr_128 runs only 3 AES rounds and is not claimed to be a CSPRNG. The same table includes many other generators (romu, sfc64, wyrand, squares, biski64) that may be separately catalogued.
caveats: Author-run, first-party numbers on an unnamed CPU, so tier C and not A. GiB/s favours generators with wide outputs (128-bit vs 32-bit), so per-call or per-byte-of-entropy comparisons are less dramatic than the headline. The README does not itself claim to beat mt19937, the comparison is read from the results table. The repo has no LICENSE file; MPL-2.0 comes from SPDX headers in source files. PractRand quality results exist in the repo but were not read here, so statistical quality is unchecked. Repo is two weeks old.
found_via: github.com/topics/random-number-generator?l=c%2B%2B listing led to planet36/randp, whose author's other repo planet36/prng-test-bench was opened via github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com

name: randomgen (NumPy-compatible bit generators: SFC64, Romu, Xoshiro256, PCG64, SFMT)
baseline: MT19937 as used by NumPy's legacy RandomState (also compared against MT19937, MT64, DSFMT inside randomgen)
workload: Time in ns to produce one random value (uint32, uint64, uniform double, exponential, normal, gamma) from each bit generator through the Python API, on Linux with an Intel Cascade Lake CPU at 3.1GHz.
claimed_speedup: uint64: Romu 2.6 ns, SFC64 2.6, Xoshiro256 2.8, SFMT 2.8, PCG64 3.2 versus MT19937 4.2 ns and NumPy RandomState 5.2 ns; uniform double: Romu 2.4, SFC64 2.5, Xoshiro256 2.7, PCG64 2.9 versus MT19937 4.0 and RandomState 5.2. The page's own overall geometric-mean score relative to RandomState: Romu(trio) 276%, Romu 268%, SFC64 259%, Xoshiro256 243%, SFMT 242%, PCG64 227%, MT19937 (via Generator) 191%.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (Family 6, Model 85, Stepping 7) at 3.1GHz, Linux
tradeoffs: Python/Cython package that needs NumPy; the C generator sources live in the repo and can be lifted into C/C++ projects, but the package itself is not a C++ library. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the NumPy docs), so parallel streams rely on distinct seeds or Weyl increments; Philox, AES and other counter-based generators are available when many streams are needed.
caveats: First-party documentation table: CPU is stated but compiler and flags are not, and no benchmark script was located in the package tree. The page does not say whether values were drawn in bulk or one call at a time, so Python-layer overhead may be included. The legacy RandomState gap on normals and exponentials is inflated by Box-Muller and log-based inversion versus ziggurat in the newer code. The page itself recommends against all Mersenne Twister variants unless backward compatibility is needed. Baseline is NumPy's C MT19937, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/mersenne-twister and https://github.com/topics/philox topic pages (both list bashtage/randomgen); then the repo page and doc/source/performance.rst via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: RANLUX++ (sibidanov/ranluxpp)
baseline: std::ranlux (GCC libstdc++ RANLUX implementation)
workload: Generation of single-precision floats from the RANLUX family: an LCG formulation of RANLUX (modulus 2^576 - 2^240 + 1, 576x576-bit modular multiplication in x86-64 assembly) versus GCC's std::ranlux and a SIMD-optimized conventional RANLUX.
claimed_speedup: README: 'generation speed achieved (20 clock/float) is order of magnitude faster than the usual approach, for example, GCC C++ RANLUX implementation where 198 clock/float is measured at Haswell CPU'; the optimized conventional RANLUX reaches 40 clock/float, and the SSE2 and AVX2 versions are 'approximately 4 and 8 times faster' than scalar.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -O3 -Iinc -mavx2, ASMSKIP enabled (from the repo Makefile)
hardware: Haswell CPU (GCC RANLUX figure) and Skylake CPU (RANLUX++ figure); microarchitecture names only, no CPU model, per README
stars_or_usage: 11 stars; later adopted in ROOT as RanluxppEngine (ROOT commit 36cc2a8 'Implement RANLUX++ generator')
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly (mulx/adcx/adox variants chosen by GCC function multiversioning), so not portable to other architectures; LGPL-3.0 (COPYING and COPYING.LESSER in repo). The win is inside the RANLUX family: RANLUX is itself far slower than mt19937/PCG/xoshiro, so this does not beat the category baselines.
caveats: First-party README numbers with only CPU microarchitecture names; the GCC figure (198 clock/float) was measured on Haswell while RANLUX++ (20 clock/float) was measured on Skylake, so the 10x claim mixes two CPUs. The accompanying paper (Computer Physics Communications 2017, arXiv 1705.03123) could not be opened in this session (arxiv.org blocked), so no peer-review upgrade to tier B. Baseline std::ranlux is not in the category baseline list. Last commit 2018-01-17.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast random number generator C++ library benchmark faster than std::mt19937 vcpkg OR conan' surfaced arXiv 1705.03123; repo opened from a follow-up search
WebSearch: 'github RANLUX++ ranluxpp Sibidanov faster than ranlux48 C++'; opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.4 -S -O3 (assembly analysis only)
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2643 v3 (3.4-3.7 GHz)
tradeoffs: Nonlinear; short minimum cycle length guarantees weaker than xoshiro; some variants have state-dependent period

name: Romu (RomuTrio/RomuQuad/RomuMono)

name: ROOT RanluxppEngine (portable RANLUX++)
baseline: ROOT TRandom1 (RANLUX); ROOT TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is faster than RANLUX++ in the same benchmark
workload: Average time per generated random double from a Google Benchmark microbenchmark (BM_Rndm calling Rndm() once per iteration, rootbench TRandomBenchmarks.cxx) for TRandom1, TRandom3, TRandomMixMax and TRandomRanluxpp, 10 repetitions with standard deviation under 1 percent.
claimed_speedup: ROOT blog 'Implementing and tuning RANLUX++ for ROOT' (2020-11-30): initial portable version about 30 ns per double, Sibidanov's assembly version about 8 ns, TRandom1 (RANLUX, single precision) about 62 ns, after tuning about 9 ns per number ('very close to the assembly version'), slightly slower than TRandom3 at about 3 ns. Derived from page data: about 6.9x faster than TRandom1 (62 ns versus 9 ns); 2x faster than TRandom1 already at the untuned 30 ns. Tuning gains reported: loop unrolling up to 30 percent, overflow handling up to 15 percent, native __int128 multiplication over 40 percent, carry propagation over 20 percent on GCC 7.5.0.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.1 (default); graph also covers Clang 9.0.1 and GCC 7.5.0 built from source; optimisation flags not stated in the post.
hardware: Single core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900, CentOS 8.2.2004
stars_or_usage: ROOT: 3.3k stars; used across high-energy physics; RANLUX++ shipped in ROOT 6.24
tradeoffs: Portable C++ (uses unsigned __int128 where available, with unrolling pragmas) instead of Sibidanov's x86 assembly; 576-bit LCG state stored as 9 x 64-bit words, and the generator advances in blocks via a multiply and modulo. It gives 48 random bits per double and passes TestU01 per the blog, but it is about 3x slower than ROOT's Mersenne Twister and the code sits inside ROOT (mathcore) with ROOT dependencies (TRandomEngine base class), so extracting it needs the src/ranluxpp helper headers. Provides RanluxppEngine24 and RanluxppEngine2048 plus compatibility engines for James/Luescher RANLUX.
caveats: The benchmark compares against TRandom1 (original RANLUX) and does not beat std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro: in the same post TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is about 3x faster. TRandom1 yields only 24-bit single-precision numbers while RANLUX++ yields 48-52 bits per double, so the work per number differs. The measured code predates correctness changes in June 2021 (commits 'Ensure full modulo operation in mod_m', 'Convert LCG state to RANLUX numbers', 'Extract only 48 bits per number', per the file history page; the blog says 52 bits per double), so the 9 ns figure was not re-measured for the shipped implementation and the tier is capped at C. Optimisation flags are not stated; the benchmark source is public (root-project/rootbench PR #200, merged 2020-12-15, 23-line file) but no results are checked in. The repo has no benchmark results for the component. The last commit shown for RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx was 2021-06-23, so the component is stable; last_commit above is the overall ROOT repo (large project, judged only for math/mathcore RanluxppEngine*).

name: rhet_RNG (xromu2jr, winner of the PRNG Battle Royale)
baseline: xoshiro256++ / xoshiro256** / xoroshiro128 variants and PCG (pcg64) among the 47 PRNGs benchmarked; std::mt19937 is not among the generators listed in the README
workload: Per the README: 47 non-cryptographic PRNGs on 9 game consoles (Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4/4 Pro/5, Xbox One/One X/Series X, Stadia 1080p/4K), throughput and latency tests with at least 256 GB of random data per test, using three range-mapping methods (biased modulo, unbiased masking with discard, Lemire fixed-point fastrange) over ranges 2 to 2^16.
claimed_speedup: No benchmark numbers appear in the repo. The README states that Romu2jr (RomuDuoJr with a NASAM-based seeding wrapper, xromu2jr.h) wins overall for game development, that the fixed-point (Lemire) range mapping beats biased modulo and unbiased masking, and that results are charts of relative speed per console (for example '2.2 implies the test was 2.2 faster than the slowest test that ran in this game console'). The charts themselves are images that are not in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: README: all tests built with 'top tier configuration presets' using the latest platform SDKs and Visual Studio 2019; exact flags unstated.
hardware: Nine game consoles (CPU models unstated)
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; the original rhet.dev blog post is widely cited in PRNG discussions (not verified here)
tradeoffs: RomuDuoJr has a 128-bit state and no guaranteed minimum period, so some seeds can end in short cycles; the README mitigates this with a NASAM-based initializer and brute-force checks (no cycles for 32-bit seeds within 2^24 bytes, 16-bit seeds within 2^36 bytes) but it is not a proof. Chaotic generators give low-quality first outputs unless seeded through a mixer. The README charts report some PractRand failures, and the author himself suggests xoshiro256++ or sfc64 when a guaranteed period matters. The header uses reinterpret_cast type punning in as<>() and either __uint128_t or __umulh for 64-bit ranges.
caveats: Tier D: the repo is an archive of a single 2.8 KB header (xromu2jr.h) plus a copy of the 2020 blog text; there are no benchmark numbers, charts or code in it, and the author says the benchmark code is kept private for console NDA reasons, so nothing is reproducible. The rhet.dev post and the Wayback copy were not fetched (blocked hosts). Licensing: the header says the wrapper is released into the public domain by its author, there is no LICENSE file in the repo, and the Romu algorithm by Mark Overton is not covered by that statement, so usability is marked mixed (no patent grant implied). The repo owner appears to be a different account from the original author (README says the header was created by RomuDuoJr at rhet.dev). Relative results are per console and mix PRNG quality and worst-case criteria chosen by the author; the 'winner' conclusion is his weighting.

name: stochastic-generation (Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02 sample sequences)
baseline: other published generators of Owen-scrambled Sobol', Halton, Faure and pmj02(bn) sequences (not named in the README)
workload: Generating low-discrepancy sample sequences (stochastic Sobol' up to 64 dimensions, Halton up to 10 dimensions, Faure, pmj02 and pmj02bn) with the method of 'Stochastic Generation of (t,s) Sample Sequences' (Helmer, Christensen, Kensler, 2021).
claimed_speedup: README: 'I don't think there are any faster or simpler open-source implementations out there' and 'the code in this library is faster than any other published method'. No timings are given. It also says a minimal 2D Sobol' implementation (Listing 2 of the paper) would be about 3x faster than this general-purpose code.

name: Cache-Aware and GPU-Accelerated SpMV (VSJ001)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpMV (CSR_ALG2)
workload: CSR SpMV effective memory bandwidth (GB/s) of a hand-written one-warp-per-row CUDA kernel versus cuSPARSE on four SuiteSparse matrices (cant, consph, pdb1HYS, webbase-1M) on an A100.
claimed_speedup: 'beats NVIDIA's cuSPARSE library by 24-56 percent on regular real-world matrices': cant 1531 vs 1172 GB/s (+30.6%), consph 1557 vs 1252 GB/s (+24.4%), pdb1HYS 1718 vs 1102 GB/s (+55.8%); cuSPARSE wins on webbase-1M (847 vs 203 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: make gpu: 'nvcc -arch=sm_80' with CUDA 12.3; CPU build 'gcc -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize'
hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (README also quotes a 1555 GB/s HBM2 peak) on the Northeastern University Explorer cluster; Intel Xeon Gold host CPUs
tradeoffs: Simple CSR-vector kernel (one warp per row, warp-shuffle reduction) with an ELL variant and a selector that skips ELL on irregular rows; CPU side adds cache tiling and AVX2 with software prefetching. Loses to cuSPARSE on irregular web-graph matrices.
caveats: Coursework-style project with four real matrices. README reports 98 to 110 percent of HBM2 peak bandwidth, which means the matrices largely fit in the A100 L2 cache, so the bandwidth numbers are cache-assisted and the win may not hold for large matrices. Only one cuSPARSE algorithm (CSR_ALG2) was compared. No LICENSE file seen. Tier A is borderline: hardware, nvcc version and architecture flag are stated and code plus CSVs are public, but only partial flags are given.

name: CVR (Compressed Vectorization-oriented sparse Row)
baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV; also MKL CSR(I) inspector-executor, ESB, VHCC and CSR5
workload: Double-precision SpMV (1000 iterations, best SMT thread count per method) on 58 sparse matrices from SNAP and the SuiteSparse collection: 30 scale-free and 28 HPC matrices, on Xeon Phi Knights Landing with MCDRAM in flat mode.
claimed_speedup: Paper (CGO 2018, included in the repo): on scale-free matrices CVR is up to 40x (2.84x on average) faster than MKL and up to 1.70x (1.33x on average) faster than the best existing approach; on HPC matrices up to 17x (1.22x on average) over MKL and up to 1.57x (1.10x on average) over the best existing approach. Table 3 domain averages, GFlop/s CVR vs MKL: web graph 7.28 vs 2.92, routing 17.11 vs 2.73, road 9.57 vs 4.24.
compiler_and_flags: Intel C/C++ compiler 17.04, flags -MIC-AVX512 -O3
hardware: Intel Xeon Phi 7250 (Knights Landing, 68 cores, 16 GB MCDRAM + 96 GB DDR4), CentOS 7.3
tradeoffs: Needs a one-time conversion from CSR to the CVR format; the paper reports the lowest preprocessing overhead among the compared formats but scale-free matrices still need many iterations to amortize it for some competitors. Written for AVX-512 (Knights Landing); building the comparison binaries needs MKL. SpMV kernel only, not a solver.
caveats: Peer-reviewed with a public artifact (spmv.cpp plus a solutions_for_comparison/ directory with build and run scripts), but the numbers are the authors' own on discontinued KNL hardware from 2017; the best thread count and parameters were picked per method. The README itself contains no numbers; they are in the paper PDF in the repo. MKL is not one of SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc. Mostly dormant since 2018 with one 2024 README edit.

name: Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM (KKSPGEMM / KKMEM)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpGEMM (CUDA 8.0.44) on P100; Intel MKL sparse-sparse multiply (MKL-INS, MKL7, MKL8 variants; intel-18.0.128) on Knights Landing
workload: Sparse matrix-matrix multiplication (symbolic plus numeric phases, 'NoReuse' case) on 81-83 SuiteSparse/UFL multiplications (mostly A*A); best time over thread counts per method; Kokkos 2.50 / Kokkos Kernels 2.60; the wiki ties the setup to the Deveci et al. paper 'Multi-threaded Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication for Many-Core and GPU Architectures'.
claimed_speedup: All figures derived from page data (I parsed the xlsx tables linked from the SpGEMM_Benchmarks wiki page, skipping their summary rows; ratio = baseline time / KKSPGEMM time per matrix, then geometric mean over matrices where both ran). P100: KKSPGEMM faster than cuSPARSE on 75 of 81 multiplications, geomean 3.61x (the table's own geomean row shows 0.441 s vs 0.122 s); faster than viennaCL CUDA on 62 of 72, geomean 1.95x; but NOT faster than Nsparse (faster on only 28 of 77, geomean ratio 0.92x). KNL flat-DDR: versus MKL-INS 1.25x (faster on 63 of 83), MKL7 1.79x (75 of 83), MKL8 2.95x (72 of 78). KNL cache mode: MKL-INS 1.19x (56 of 83), MKL7 2.25x (80 of 83), MKL8 3.75x (77 of 78). Power8 OpenMP versus viennaCL: 2.79x (78 of 83).
compiler_and_flags: P100 runs: nvcc_wrapper (CUDA 8.0.44) with gcc 5.4.0, CXXFLAGS='-Wall -pedantic -Werror -O3 -g -Wshadow -Wsign-compare -Wignored-qualifiers -Wempty-body -Wclobbered -Wuninitialized', KOKKOS_ARCHS=Pascal60,Power8, cuSPARSE TPL, eti-only, double/int; KNL runs: icpc (Intel 18.2.199) with the same flags, KOKKOS_ARCHS=KNL, MKL TPL; OMP_PROC_BIND=spread, OMP_PLACES=threads; first run discarded as warm-up, 6 runs.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla P100-SXM2-16GB (host Power8, machine 'White'); Intel Knights Landing 68-core nodes (machine 'Bowman', up to 256 threads, quadrant mode); Power8 for the viennaCL comparison. Exact CPU SKUs not stated.
tradeoffs: Templated C++ on top of Kokkos (needs the Kokkos library, explicit template instantiation 'eti-only' builds); one source targets OpenMP, CUDA and other Kokkos backends instead of hand-tuned vendor code. Also wraps cuSPARSE, MKL, cuBLAS and MAGMA as optional TPLs. Covers BLAS, sparse BLAS, graph (coloring, triangle counting), Gauss-Seidel and batched kernels. Performance depends on the Kokkos backend and architecture flags chosen at build time.
caveats: Results are from 2018 (Kokkos 2.50, CUDA 8, KNL and P100 hardware, MKL 18.0, cuSPARSE of that CUDA); modern cuSPARSE/MKL SpGEMM may differ. On P100 KKSPGEMM is on average slower than Nsparse (v1.2), so it is not the fastest GPU SpGEMM there. None of the baselines is in the catalog's listed set (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), and the wiki's SpMV benchmark page compares only against Kokkos Kernels' own reference implementation, so SpMV carries no incumbent comparison. Per-matrix times are best over thread counts. CPU SKU is not given (only architecture names), so a strict reading of 'hardware stated' would give B. The wiki is marked deprecated (new docs on kokkos.org, which I could not open); xlsx tables used: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/kokkos/kokkos-kernels/figures/spgemm_benchmark/P100-table.xlsx and .../knl-ddr-table.xlsx, .../knl-cache-table.xlsx, .../power8-table.xlsx; setup page https://raw.githubusercontent.com/wiki/kokkos/kokkos-kernels/p100_configure.md. The tables also contain their own geomean summary rows, which I excluded from my paired ratios; the P100 sheet is oddly named 'Power8' inside the xlsx but its columns are the P100 runs.

name: ParAMD (parallel approximate minimum degree ordering)
baseline: SuiteSparse AMD (single-threaded approximate minimum degree fill-reducing ordering)
workload: Fill-reducing AMD ordering time and fill-in on 9 SuiteSparse Matrix Collection matrices (pre2, nd24k, ldoor, dielFilterV3real, Flan_1565, HV15R, Queen_4147, stokes, nlpkkt240); median of five random row permutations, ParAMD at 1 and 64 threads versus SuiteSparse AMD.
claimed_speedup: 64 threads: 2.85x (nd24k) to 8.51x (nlpkkt240) faster than SuiteSparse AMD (pre2 3.25x, ldoor 4.64x, dielFilterV3real 5.92x, Flan_1565 6.11x, HV15R 6.21x, Queen_4147 6.18x, stokes 7.95x). Single thread: 0.44x to 1.01x, i.e. slower than SuiteSparse on 8 of 9 matrices. Fill-in ratio versus SuiteSparse at 64 threads: 0.98x to 1.16x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC v13.2.1 (must support '#pragma omp atomic compare'), OpenMP, CMake default build type Release; scripts/ in the repo (all.sh, scaling.sh) reproduce the table
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (64 cores) for the committed exemplar outputs; README says benchmarks need at least 64 physical cores and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Approximate parallel variant: ordering quality is slightly worse (fill-in up to 1.16x SuiteSparse AMD in the committed table). Needs many cores to pay off; at one thread it is slower than SuiteSparse AMD. Provides libparamd.so, a paramd.h header and a CLI; reads Matrix Market input; OpenMP; relaxation factors (mult, lim, mem) are tunable.
caveats: Authors' own benchmark (PASSIONLab, accompanying arXiv preprint 2504.17097 was not opened). The committed plots/scaling.csv is one exemplar run on one machine. The headline speedups compare 64 threads to the single-threaded SuiteSparse AMD, so they measure parallel scaling, not per-core efficiency. SuiteSparse AMD version and its build flags are not stated in the README. Repository is young (4 commits, April to November 2025) and has few users.

name: sparsam
baseline: GTSAM 4.2 (also Ceres 2.2)
workload: End-to-end Gauss-Newton/LM optimization of the 2D M3500 pose graph using sparsam's own block-sparse Cholesky with AMD ordering, versus GTSAM 4.2; bundle adjustment on BAL Ladybug versus Ceres 2.2.
claimed_speedup: README: on M3500 sparsam's GN/LM is 1.7-2.1x faster end-to-end than GTSAM 4.2 at final chi-squared parity of 0.009%. Against Ceres 2.2 on BAL Ladybug bundle adjustment sparsam is slower in wall clock (1.74 s vs 0.67 s on ladybug-49, 1.57 s vs 0.48 s on ladybug-73, 9.9 s vs 4.9 s on ladybug-138, 26.5 s vs 24.0 s on ladybug-318) but 552 vs 1091 ms per iteration on ladybug-318.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13 -O3, single-threaded (README headline results)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX
tradeoffs: SLAM and estimation backend written from scratch in C++20 using only the standard library and Eigen dense fixed-size types; own CSR-of-blocks storage, AMD/RCM ordering and simplicial block Cholesky. Not a general sparse solver API. Benchmarks need GTSAM and Ceres built behind an off-by-default CMake flag.
caveats: Mixed result that the README itself states: Ceres wins wall clock on bundle adjustment, and on fill-heavy 3D pose graphs GTSAM's per-iteration linear algebra is about 3-5x faster than sparsam's simplicial block Cholesky. The M3500 speedup is end to end (including iteration counts and damping strategy), not a like-for-like factorization time. Author-run, single machine, GTSAM/Ceres build flags not stated in the README, and the project is weeks old with 1 star. Category fit is loose (nonlinear least-squares/SLAM backend whose core is sparse Cholesky); baselines are not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc.

name: ALP/GraphBLAS (nonblocking backend)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS and Eigen
workload: PageRank, conjugate gradient and sparse DNN inference on ten sparse matrices (per a search-result excerpt of the paper), ALP/GraphBLAS nonblocking execution compared with Eigen and SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS.
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (Mastoras, Anagnostidis, Yzelman, ACM TACO 20(1), 2022, doi 10.1145/3561652) reports the nonblocking ALP/GraphBLAS faster than both Eigen and SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS on PageRank, CG and sparse DNN inference. Figures are not verified here: see caveats.
stars_or_usage: 33 stars; PyPI package alp-graphblas (pyalp bindings, backends pyalp_ref, pyalp_omp, pyalp_nonblocking)
tradeoffs: Header-based C++11 framework needing OpenMP, libnuma, pthreads and CMake; run-time fusion of linear-algebra primitives (nonblocking mode) and shared/distributed-memory backends. GraphBLAS-style API rather than an Eigen- or PETSc-style API.

The only figures I saw were in a search-result excerpt of the abstract: up to 12.2x over Eigen and 16.1x over SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS, and up to 5.13x over ALP's own blocking mode. A verifier must open the paper to confirm the numbers, matrices, CPU, compiler and flags. Gains are specific to algorithms that chain GraphBLAS primitives and benefit from fusion, so single-kernel speedups are likely smaller.

name: AmgT (tensor-core AMG)
baseline: HYPRE (GPU build calling cuSPARSE)
workload: Algebraic multigrid solves on SuiteSparse matrices where AmgT replaces HYPRE's SpGEMM (setup phase) and SpMV (solve phase) with tensor-core kernels over a new mBSR storage format, in FP64 and mixed precision; the repo builds three executables (AmgT_FP64, AmgT_Mixed, and cuSPARSE = HYPRE baseline).
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'24): AmgT outperforms the original GPU version of HYPRE by a factor of on geomean 1.46x, 1.32x and 2.24x (up to 2.10x, 2.06x and 3.67x) on NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 GPUs, respectively. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text; which phase or total time they cover is not stated there.)
compiler_and_flags: compile.sh: CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.0; HYPRE configured with --with-cuda --enable-unified-memory and --with-gpu-arch='80 80' (A100) or '90 90' (H100); -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80 (or compute_90); README advises CUDA 12.2+ and OpenMPI 4.0+. No explicit CXX optimization flags are visible in compile.sh.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 (per the paper text returned by search); repo recommends compute capability 8.0; host CPU not verified
tradeoffs: Implemented inside a modified copy of HYPRE (AmgT_HYPRE/), not a standalone library: using it means taking that fork or porting the mBSR data structure (seq_mv.h), SpGEMM (csr_spgemm_device.c) and SpMV (csr_matvec_device.c). The variant is chosen at build time by copying config_files/<variant>.h over seq_mv.h. Needs tensor-core GPUs (compute capability 8.0 or newer) for the main gains; the mixed-precision mode changes numerics. The embedded HYPRE code carries its own license files, which I did not inspect.
caveats: The paper could not be opened (dl.acm.org, ieeexplore, ssslab.cn are egress-blocked); the benchmark_url was returned by WebSearch and the numbers come from that result's abstract-level text ('snippet only'). The repo README has no numbers and the repo has no result tables, but it does contain the HYPRE+cuSPARSE baseline executable, so the HYPRE comparison is reproducible from repo code; no AmgX comparison was found. Hardware CPU model, HYPRE version and per-matrix problem set were not verified, so B rather than A. The 2.24x on MI210 comes from a different GPU vendor path than the tensor-core story. FP64 versus mixed-precision split of the quoted geomeans is not stated in the snippet. Not a GitHub fork, so is_fork_of is null even though it embeds modified HYPRE.

The README does not say which GPU or aggregation the 5.26x/4.00x refer to. cuSPARSE baseline is the CUDA 8-10.2 era SpTRSV; newer cuSPARSE versions were not tested. Authors note the win is for matrices with many components per level and few nonzeros per row. Last commit 2021. Host CPU model not stated, so not tier A.

compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper text (cuSPARSE v12.4 named as baseline); FP64 values, 16x16 sub-blocks
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (40 GB, 1.56 TB/s) and NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB, 1.01 TB/s); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: GPU-only (NVIDIA), needs conversion of CSR into the CB 2D block format (preprocessing cost, extra metadata); CPU-side aggregation of mixed-type data. Only CB-SpMV is released; CB-SpMM and CB-SpGEMM are 'coming soon (under review)'.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ICS 2025) with code in the repo, but compiler, flags and host CPU are not stated, so B rather than A. The lead's snippet assigned 3.95x to A100 and 3.06x to RTX 4090 for TileSpMV and that matches the paper, but cuSPARSE-BSR is a blocked-format baseline (not cuSPARSE CSR), so the cuSPARSE number is against its BSR path with best-of-four block sizes. Averages are of per-matrix speedups. The advantage over DASP on A100 is only 1.21x. A recent commit (2026-09-02, 'bug fix and opt preprocess') postdates the paper, so numbers may differ from the current code. Not a CPU baseline: SuiteSparse, Eigen and PETSc are not compared.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/xing-cong/CB-Sparse README and PDF fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com/hpcrl/ICS2025-webpage

name: CHOLMOD (SuiteSparse supernodal sparse Cholesky, via Eigen::CholmodSupernodalLLT)
baseline: Eigen::SimplicialLLT and Eigen::SimplicialLDLT (Eigen's built-in sparse Cholesky); Eigen::SparseLU also in the table
workload: Factorization time of SPD k-harmonic diffusion systems (k=1,2,3) on the 720K-vertex xyzrgb_dragon triangle mesh, Eigen wrappers around each solver.
claimed_speedup: Factor time vs Eigen::SimplicialLLT: 0.86 s vs 1.5 s for harmonic (about 1.7x, derived from page data), 1.7 s vs 12 s for biharmonic (about 7x, derived), 3.3 s vs 41 s for triharmonic (about 12x, derived); Eigen::SparseLU needed 4.8 s, 31 s and 130 s. Solve phase only about 1.2x to 1.4x better (0.1 s vs 0.12 s harmonic).
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (compiler and version not stated)
hardware: MacBook, 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7, 32 GB RAM
license: GPL-2.0-or-later (CHOLMOD Supernodal module); LGPL-2.1-or-later for CHOLMOD's other modules
tradeoffs: Supernodal module is GPL; needs BLAS/LAPACK; the Eigen wrapper adds a SuiteSparse dependency; factorization only for SPD matrices (LDL^T variant also exists).
caveats: CHOLMOD is itself the incumbent for this category (SuiteSparse), so this entry records it as the shootout winner over Eigen's own simplicial solvers rather than as a new library. Informal single-author benchmark: one mesh, one laptop, compiler not stated, README says 'YMMV'. Errors differ slightly across solvers (L-infinity 1e-10 to 1e-4 depending on k). Eigen::PardisoLLT also beats Eigen simplicial on k=2 and k=3 but is proprietary; catamari::SparseLDL (MPL-2.0) was not faster than Eigen simplicial. Per-module licences were not opened beyond the SuiteSparse page note that some modules are GPL.

name: cuBool (sparse Boolean linear algebra on CUDA)
baseline: SuiteSparse on CPU (README does not say which package; GraphBLAS likely)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix multiplication M*M and element-wise addition M+M^2 on 10 SuiteSparse graphs (62K to 2.2M rows), SpBench harness, operation time only with data already resident.
claimed_speedup: SpBench README table, time in ms, cuBool vs SuiteSparse for M*M: 23.2 vs 257.6 on amazon0312 (about 11x, derived from page data), 33.3 vs 369.5 on amazon-2008 (11x), 41.8 vs 673.3 on web-Google (16x), 18.1 vs 66.6 on roadNet-PA (3.7x), 1.9 vs 7.9 on wing (4.2x), 35.3 vs 90.9 on netherlands_osm (2.6x), 2.4 vs 3.1 on luxembourg_osm (1.3x); element-wise addition 11.4 vs 37.2 on amazon0312 (3.3x) and 24.8 vs 77.5 on web-Google (3.1x).

hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 3.40 GHz, 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB, Ubuntu 20.04

caveats: GPU against CPU, which SpBench itself calls 'not entirely fair'; some compared libraries emulate Boolean operations with floats; SuiteSparse package, version and thread count not stated; cuSPARSE and clBool beat cuBool on some rows (for example luxembourg_osm and several addition rows). Benchmark is by the same project family; the 2021 GrAPL paper linked from the README was not opened. name: DASP (dense-tensor-core SpMV)
baseline: cuSPARSE CSR SpMV (CUSPARSE_SPMV_ALG_DEFAULT); also CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR and cuSPARSE BSR in the paper
workload: General sparse matrix-vector multiplication (y = Ax) on SuiteSparse matrices in FP64 and FP16 on NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs, using tensor-core MMA units; the repo's harness times cuSPARSE and DASP for 1000 iterations after 100 warm-ups for a given .mtx file.
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'23) FP64 on A100: DASP outperforms CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR, cuSPARSE BSR and cuSPARSE CSR by a factor of on average 1.46x, 2.09x, 3.29x, 2.08x and 1.52x (up to 12.64x, 17.48x, 90.59x, 283.92x and 6.94x), respectively. FP16 versus cuSPARSE: on average 1.70x and 1.75x (up to 26.47x and 65.94x) on A100 and H800. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text for the paper; see caveats.)
compiler_and_flags: From the repo Makefile: nvcc from CUDA 12.0 with host gcc 12.2, -O3 -m64 -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80, -Xcompiler -fopenmp-simd, linked with -lcusparse -lcublas
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs (per the paper text returned by search); the repo recommends a GPU with compute capability 8.0. Host CPU model not verified.
tradeoffs: Needs NVIDIA GPUs with MMA tensor-core support (compute capability 8.0 or newer; FP64 and FP16 variants built from separate mains: make double, make half). Research code driven by Matrix Market files, not a library API. Rows are grouped into long, medium and short categories and repacked into MMA-sized blocks, which adds preprocessing and padding (fill-zero) data. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies to anything built on the code.
caveats: The paper PDF could not be opened (dl.acm.org, ssslab.cn and other publishers are egress-blocked here); the benchmark_url was returned by WebSearch and the speedup numbers above come from that result's text (abstract-level, 'snippet only'), including the A100-only list of averages. The repo itself holds no result tables; I read its harness (src/main_f64.cu, src/dasp_f64.h): it times only the SpMV kernels, and the DASP row reordering / format conversion is not part of the timed loop (cuSPARSE buffer setup is also timed separately), so gains only pay off when the same matrix is multiplied many times. The repo has no scripts for the CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR or BSR baselines, so only the cuSPARSE comparison is reproducible from the repo. cuSPARSE version used in the paper is not verified. Could move to tier A if the paper's setup table lists CPU model and library versions. Large 'up to' ratios (283.92x vs BSR) are outliers; averages are the meaningful figures.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/DASP and one WebSearch query for the SC'23 paper numbers

name: Ocean SpGEMM (CornellHPC)
baseline: spECK (primary) and OpSparse; also TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM
workload: GPU SpGEMM (C = A*B) on 337 square SuiteSparse matrices on A100, plus H100 and 64 rectangular matrices; replaces the symbolic pass with HyperLogLog estimation.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of arXiv 2604.19004 abstract: on A100 over 337 square matrices Ocean achieves 1.4x, 2.6x, 3.5x and 2.0x over spECK, opSparse, TileSpGEMM and HSMU-SpGEMM; consistent speedup on H100 and 64 rectangular matrices; overall 1.4x-2.8x on A100 and H100.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit 12.4 or later; Makefile with sm_xx compute capability, NUM_SM and SHARED_MEMORY_KB set by hand (flags not stated in README)
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and H100 (tested only on these)
tradeoffs: Requires compute capability 8.0+ and CUDA 12.4+, manual hardware constants in include/Common.h, matrices must be converted to a custom .csr format with the bundled convert tool; README warns of likely compile or runtime errors on untested hardware. Part of the code is adapted from spECK; uses nlohmann/json and murmur3.

Paper (ICS 2026, doi 10.1145/3797905.3807868) is peer reviewed but arXiv, doi.org and alphaxiv were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the speedups are from WebSearch snippets and the cuSPARSE comparison, per-case numbers, CPU and flags could not be checked. The values '7.35x/1.43x/1.52x' in the lead are OpSparse's own reported averages over cuSPARSE, nsparse and spECK (OpSparse paper, arXiv 2206.07244), not Ocean results, and should not be attributed to Ocean. README says to use spECK output as ground truth and warns numerical comparison may fail on some matrices due to floating point error. No CPU baseline (SuiteSparse CPU, Eigen, PETSc) is compared.

name: PanguLU
baseline: SuperLU_DIST
workload: Distributed sparse LU factorization and solve of sparse test matrices on CPU+GPU clusters (up to 128 NVIDIA A100 and 128 AMD MI50 GPUs, per a search-result excerpt of the SC'23 paper abstract).
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (PanguLU, SC '23) reports speedups over SuperLU_DIST on 128-GPU heterogeneous platforms. Exact figures are not verified here: see caveats.
tradeoffs: Written in C with MPI, OpenMP and CUDA; regular 2D block-cyclic layout with sparse blocks and synchronisation-free communication; optional METIS and MC64 reordering; real and complex, single and double precision. AGPL-3.0 copyleft. Tested with MPICH 4.3.0, CUDA 12.9, OpenBLAS 0.3.26 per README.
caveats: I could not open the paper (dl.acm.org, arxiv.org and researchgate.net are blocked here) and the GitHub README has no performance numbers. The figures I saw were in a search-result excerpt: up to 11.70x (128 A100) and 17.97x (128 MI50) over SuperLU_DIST, with scaling of 47.51x and 74.84x over one GPU. A verifier must confirm these, the SuperLU_DIST version, matrices, compiler and flags. Distributed heterogeneous-system result, so single-node CPU users may see very different ratios. SuperLU_DIST is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list (PETSc can call it). Last commit is 14 months before the run date.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github sparse LU direct solver "faster than SuperLU_DIST" open source' then 'PanguLU sparse LU distributed github SuperLU_DIST speedup'; repo page, README and commit list opened

name: PIQP
baseline: OSQP
workload: Convex QP solve time on the Maros-Meszaros test set (138 problems; 76-problem sparse subset), shifted geometric mean of runtime over four accuracy settings, run through the qpsolvers Python wrappers.
claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0, Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean with PIQP = 1.0: OSQP 12.7 (default), 16.1 (high accuracy), 52.8 (low), 51.9 (mid); sparse subset (76 problems): OSQP 9.5 / 17.4 / 30.0 / 56.0. Success rate at default settings 95.7% for PIQP vs 43.5% for OSQP. First-party piqp_benchmarks (shifted geometric means, PIQP = 1.0): OSQP 7.55 at low accuracy and 42.66 at high accuracy.
hardware: qpbenchmark run: Intel Core i7-6500U @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs). First-party piqp_benchmarks: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X 64-core @ 4.3GHz.
tradeoffs: Convex QPs only. Header-only C++14 built on Eigen, with dense, sparse and multistage backends; C/C++, Python, Matlab/Octave and R interfaces. Proximal interior-point method, so it needs sparse/dense LDL factorizations per iteration.
caveats: Category fit is loose: this is a QP optimization solver, not a sparse linear-system solver, and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list. The qpbenchmark was run through prebuilt Python wheels (solver versions piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0, qpsolvers 4.3.3), so no compiler or flags apply. Its own known-limitations list includes CPU thermal throttling (issue 88). Failed solves are counted at the 1000 s time limit, which inflates the ratios of solvers that fail often. Results are shifted geometric means on one test set; ProxQP's own benchmark (different problem classes) shows ProxQP ahead of OSQP instead, so rankings depend on the suite.
found_via: PyPI JSON https://pypi.org/pypi/piqp/json (after PyPI name scan for qpsolvers / qpsolvers_benchmark), then the qpsolvers Maros-Meszaros results page and https://github.com/PREDICT-EPFL/piqp_benchmarks

name: QPALM
baseline: OSQP
workload: Convex QP solve time on the Maros-Meszaros test set (138 problems; 76-problem sparse subset), shifted geometric mean of runtime over four accuracy settings, run through the qpsolvers Python wrappers.
claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0, Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean (best solver = 1.0, which is PIQP): QPALM 3.6 vs OSQP 12.7 (default), 4.8 vs 16.1 (high accuracy), 3.4 vs 52.8 (low), 2.2 vs 51.9 (mid). Sparse subset (76 problems): QPALM 3.2 vs OSQP 9.5 (default), 4.3 vs 17.4, 3.1 vs 30.0, 1.8 vs 56.0. Success rate at default settings 55.8% vs 43.5% for OSQP.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6500U @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs), run by a third party (qpsolvers maintainer)
tradeoffs: Proximal augmented-Lagrangian QP solver that also handles nonconvex QPs; C core with C++, Python, Julia, Matlab and Fortran interfaces; LGPL copyleft.
caveats: Category fit is loose: QP optimization solver, not a linear-system solver; OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list. Result is from prebuilt Python wheels (qpalm 1.2.3, osqp 0.6.7.post0), so no compiler or flags; known limitation of the suite includes CPU thermal throttling. QPALM is itself about 2-5x slower than PIQP in the same table. The QPALM repo page opened only gave paper references, no numbers of its own. Failed solves are counted at the 1000 s time limit.

name: SPC5 (block-based SpMV kernels for AVX-512 and ARM SVE)
baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV (sequential column of the results CSV)
workload: Sequential SpMV y=Ax over 23 SuiteSparse matrices in double and float on AVX-512, SPC5 kernels 1rVc/2rVc/4rVc/8rVc compared with MKL CSR, in GFlop/s.
claimed_speedup: From results/results-avx-2.csv, taking the best of the four SPC5 sequential kernels per matrix against the MKL column (derived from page data): median 1.23x in double and 1.49x in float, geometric mean 1.18x and 1.45x, SPC5 ahead on 16 of 23 matrices in double and 17 of 23 in float, up to 1.90x (double) and 3.00x (float), but slower on others (worst 0.45x double, 0.41x float).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.2.0 with MKL 2022.0.2 (from jobs-plafrim.sh); CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE -DUSE_AVX512=ON -DCPU=CNL; OpenMP with OMP_PROC_BIND=true
hardware: PlaFRIM 'bora' Intel Cascade Lake nodes (SLURM constraint bora&intel&cascadelake, 36 CPUs per task); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a conversion from CSR to SPC5's block formats; AVX-512 or ARM SVE only (SVE emulated on x86 through FARM); C++17; compact code meant to be copied (spc5.hpp).
caveats: The best kernel is picked per matrix after the fact, which flatters SPC5; the CSV has an MKL column only for sequential runs (parallel SPC5 columns have no MKL counterpart). Conversion cost is not examined in the numbers I read. Results are a 2023 re-run, not the numbers of the 2018 PeerJ CS paper (paper page could not be opened, peerj.com is blocked here). CPU class only, no model.

name: apxchol (parallel approximate-Cholesky PCG for Laplacian and SDDM systems)
baseline: hypre BoomerAMG (CPU and GPU builds); AMGCL, RCHOL and ParAC are also in the comparison
workload: Setup plus solve time to 1e-8 true residual of the original system on 27 matrices (grids, interior-point matrices, SuiteSparse/SNAP graphs), one right-hand side, 72 threads on a GH200 node, median-total repetition after a warmup.
claimed_speedup: Derived from benchmarks/daint/results.csv (total time, CPU apxchol 'bg+tree' vs competitor): geometric-mean 5.7x faster than CPU BoomerAMG (median 4.6x, min 1.6x, max 123x, faster on all 26 matrices where both finished); 2.4x geometric mean vs CPU AMGCL (median 1.2x, faster on 21 of 27, slower on 6); 33x vs ParAC; GPU apxchol vs GPU BoomerAMG only 1.04x geometric mean (faster on 14 of 26).

AMGCL is faster on 6 of 27 matrices and GPU apxchol is at parity with GPU BoomerAMG. BSD-4-Clause has the advertising clause; check OSI status before relying on 'copyable'. name: CKTSO (parallel sparse direct solver for circuit simulation)
language: C (prebuilt shared libraries with a C header; source not published)
baseline: KLU from SuiteSparse (sequential, approximate minimum degree ordering); README also names NICSLU, Intel MKL PARDISO and two GPU-based sparse solvers
workload: LU factorization and solve of 66 circuit matrices from the SuiteSparse collection (dimensions 1K to 5M).
claimed_speedup: README: on average more than 3X faster than KLU when sequential and more than 25X faster with 16 threads; on average faster than KLU, NICSLU, Intel MKL PARDISO and two GPU solvers for circuit matrices (detailed tables are in doc/results.pdf, not opened).
tradeoffs: x86-64 binaries only (CentOS 6/7, Rocky 8, Windows 7 x64); needs a license key file (license/cktso.lic) next to the library; specialised for SPICE-style circuit matrices; races 10 reordering methods, so analysis is slow by design.
caveats: Repository ships compiled libraries, a header, demos and docs, not source, and the licence is a key file whose terms were not visible, so it is not OSI-open and cannot be audited. name: CKTSO-GPU

claimed_speedup: Re-factorization: CKTSO-GPU is 28.80X (arithmetic mean) / 13.29X (geometric mean) faster than KLU and 12.01X / 6.11X faster than CKTSO (1 thread). Solving: 2.41X / 1.72X faster than KLU and 1.98X / 1.46X faster than CKTSO (1 thread). Per-matrix times appear only as bar charts.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.5 and nvcc 11.0 on CentOS 7.9.2009 x64 (optimization flags not stated); 32-bit integer interface
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6130 (16 cores, 2.1 GHz), NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 (24 GB), 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Closed-source: the repo ships only prebuilt x86-64 libraries (libcktsogpu.so, cktsogpu.dll, plus _l 64-bit-integer variants), a header, and demo sources; it also needs the CKTSO library and its cktso.lic from the sibling repo. NVIDIA/CUDA only. Per its own user guide it only helps slightly-dense circuit matrices (recommended when flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50) and cannot efficiently accelerate highly sparse circuit matrices; plain multicore CKTSO is best for those. One right-hand side per solve call. Pivoting factorization still runs on the CPU; only re-factorization and solve run on the GPU.
caveats: First-party results.pdf (version 20221207) only; no benchmark code is public and the solver source is not available, so this cannot be rerun. The GPU is compared only with CKTSO on ONE thread and with sequential KLU, not with multithreaded CKTSO, NICSLU, cuSOLVER or GLU, so the speedup is partly a GPU-vs-one-core comparison. The 29 matrices were selected for high Flops/NZ(L+U) (> 50), which favours the GPU. KLU is given CKTSO's ordering. Whether host-device transfers are included in the GPU times is not stated. A readme in the repo's disabledL1cache folder says some GPUs (V100 named) give wrong results unless L1 cache is disabled, at about 20% performance loss. No license text in the repo (reference only). Repo last updated 2023-04-01. Dates of last commit were read from the GitHub commits page.

The same repo also offers SupernodalLDLT (README and doc/SupernodalLDLT.md claim about 2x faster factorization than its own LU on symmetric 3D Laplacians and 6.5x vs Eigen::SimplicialLDLT at n=64000, though SimplicialLDLT wins on analyze time) and SupernodalLU/LeftRightLU, which the docs say are typically 2-3x slower and denser than Eigen::SparseLU on general matrices (but more robust on some matrices Eigen::SparseLU fails on) and about 1.5-1.8x behind MKL PARDISO.

Eigen::SparseQR is a weak baseline (the docs say it never permutes rows, so it has huge fill and wrong rank on badly scaled matrices); there is no comparison against SuiteSparseQR (SPQR), the real incumbent for sparse QR. Matrices where Eigen timed out are excluded from the 59x median. The LU solvers are slower than Eigen::SparseLU on general matrices, so the speedup claim applies to QR and symmetric LDLT only.

language: C (C API header with extern "C", closed-source prebuilt library)
baseline: Intel MKL PARDISO
workload: Parallel sparse LU solve (preprocessing, numerical factorization, forward-backward substitution) of 37 SuiteSparse Matrix Collection matrices with dimensions 525,825 to 5,558,326, wall time with 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: One-time solve: 1.70X faster than Intel MKL PARDISO on geometric mean in total time (preprocessing + factorization + solve); 2.36X faster in numerical factorization, 1.48X faster in preprocessing, but forward-backward substitution 18% slower. Repeated solve with identical sparsity pattern: 2.90X faster in numerical factorization, 2.53X faster in factorization + solve total, forward-backward substitution 20% slower. Also claims an order of magnitude higher accuracy (residual) on geometric mean.
compiler_and_flags: Test code compiled with gcc 13.3.0 (flags not stated); HYLU library compiled with gcc 8.5.0 on Rocky Linux 8.10 (flags not stated); MKL 2025.3; HYLU version 20260331
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6130 @ 2.1GHz, 256GB memory, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, 16 threads
tradeoffs: Closed source: the repo ships one C header (include/) plus prebuilt x64 libraries (centos7_x64_mkl, centos7_x64_openblas, win7_x64_mkl, win7_x64_openblas) and a demo; no solver source. Needs an x64 CPU with AVX2 and FMA; Windows or Linux only (README names Windows 7/10/11 and CentOS 7/8, other mainstream Linux said to work). Supports unsymmetric, symmetric indefinite and symmetric positive-definite matrices, real and complex, 32-bit and 64-bit index APIs. Forward-backward substitution is slower than MKL PARDISO (18-20% on geometric mean), so the win comes from preprocessing and factorization.
caveats: First-party evidence only: README and doc/results.pdf by the author, plus the author's arXiv preprint 2509.07690 (not opened; arXiv is unreachable from this environment). Benchmark code is not public (only demo/ is in the repo), and compiler flags are not stated, so this cannot be Tier A. No license file or license statement was found in the repo listing or README, and only binaries are provided, so the code cannot be copied or reimplemented from source; usability is reference and has_code is false (no source). Baseline is Intel MKL PARDISO, not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc, so there is no direct comparison against the category baselines. The matrix set is limited to 37 large SuiteSparse matrices (n >= 525,825), and the results.pdf was produced with HYLU version 20260331 while the README's latest version is 20260930. Repo history runs from 2025-09-12 (initial release) to 2026-09-30. The README quotes 1.70X (total, one-time) and 2.53X (repeated, factorization + solve); results.pdf additionally gives the 2.36X and 2.90X numerical-factorization figures. A sibling project by the same author, CKTSO, is already catalogued (https://github.com/chenxm1986/cktso).

Host-device copies of the matrix each solve unless updateRHS is changed.
caveats: OGL contains no solver kernels of its own, so it is largely a Ginkgo wrapper and probably should fold into the existing Ginkgo entry as a duplicate or integration. The only performance figure found is a WebSearch snippet of the Meccanica paper (Olenik, Koch, Boutanios, Anzt, doi 10.1007/s11012-024-01806-1) saying the largest GPU-versus-CPU speedup was about 15x on one machine and speedup grows with problem size; link.springer.com is blocked here so the paper was not opened (snippet only), and the CPU baseline solver, compiler and hardware are unknown. Tier set to C because the numbers could not be checked on an opened page. License: README SPDX header is GPL-3.0-or-later and LICENSES/ also holds MIT and Unlicense texts (REUSE layout), so some files carry different terms.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/hpsim/OGL README, https://github.com/hpsim/OGL_DATA README, and WebSearch for the OGL Meccanica paper

name: ProxQP (ProxSuite)
baseline: OSQP (also compared against Gurobi, MOSEK, qpOASES, quadprog)
workload: Randomly generated dense and sparse (about 15% density) convex QPs and the hard Maros-Meszaros problems, shifted geometric mean of solve time at high accuracy (eps 1e-9) and low accuracy (1e-3).
claimed_speedup: First-party proxqp_benchmark, shifted geometric means with PROXQP = 1.0, high accuracy: dense random QPs OSQP 18.2, qpOASES 282.6, quadprog 20.4; sparse (~15%) random QPs OSQP 3.5, qpOASES 260.6, quadprog 19.3; Maros-Meszaros OSQP 14.2, qpOASES 4.5, Gurobi 114.2 (low accuracy 1e-3: OSQP 108.5, qpOASES 17.1).
hardware: 11th Gen Intel Core i7-11850H @ 2.50GHz
stars_or_usage: 594 stars; vcpkg port proxsuite; PyPI proxsuite
tradeoffs: Dense and sparse backends, Eigen-based, vectorized and allocation-free updates, Python bindings; targets robotics (MPC) use. Convex QPs.
caveats: First-party benchmark (tier C): the proxqp_benchmark scripts are public and the CPU is named, but no compiler, flags or solver versions are given. The benchmark covers the dense ProxQP backend only. The independent qpbenchmark (Maros-Meszaros, i7-6500U) is mixed: runtime shifted geometric mean 53.3 for ProxQP vs 12.7 for OSQP at default settings (ProxQP slower), but 5.9 vs 16.1 at high accuracy, 36.0 vs 52.8 at low and 19.2 vs 51.9 at mid (ProxQP faster); ProxQP success rate 73.2% vs OSQP 43.5% at default. Category fit is loose (QP optimization, not linear-system solving) and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list.
