name: RA-SpMM (regime-aware GPU SpMM router for GNN workloads)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpMM (FP32, cusparseSpMM)
workload: Sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) with CSR sparse matrix and feature width N in {64,128,256,512} over 51 graphs (26 real, 25 synthetic) = 192 configurations on an RTX 3090; a seven-rule decision tree dispatches each call to one of five CSR or tensor-core tile kernels; warm protocol is 50 warmup + 200 timed CUDA-event iterations on both sides.
claimed_speedup: 1.702x warm geomean speedup over FP32 cuSPARSE (oracle 1.706x, 173/192 oracle hits); precision-matched speedup 1.222x; cold first-call 2.269x; GNN training step vs cuSPARSE backend 1.37x/1.26x/1.26x warm geomean (GCN/SAGE/GIN), up to 3.24x on Reddit; RTX 4090 transfer 1.515x warm.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 with -arch=sm_86 (setup.py, RA_SM_ARCH env var), CUDA 11.8 and matching PyTorch; CUDA 12.1 for the RTX 4090 sweep
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (primary) and RTX 4090 (cross-architecture); host CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA GPU only with PyTorch bindings; tile kernels need a one-time format build (1 ms to 36 ms geomean, worst 1.5 s per RESULTS.md) and tensor-core FP16/TF32 paths, so results are not bit-identical to FP32 cuSPARSE; a cuSPARSE guardrail covers inputs no specialist improves.
caveats: Paper is under review at Future Generation Computer Systems (README), so not peer reviewed yet: tier C although code, flags, per-table CSVs (CC-BY-4.0) and a reproduce script are public; host CPU model is missing. The headline 1.702x compares FP16/TF32 tensor-core kernels against FP32 cuSPARSE; precision-matched speedup is 1.222x (RESULTS.md: 1.053x on the RTX 4090). RESULTS.md also reports frozen-router validation on 9 unseen graphs at only 1.197x, FlashSparse being faster than the RA-SpMM router (1.28x geomean over 190 configs; FlashSparse faster on 134, router on 56), and a worst-case router/oracle ratio of 0.868x. Self-selected benchmark suite of GNN-style graphs; baseline cuSPARSE is not one of SuiteSparse/Eigen sparse/PETSc.
found_via: Blogs / talks: engineering-blog hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED and no blog post or talk surfaced this project; found on the github.com/topics/spmm topic page; opened repo, README, RESULTS.md, setup.py and commits page.

name: RSLAB (pure-Rust sparse LDL^T, LU and KLU solver)
baseline: Intel MKL PARDISO
workload: Wall time relative to PARDISO on 28 systems exported from production codes (6 FEM curl-curl, 2 power grid, 7 MoM near field, 13 SuiteSparse circuits), 12 threads each, geometric mean per class.
claimed_speedup: Ratios to PARDISO time (below 1 is faster): solve 0.34 / 0.43 / 0.37 / 0.30 on the four classes (about 2.3x to 3.3x faster, derived from page data); factor 1.35 / 3.97 / 0.95 / 4.76 and refactor 1.38 / 4.28 / 0.90 / 1.83 (faster only on MoM near field); one-shot analysis+factor+solve 1.05 / 1.06 / 0.74 / 1.12 (faster only on MoM near field).
hardware: 12 threads; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: No BLAS, LAPACK or MKL needed; factor is bit-identical for every thread count; Python bindings (pip install rslab); built-in Krylov solvers use the factor as preconditioner; Threads::Auto is capped at 4 workers by default.
caveats: Mixed result: the win is the solve phase; factorization and one-shot time are slower than PARDISO on three of four classes. The corpus is exported from production codes and the benchmark scripts take a corpus path, so the table cannot be reproduced from the README alone. CPU model, Rust version and flags are not given. MKL PARDISO is a proprietary baseline. The project started from the feral crate (MIT) and its commit history is very recent.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/sparse-linear-solver listing led to milanofthe/rslab; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: sparse_dot_topn
baseline: SciPy sparse CSR matrix multiplication (scipy.sparse A.dot(B), SciPy 1.12.0)
workload: Sparse matrix product A.dot(B) of two TF-IDF CSR matrices of shape (20,000 x 193,190) by (193,190 x 20,000) built from SEC EDGAR company names, with and without keeping only the top-n values per row; 30 repeats.
claimed_speedup: Apple M2 Pro, 8 threads: plain sp_matmul 5.1x faster than SciPy (0.032 s vs 0.165 s min time); sp_matmul_topn with top_n=10 and 8 threads 6.9x faster (0.024 s). Intel i9 2.3 GHz 8-core, 8 threads: sp_matmul 3.4x. Single-thread plain product about 1.0x on M2 Pro.
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M2 Pro (32GB RAM); MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 (16GB RAM)
tradeoffs: Python package with a C++17 extension (OpenMP vendored); uses a max-heap to keep memory low when only the top-n entries per row are needed. Result type and API differ from plain SciPy products. Not a general SpGEMM replacement.
caveats: First-party benchmark (tier C): bench code is public and hardware is named but compiler and flags are not. SciPy's sparse matmul is single-threaded, so almost all of the speedup comes from multithreading; single-thread plain product is about 1.0x. The top-n variant is slower than SciPy for large n (for example 6.2x slower at top_n=1000 on one thread on the M2 Pro). SciPy CSR matmul is not SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc, so baseline_in_list is false and the category fit is partial.
found_via: PyPI JSON scan of sparse-related package descriptions (https://pypi.org/pypi/sparse-dot-topn/json): line 'up to 6 times faster'

name: SparseX (CSX-format SpMV library with LLVM runtime code generation)
baseline: Intel MKL inspector-executor SpMV (and CSR SpMV)
workload: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on multicore CPUs; the Compressed Sparse eXtended (CSX) format stores dense substructures compactly to cut memory bandwidth and emits specialised kernels per matrix.
claimed_speedup: For HPC matrices, up to 19.5x over the MKL inspector-executor SpMV kernel (1.6x on average) (snippet only).
tradeoffs: Needs LLVM/Clang >= 4.0, Boost >= 1.48 (regex, serialization, system), numactl and gcc >= 4.8 (README); autotools build; format conversion and tuning step before the first multiply, so it pays off only for repeated SpMV (iterative solvers).
caveats: Numbers come from a WebSearch result snippet only; the paper/page itself was not opened (arxiv, ACM, IEEE and researchgate hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED in this environment), so tier is capped at C. The snippet came from a WebSearch summary of SparseX-related papers and its attribution to the SparseX TOMS paper was not verified. A different snippet (a 2025 third-party paper on index/value compression for SpMV) says SparseX is mainly able to reliably speed up SpMV for large matrices, median speedup 13 percent and geometric mean 7.7 percent; the baseline of that figure was not visible. The repo README itself carries no benchmark numbers and cites the TOMS, TPDS, IPDPS'13 and PPoPP'11 papers. Last commit 2018, so MKL has had many releases since.
found_via: Blogs / talks: engineering-blog hosts are EGRESS_BLOCKED and no blog post or talk surfaced this project; found via WebSearch query 'SparseX CSX SpMV library faster than Intel MKL multicore speedup CSR' after the repo appeared on github.com/topics/spmv; opened repo, README and commits page.

name: SPbLA (sparse Boolean linear algebra on GPU; cuBool and clBool backends)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (CPU) plus CUSP, cuSPARSE and clSPARSE (GPU)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix multiplication M x M and element-wise addition M + M^2 on 10 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graph matrices (e.g. amazon-2008, web-Google, roadNet-CA, netherlands_osm); time in ms and memory in MB; GTX 1070 GPU versus i7-6700 CPU.
claimed_speedup: Paper: Boolean-specialized operations 'can be up to 5 times faster and consume up to 4 times less memory' than generic non-Boolean operations from CUSP or cuSPARSE. From Table II (M x M, derived from page data): cuBool 1.9 ms vs SuiteSparse 7.9 ms on matrix 0, 23.2 vs 257.6 ms on matrix 2, 33.3 vs 369.5 ms on matrix 3, 41.8 vs 673.3 ms on matrix 4 (about 4x to 16x); cuSPARSE took 4761.3 ms on matrix 4. Not uniformly faster: cuSPARSE is faster on matrix 1 (1.7 vs 2.4 ms) and CUSP/cuSPARSE are often as fast or faster for M + M^2 (Table III), where cuBool's advantage is lower memory.
hardware: Ubuntu 20.04, Intel Core i7-6700 3.40GHz, 64 GB DDR4, GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB
tradeoffs: Boolean (structure-only) matrices only; CUDA (cuBool) and OpenCL (clBool) backends plus a CPU fallback, Python bindings. Much lower peak GPU memory than the generic libraries in the paper's tables. The GPU baselines treat nonzero floats as true, so they do more work per element than a Boolean kernel.
caveats: Paper PDF text does not state its venue (it sits in a 2021/GRAPL folder of the YaccConstructor/articles repo), so peer review is unconfirmed and the tier stays C; B if the workshop venue is confirmed. The baseline comparison is GPU versus a CPU library and a Boolean kernel versus non-Boolean kernels, which the SpBench README itself calls 'not entirely fair'. Compiler and flags not stated. Public benchmark code exists at https://github.com/EgorOrachyov/SpBench (opened) but was not rerun.

language: Fortran (with C interface; GPU build via CUDA)
baseline: HSL_MA97, MUMPS, PARDISO (named by the task lead only; the paper's actual baselines could not be verified)

Environment variables OMP_CANCELLATION=TRUE and OMP_PROC_BIND=TRUE must be set or SSIDS fails with error flag -53. Per its docs the solve phase is performed in serial at present. Does posdef Cholesky or indefinite factorization with 1x1 and 2x2 pivots; leaf subtrees are pre-assigned to NUMA regions or GPUs.
caveats: Evidence not reachable: the SSIDS GPU paper (TOMS 2016; preprint RAL-P-2014-006 on epubs.stfc.ac.uk) and the CPU a-posteriori-pivoting report cited in the docs are on egress-blocked hosts (epubs.stfc.ac.uk, numerical.rl.ac.uk, doi.org), and my WebSearch budget was spent on other projects, so no baseline names or ratios are verified. A verifier with access to the TOMS paper could probably re-tier to B (peer reviewed, hardware described in the paper, comparison against HSL codes). The baselines named in the task lead are not in the catalog's list for this category (SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse, PETSc), so baseline_in_list is false. The ChangeLog entry of 2016-09-23 says SSIDS v2 added CPU, multi-GPU and heterogeneous execution.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/ralna/spral (README, LICENCE, ChangeLog, docs/Fortran/ssids.rst)

name: SyLVER (NLAFET)
baseline: SPRAL SSIDS / HSL MA87 / PARDISO (no comparison found in the repo)
workload: Sparse symmetric positive-definite (Cholesky) and indefinite (LDL^T) direct factorization on multicore and GPU through the StarPU runtime; no benchmark in the repo.
claimed_speedup: None. The README and doc/source pages (purpose.rst, introduction.rst) describe DAG-based algorithms that 'enable an efficient exploitation of multicore CPU architectures and GPU-accelerated systems' with no numbers.
tradeoffs: Requires StarPU 1.3+, SPRAL (submodule), MeTiS, hwloc and a sequential BLAS/LAPACK (MKL or ESSL recommended); optional CUDA. Mixed C++ and Fortran 2003 sources (test drivers are .F90). Developed for the EU H2020 NLAFET project; last commit May 2020.
caveats: No numbers in README, doc/source or drivers (drivers hold only spldlt_test.F90, spldlt_test_debug.F90, splu_test.F90). NLAFET deliverable and working-note PDFs on www.nlafet.eu (for example WN21 Duff-Hogg-Lopez on sparse Cholesky with a task-flow implementation) were returned by WebSearch but nlafet.eu is blocked here, so no paper numbers were read. SyLVER is the StarPU-based successor of SPRAL SSIDS, so SPRAL SSIDS is its natural baseline, and that is a library also listed under this category by other entries. Language label is inferred from the file listing (src/, include/sylver, Fortran drivers); the GitHub language bar was not shown.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/NLAFET/SyLVER README, doc/source, drivers directory and WebSearch for SyLVER vs SPRAL/PARDISO papers

name: TACO (Tensor Algebra Compiler)
baseline: hand-optimized sparse linear algebra and sparse tensor kernels in widely used libraries (the README does not name them; Eigen and Intel MKL are the likely comparison targets but this was not confirmed on an opened page)
workload: Generated kernels for sparse tensor algebra and sparse linear algebra expressions on CPUs and GPUs; no specific benchmark is stated on the repo page.
claimed_speedup: 'performance competitive with hand-optimized kernels in widely used libraries for both sparse tensor algebra and sparse linear algebra' (README; no numbers, and 'competitive' is not a claim of being faster)
tradeoffs: Usable as a C++ library to load tensors and compute expressions, or as a code generator that emits C functions for a given expression and format. The README links the OOPSLA 2017 paper and two technical reports (arXiv 1802.10574 on optimization, 1804.10112 on formats) for details.
caveats: Only entry in this run with no numbers; included as the single tier D because the project is notable. arxiv.org, tensor-compiler.org and the paper PDFs were blocked in this environment, so the paper speedups against named libraries could not be opened; the verifier should read the OOPSLA paper and arXiv 1802.10574 for exact baselines and ratios. The README only claims parity ('competitive'), not a win.

name: TileSpMV
baseline: cuSPARSE, CSR5 and merge-based SpMV (per the task lead; the exact baselines and ratios could not be verified)
workload: SpMV on GPUs over the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection using 16x16 sparse tiles with seven warp-level kernels (CSR, COO, ELL, HYB, dense, dense row, dense column) and per-tile format selection; paper is IPDPS 2021.
claimed_speedup: No numbers available to me. A WebSearch result summary says only that TileSpMV 'is faster than state-of-the-art SpMV methods in most matrices of the full SuiteSparse Matrix Collection'. The repo README has no performance numbers.
compiler_and_flags: From src/Makefile: nvcc, CUDA 11.1 path, -O3 -w -arch=compute_61 -code=sm_86 -gencode=arch=compute_61,code=sm_86, -Xcompiler -fopenmp -O3, MAT_VAL_TYPE=double
hardware: README: NVIDIA Tesla K40 'as tested', CUDA 11.1, Ubuntu 18.04/20.04; paper hardware not verified
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPUs only (compute capability 3.5 or newer). Matrices are first converted to a tiled format (csr2tile), and very sparse tiles are split into a separate matrix; conversion cost and the extra format memory are tradeoffs. Research code driven by a Matrix Market file (./test -d 0 matrix.mtx). Bundles the CSR5 CUDA code under src/external/CSR5_cuda.
caveats: Evidence is a peer-reviewed IPDPS 2021 paper (Niu, Lu, Dong, Jin, Liu, Tan, pp. 68-78) whose full text and abstract numbers I could not open (IEEE, ACM, Semantic Scholar and ResearchGate are egress-blocked; the single WebSearch snippet had no ratios), so I record no speedup and tier D. A verifier with paper access could likely re-tier to B. The repo's src/main.cu includes the CSR5 headers but I found no cuSPARSE or merge-SpMV comparison output in it, so the repo itself does not reproduce a comparison. Context: the DASP paper (SC'23, same lab) reports DASP beating TileSpMV by 2.09x on average in FP64 on A100 (search-result text only), so TileSpMV is no longer the lab's fastest method. Makefile arch flags are mixed (compute_61 virtual arch with sm_86 code).
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/SuperScientificSoftwareLaboratory/TileSpMV and one WebSearch query for the IPDPS'21 paper (no numbers surfaced)
